ELECTRO TECHNICAL OFFICER
MMD EXAMINATION — STUDY NOTES
ELECTRICAL SECTION — ALL TOPICS
Exam-Oriented | Mark-Wise | Memory Techniques
Based on Question Bank: 2023–2025

SECTION I — ELECTRICAL MACHINES & POWER
SYSTEMS
TOPIC 1: Semiconductor Devices (★★★★★ Most Repeated)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: What are semiconductor devices? Advantages over thermionic devices?
Describe working principle and application of: Zener Diode, Transistor, Photocell, Thyristor. (16 marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: Repeated in: Jun 2025, Oct 2025, Dec 2025, Jun 2024, Oct 2023, and 8+ more
papers
📋 Mark Division: Definition + Advantages = 4 marks | Each device (×4) = 3 marks each = 12
marks | TOTAL = 16 marks
1.1 What is a Semiconductor?
A semiconductor is a material with electrical conductivity between a conductor and an insulator. Its
conductivity can be controlled by adding impurities (doping).
• Examples: Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge)
• N-type doping: adds extra electrons (negative carriers)
• P-type doping: creates holes (positive carriers)
• When P and N types are joined: forms a P-N Junction
1.2 Advantages Over Thermionic Devices
Semiconductor Device Thermionic Device (Vacuum Tube)
No heating required — works instantly Requires filament heating & warm-up time
Very small and lightweight Bulky and large
Low power consumption High power consumption
Long operational life, robust Fragile, shorter lifespan
Low operating voltage Requires high voltages
Low cost, mass-producible Expensive to manufacture
💡 MEMORY TIP: 4 key advantages = No Heat, Small, Low Power, Long Life — 'HSPL'
1.3 Zener Diode (3 marks)
Working Principle:
A specially doped P-N junction designed to operate in REVERSE BIAS. When reverse voltage reaches
the Zener breakdown voltage (Vz), current flows freely but the voltage remains constant — this is the
Zener effect.

Key Characteristics:
• Conducts in reverse bias at a precise voltage (Vz)
• Voltage across it stays constant even if current changes
• Acts as voltage regulator
Marine Application:
• Voltage regulator circuits in ship's AVR (Automatic Voltage Regulator)
• Overvoltage protection in control circuits
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'Zener = Zero variation in voltage' — it LOCKS the output voltage
✏️ EXAM TIP: Always draw a simple circuit showing Zener in reverse bias with load resistor
1.4 Transistor (3 marks)
Working Principle:
A three-layer semiconductor device: Emitter-Base-Collector (E-B-C). A small current at the Base
CONTROLS a large current from Collector to Emitter. Two types: NPN and PNP.
Key Characteristics:
• Acts as current amplifier: Ic = β × Ib (β = current gain, typically 50-300)
• Can also act as electronic switch (ON/OFF)
• NPN: current flows Collector → Emitter when base is positive
Marine Applications:
• Signal amplification in navigation equipment
• Switching in automation and control panels
• Oscillator circuits in radio equipment
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'Transfer + Resistor = Transistor' — Small signal IN at Base → Big signal OUT at
Collector
1.5 Photocell (3 marks)
Working Principle:
Converts light energy into electrical energy using the photoelectric effect. When light falls on the
semiconductor surface, photons release electrons, creating a current. More light intensity = more
current produced.
Types:
• Photodiode: reverse biased, current increases with light
• Phototransistor: light replaces base current, higher sensitivity
Marine Applications:
• Flame detectors in fire detection systems
• Smoke detectors — smoke blocks light path → alarm triggers
• Automatic navigation light control (dusk/dawn switching)
• Cargo hold smoke detection systems
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'Photo = Light, Cell = Generates Power' — Onboard: smoke blocks light →
alarm!
1.6 Thyristor / SCR — Silicon Controlled Rectifier (3 marks)

Working Principle:
A four-layer PNPN semiconductor device with three terminals: Anode (A), Cathode (K), and Gate (G). It
remains OFF until a trigger pulse is applied to the Gate. Once triggered, it stays ON even without the
gate signal. It turns OFF only when current drops below the holding current (Ih).
Key Characteristics:
• Works as a controlled switch — ON/OFF based on Gate pulse
• Can handle very high currents and voltages
• Once fired, gate loses control — turns off only by reducing current
Marine Applications:
• Motor speed control for cargo pumps, winches, bow thrusters
• Soft starters for large induction motors
• Power converters and variable frequency drives (VFD)
• Battery charging circuits
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'Thyristor = Light switch with a latch' — Gate = doorbell (rings once) → door
stays open until power removed
1.7 Exam Answer Structure
📋 For 16 marks: Para 1 — Define semiconductor (2 lines) | Para 2 — Table of 4 advantages |
Para 3-6 — Each device: definition, working, diagram, marine application
✏️ EXAM TIP: Always mention MARINE/SHIPBOARD application for every device —
examiners specifically look for this!

TOPIC 2: Diesel Electric Propulsion (★★★★★ Highly Repeated)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: Diesel electric propulsion is being chosen as power plant for wide variety of
vessels. (a) Sketch a simple layout. (b) Explain advantages of selecting such a plant. (16 marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: Repeated in: Jun 2025, Dec 2025, Nov 2023, Jun 2024, Jul 2019, Dec 2019 and
more
📋 Mark Division: Layout sketch = 8 marks | Advantages = 8 marks | TOTAL = 16 marks
2.1 What is Diesel Electric Propulsion?
Instead of directly coupling a diesel engine to the propeller shaft, diesel generators produce
ELECTRICAL POWER which drives electric motors connected to the propeller shaft. The propulsion
motor is powered electrically, not mechanically.
2.2 Layout of Diesel Electric Propulsion System
Main Components (draw these in your sketch):
1. Diesel Prime Movers (2-4 generators running in parallel)
2. Main Switchboard (MSB) — distributes power
3. Propulsion Transformer (if required)
4. Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) / Power Converter
5. Propulsion Motor (AC or DC)
6. Propeller Shaft + CPP or FPP
7. Ship Service Loads (lighting, pumps, HVAC etc.)
Simple Layout Description for Sketch:
[Diesel Gensets 1,2,3] → [Main Switchboard] → [Converter/VFD] → [Propulsion Motor] → [Propeller]
Also from MSB: → [Ship Service Loads]
✏️ EXAM TIP: In exam sketch: label all components clearly. Show generators in parallel to
MSB. Show VFD between MSB and motor. Show propeller at end.
2.3 Advantages of Diesel Electric Propulsion
Advantage Explanation
Flexibility of generator operation Run only the generators needed for load — saves fuel at low
speeds
Efficient fuel consumption Generators always run at optimal RPM regardless of propeller
speed
Better maneuverability Quick, precise speed and direction control via electric motor
Reduced engine room space Generators can be placed anywhere — no shaft tunnel needed
Lower maintenance Fewer running hours on each engine, wear reduced

Dynamic Positioning (DP) Essential for DP vessels — precise thrust control required
Redundancy Multiple generators — one failure doesn't stop propulsion
Quieter operation Less vibration transmitted to hull — ideal for cruise/research
ships
Azimuth thruster compatibility Easily drives pod propulsion systems (Azipods)
💡 MEMORY TIP: Remember 5 top advantages: Fuel Efficiency, Flexibility, Maneuverability,
Redundancy, DP Capability — 'FFMRD'
✏️ EXAM TIP: Mention ship types that use it: Cruise ships, DP vessels, Ferries, Icebreakers,
Research vessels — scores extra marks

TOPIC 3: Emergency Source of Electrical Power (★★★★★ Very Repeated)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: With reference to emergency source of electrical power in cargo ships: (a)
Describe a typical power source (8 marks) (b) Give list of essential services and explain how installation
can be periodically tested (8 marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: Repeated in: Jun 2025, Dec 2025, Jul 2019, Dec 2019, Mar 2021, Nov 2023,
Jun 2024 and more
📋 Mark Division: Power source description = 8 marks | Essential services + Testing = 8
marks | TOTAL = 16 marks
3.1 Emergency Source — Requirements (SOLAS)
SOLAS requires every ship to have an independent emergency source of electrical power capable of
operating essential services for a minimum period after main power failure.
Types of Emergency Power Sources:
• Emergency Generator (most common) — diesel driven
• Battery (for small vessels or as transitional source)
• Emergency Generator + Battery combination
3.2 Emergency Generator — Details
Parameter Requirement
Location Above bulkhead deck, outside machinery spaces
Starting Auto-start within 45 seconds of main power failure
Fuel Separate day tank (18 hours minimum for cargo ships)
Independence Must NOT depend on main machinery for cooling/lubrication
Testing Load tested monthly, started weekly (no-load)
Capacity Must supply all essential services simultaneously
3.3 Essential Services to be Supplied
Navigation & Communication:
• Navigation lights
• Internal communication (PA system, telephone)
• GMDSS radio equipment
• Radar (at least one)
• Navigational instruments
Safety Systems:
• Fire detection and alarm system
• Fire pumps and sprinkler pumps
• Emergency bilge pump

• Watertight door controls
• Lifeboat launching equipment
Other Essential Services:
• Emergency lighting (accommodation, escape routes, bridge, engine room)
• Steering gear (transitional supply)
• Day tank fuel transfer pumps
3.4 Periodic Testing Procedure
8. Weekly test: Start emergency generator under no load — verify auto-start
9. Monthly test: Run under load for minimum 30 minutes
10. Simulate main power failure: trip main breaker, verify auto-changeover
11. Check battery starting system and charge condition
12. Verify automatic changeover switch operation
13. Test all essential services on emergency supply
14. Record all tests in Engine Room Log Book
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'SOLAS says 45 seconds' — emergency gen must AUTO-START within 45
seconds of failure
✏️ EXAM TIP: List at least 8 essential services in exam — navigation, fire, bilge, comms,
lighting, steering, doors, lifeboat

TOPIC 4: Alternators — Parallel Operation & Voltage Regulation (★★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) Describe two methods of determining voltage regulation of 3-phase alternator
(8 marks) (b) Two alternators connected in parallel — what happens when excitation of one machine is
increased? (8 marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) True power, Apparent power and power factor (8 marks) (b) Alternator rated
750 KVA at 0.85 PF — find maximum load in kW. Is it overloaded at 620kW, 0.80 PF? (8 marks)
📋 Mark Division: Varies — typically 8+8 = 16 marks or 6+10 = 16 marks
4.1 Voltage Regulation — Definition
Voltage Regulation (VR%) = [(V_no-load - V_full-load) / V_full-load] × 100
It measures how much the terminal voltage changes from no-load to full-load conditions.
4.2 Methods of Determining Voltage Regulation
Method 1 — EMF Method (Synchronous Impedance Method):
15. Perform Open Circuit Test: measure OC voltage vs field current
16. Perform Short Circuit Test: measure SC current vs field current
17. Calculate Synchronous Impedance: Zs = Voc/Isc
18. Determine Ra (armature resistance) by DC test
19. Calculate Xs (synchronous reactance) = √(Zs² - Ra²)
20. Use phasor diagram to find no-load EMF (E0)
21. VR% = [(E0 - V) / V] × 100
Method 2 — MMF Method (Ampere-Turn Method):
22. Obtain Open Circuit Characteristic (OCC)
23. Obtain Short Circuit Characteristic (SCC)
24. Find field current for full-load current from SCC
25. Combine field currents using phasor diagram
26. Find corresponding voltage from OCC
27. Calculate VR%
EMF Method MMF Method
Simple calculation More accurate
Gives pessimistic (high) result Gives optimistic (low) result
Uses impedance triangle Uses MMF phasor diagram
4.3 Parallel Operation of Alternators
Conditions for Paralleling (MUST know all 4):

Condition Purpose
Same terminal voltage Prevent circulating currents
Same frequency Prevent hunting/instability
Same phase sequence Prevent phase-to-phase short circuit
Same phase angle (in-phase) Smooth transfer of load
Effect of Increasing Excitation of One Alternator:
• Increasing excitation → Increases reactive power (KVAR) output of that machine
• Terminal voltage of the busbar tends to RISE
• The other alternator's reactive power output DECREASES
• Active power (KW) sharing remains UNCHANGED
• Power factor of the excited machine becomes more LAGGING
• Power factor of the other machine becomes more LEADING
💡 MEMORY TIP: Excitation controls REACTIVE POWER (KVAR) and Voltage. Prime mover speed
controls ACTIVE POWER (KW).
4.4 Power Factor, True Power, Apparent Power
Definitions:
• Apparent Power (S) = V × I (measured in KVA) — total power supplied
• True/Active Power (P) = V × I × cos φ (measured in KW) — useful work done
• Reactive Power (Q) = V × I × sin φ (measured in KVAR) — power stored/released
• Power Factor (PF) = P/S = cos φ (dimensionless, 0 to 1)
Worked Example (Alternator rated 750 KVA at 0.85 PF):
Maximum KW = KVA × PF = 750 × 0.85 = 637.5 kW
At 620 kW, 0.80 PF: KVA used = 620/0.80 = 775 KVA > 750 KVA → OVERLOADED on KVA
✏️ EXAM TIP: Always check BOTH KW and KVA limits. A machine can be within KW limit
but overloaded on KVA!

TOPIC 5: Brushless Alternator (★★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: Explain with neat diagram the operation of a Brushless Alternator. What would
happen if one of the rotating diodes fails and becomes: (a) An open circuit? (b) A short circuit? (16
marks)
📋 Mark Division: Diagram + Operation = 10 marks | Open circuit failure = 3 marks | Short
circuit failure = 3 marks
5.1 Construction and Operation
Components:
28. Main Stator (output winding) — stationary, produces 3-phase output
29. Main Rotor (rotating field winding) — carries DC excitation
30. Exciter Stator (stationary AC winding) — fixed field
31. Exciter Rotor (rotating AC armature) — produces AC on the shaft
32. Rotating Rectifier (diode bridge) — mounted on shaft, converts AC to DC
33. AVR (Automatic Voltage Regulator) — senses output, controls exciter field
Working Sequence:
34. AVR senses output voltage and controls current to Exciter Stator
35. Exciter Stator creates a rotating magnetic field
36. Exciter Rotor (on shaft) cuts this field → AC voltage induced
37. Rotating Rectifier converts this AC to DC (no brushes or slip rings needed)
38. This DC feeds the Main Rotor field winding
39. Main Rotor field rotates → cuts Main Stator conductors → 3-phase AC output
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'No brushes = No sparks = Safe for hazardous areas' — no carbon dust, no
maintenance on brushes
5.2 Failure of Rotating Diode
(a) Open Circuit Failure:
• One diode stops conducting — reduces DC supply to main rotor
• Main rotor field becomes pulsating (AC ripple on DC)
• Output voltage drops and becomes unstable
• Heavy AC ripple causes overheating of rotor
• Output has large harmonic content — 3× ripple frequency visible
• AVR tries to compensate → exciter overloads
(b) Short Circuit Failure:
• Short circuit diode bypasses part of rectifier bridge
• AC current now flows in main rotor winding
• Causes severe overheating of rotor and exciter

• Output voltage fluctuates heavily — large AC component on output
• Fuse in diode circuit may blow
• Can cause complete loss of excitation if not detected quickly
✏️ EXAM TIP: For both failures: state effect on output voltage, heat generation, and AVR
response. Draw simple block diagram of brushless alternator.

TOPIC 6: Induction Motors — Principle, Slip & Star-Delta Starting (★★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) Briefly explain principle of operation of induction motors (4 marks) (b) What is
slip for an induction motor? (4 marks) (c) Draw simple ladder logic diagram of star delta starting (8
marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: With reference to three phase induction motors: (a) Explain crawling and
cogging (6 marks) (b) 4-pole motor, 50Hz — calculate synchronous speed, rotor speed at 4% slip, rotor
frequency at 600 r/min (10 marks)
📋 Mark Division: Principle = 4 | Slip = 4 | Star-delta = 8 | OR Crawling/Cogging = 6 |
Calculations = 10
6.1 Principle of Operation
40. Three-phase AC supply applied to stator windings
41. This creates a ROTATING MAGNETIC FIELD (RMF) at synchronous speed
42. RMF cuts rotor conductors → EMF induced in rotor (transformer action)
43. Rotor current flows (rotor is short-circuited)
44. Current-carrying rotor in magnetic field → Force produced (F = BIL)
45. Rotor rotates in direction of RMF — but always SLOWER than RMF (slip)
Synchronous Speed formula:
Ns = 120f / P
Where: f = frequency (Hz), P = number of poles
Example: 4-pole, 50Hz motor: Ns = 120×50/4 = 1500 RPM
6.2 Slip
Slip = (Ns - Nr) / Ns × 100%
Where: Ns = Synchronous speed, Nr = Rotor speed
• At no load: slip ≈ 0.5-2% (small)
• At full load: slip ≈ 3-8%
• At standstill (starting): slip = 100%
• Slip must be >0 for induction motor to work — rotor must lag behind RMF
Worked Example (4-pole, 50Hz):
Synchronous speed: Ns = 120×50/4 = 1500 RPM
Rotor speed at 4% slip: Nr = Ns(1-s) = 1500(1-0.04) = 1440 RPM
When Nr = 600 RPM: Slip = (1500-600)/1500 = 0.6 = 60%
Rotor frequency = slip × supply frequency = 0.6 × 50 = 30 Hz
💡 MEMORY TIP: Rotor frequency formula: fr = s × fs — at standstill fr = 50Hz, at full speed fr ≈ 2-
3Hz

6.3 Star-Delta Starting
Why needed?
Direct online (DOL) start draws 6-8 times full load current — causes voltage dip on switchboard,
mechanical shock to coupling.
Star-Delta reduces starting current to 1/3 of DOL current.
Sequence of Operation:
46. Start in STAR connection — stator voltage reduced to V/√3
47. Motor accelerates — at 70-80% of full speed
48. Timer operates — opens star contactor
49. Brief pause (overlap period)
50. DELTA contactor closes — full voltage applied
51. Motor reaches full speed in delta
Contactors Required: Main Contactor (K1), Star Contactor (K2), Delta Contactor (K3)
Interlock: K2 and K3 must be interlocked — NEVER close together (short circuit!)
Star-Delta Comparison:
Parameter Star (Starting) Delta (Running)
Voltage across winding VL/√3 = 58% of line voltage Full line voltage VL
Starting current 1/3 of DOL current Full current
Starting torque 1/3 of DOL torque Full torque
6.4 Crawling and Cogging
Crawling:
Induction motor tends to run stably at a very low speed (about 1/7 of synchronous speed) instead of
accelerating to full speed. This is caused by harmonic flux (7th harmonic) creating a dip in the torque-
speed curve at that speed.
• Caused by: harmonic components in air-gap flux
• Effect: Motor runs continuously at low speed — noisy operation
• Prevention: Skewing of rotor slots
Cogging (Magnetic Locking):
Induction motor refuses to start — rotor locks with stator teeth magnetically. Occurs when the number
of rotor slots equals or is a multiple of stator slots.
• Caused by: alignment of rotor and stator teeth causing magnetic attraction
• Effect: Motor won't start from rest — zero starting torque
• Prevention: Skewing of rotor slots, choosing correct slot combination
💡 MEMORY TIP: 'Crawling = Car stuck in first gear' | 'Cogging = Teeth locked together like gears'

TOPIC 7: Overcurrent Protection (★★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) Explain three methods of overcurrent protection for electrical circuit (8 marks)
(b) Explain with diagram the meaning of inverse current time characteristic (8 marks)
📋 Mark Division: 3 methods = 8 marks (approx 2.5 each) | Inverse time characteristic = 8
marks
7.1 Methods of Overcurrent Protection
Method 1 — Fuses:
• A thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds rating
• Types: Rewireable fuse, Cartridge fuse, HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuse
• HRC fuse: filled with quartz powder — can interrupt very high fault currents safely
• Advantage: Simple, cheap | Disadvantage: Single use, no auto-reset
Method 2 — Miniature Circuit Breaker (MCB):
• Operates on thermal (bimetallic strip) and magnetic (solenoid) principles
• Thermal element: trips on sustained overload (slow response)
• Magnetic element: trips instantly on short circuit (fast response)
• Advantage: Resettable, dual protection | Used for: final circuits
Method 3 — Moulded Case Circuit Breaker (MCCB) / Air Circuit Breaker (ACB):
• Used for high current circuits on main switchboard
• Fitted with overcurrent relay + trip coil mechanism
• Adjustable current settings
• ACB: arcing contacts quenched by arc chutes
• Used for: main feeder circuits, generator protection, motor feeders
7.2 Inverse Current Time Characteristic
Definition:
The operating time of a protective device is INVERSELY proportional to the magnitude of the
overcurrent. Higher the fault current → Faster the trip.
Three zones of the characteristic curve:
52. Normal zone: Current ≤ rated current → No trip
53. Overload zone: Small overcurrent → Slow trip (allows motor starting)
54. Short circuit zone: Very high current → Instantaneous trip
Why Inverse Time Characteristic is Important:
• Allows motor starting current (high but brief) without nuisance tripping
• Provides time-graded protection — downstream device trips before upstream
• Protects against sustained overloads without interrupting starting transients

Preferential Tripping on Shipboard:
• Non-essential loads trip first, then essential loads, main generators last
• Ensures vital services maintained during partial power loss
✏️ EXAM TIP: Draw the inverse time characteristic curve — X axis = current (multiples of
rated), Y axis = time in seconds. Show three zones: normal, overload, short circuit.

TOPIC 8: Shore Electrical Supply Connection (★★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: With reference to provision of shore electrical supply to a ship: (a) Sketch
arrangement for taking A.C. shore supply and checks prior to shore connection (8 marks) (b) Describe
methods of safely connecting arrangement to shore supply (8 marks)
📋 Mark Division: Sketch + Checks = 8 marks | Safe connection procedure = 8 marks
8.1 Shore Supply Arrangement Components
55. Shore supply cable (via shore box/pedestal)
56. Shore connection box on ship (with circuit breaker)
57. Shore supply transformer (if voltage differs)
58. Frequency converter (if frequency differs — 50Hz/60Hz)
59. Phase sequence indicator
60. Synchronizing panel / paralleling breaker
61. Main switchboard connection
8.2 Checks Before Taking Shore Connection
Electrical Checks:
62. Verify shore supply voltage matches ship's system voltage
63. Check frequency compatibility (50Hz or 60Hz)
64. Verify phase sequence matches ship (use phase sequence meter)
65. Check insulation resistance of shore cable
66. Verify shore supply is isolated/de-energized before connecting cable
Safety Checks:
67. Ensure shore cable is rated for ship's maximum load
68. Check cable for damage, proper plugs/sockets
69. Verify earth/ground connection is made FIRST
70. Check for correct polarity
71. Verify all personnel are clear of connection
8.3 Procedure for Connecting Shore Supply
72. De-energize shore supply before connecting cable
73. Connect earth wire FIRST
74. Connect shore cable to ship's shore connection box
75. Verify all checks complete
76. Energize shore supply from shore end
77. Check voltage, frequency, phase sequence on ship's panel
78. Close shore supply breaker on ship
79. Parallel shore supply with ship's generators (if needed) OR
80. Transfer load from ship's generators to shore supply
81. Shut down ship's generators after load transfer

💡 MEMORY TIP: 'Earth first, live last' — always connect/disconnect in this sequence
✏️ EXAM TIP: Mention phase sequence check specifically — a wrong phase sequence can
reverse motor rotation and damage equipment

SECTION II — CIRCUIT THEORY & ELECTRICAL
MACHINES
TOPIC 9: Transformers — Losses, Efficiency & Liquid-Cooled Hazards
(★★★★★ Most Repeated in Sec II)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) Explain potential hazards if liquid-cooled transformers are used (6 marks) (b)
What are losses in transformers? Mention factors affecting these losses. In a 25 KVA, 3300/233V, iron
loss = 350W, Cu loss = 400W. Calculate efficiency at half-full load, 0.8 PF. (10 marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: Repeated in: Feb 2025, Apr 2025, Jul 2025, Nov 2025, Dec 2025, Oct 2024 and
8+ more papers
📋 Mark Division: Hazards = 6 marks | Losses theory = 4 marks | Calculation = 6 marks |
TOTAL = 16 marks
9.1 Liquid-Cooled Transformer Hazards
The cooling liquid (transformer oil / synthetic fluid) creates these hazards:
Hazard Explanation
Fire risk Transformer oil is flammable — oil leak near hot parts can ignite
Explosion risk Overheating causes gas buildup → Buchholz relay operates but if
delayed, explosion possible
Environmental pollution Oil spill contaminates bilge water — MARPOL violation
Toxic fumes Some cooling fluids (PCBs — now banned) produce toxic gases
when heated
Electric shock Oil degradation reduces insulation → tracking and flashover risk
Slip hazard Leaking oil on deck creates slipping danger for crew
Precautions for Liquid-Cooled Transformers:
• Fitted with oil conservator and Buchholz relay for gas detection
• Bunded/drip trays to contain oil spills
• Regular oil testing (dielectric strength, acidity, moisture content)
• Fire suppression system in transformer room
9.2 Transformer Losses
Type 1 — Iron/Core Losses (Constant losses):
• Hysteresis loss: due to reversal of magnetic domains in core — depends on frequency and flux
density
• Eddy current loss: due to circulating currents in core — reduced by laminating the core

• Total iron loss is CONSTANT — independent of load
Type 2 — Copper/I²R Losses (Variable losses):
• Due to resistance of primary and secondary windings
• Increases with square of current: Pcu = I² × R
• At half load: copper loss = (1/2)² × full load Cu loss = 1/4 × full load Cu loss
Factors Affecting Losses:
Loss Type Affected By
Hysteresis loss Frequency, max flux density, core material (grain-oriented
silicon steel reduces it)
Eddy current loss Frequency², flux density², lamination thickness
Copper loss Load current², winding resistance, temperature
9.3 Efficiency Calculation — Worked Example
Given: 25 KVA, 3300/233V, Iron loss (Pi) = 350W, Full load Cu loss (Pcu_FL) = 400W, Load = half,
PF = 0.8
Step 1: Find Cu loss at half load
Cu loss at half load = (1/2)² × 400 = 0.25 × 400 = 100W
Step 2: Find output power at half load
Output = (1/2) × KVA × PF = 0.5 × 25000 × 0.8 = 10,000W = 10kW
Step 3: Find total losses
Total losses = Iron loss + Cu loss = 350 + 100 = 450W
Step 4: Find input power
Input = Output + Losses = 10,000 + 450 = 10,450W
Step 5: Calculate efficiency
η = (Output/Input) × 100 = (10,000/10,450) × 100 = 95.7%
💡 MEMORY TIP: At half load: Cu loss = (0.5)² × FL Cu loss = 0.25 × FL Cu loss. Iron loss stays the
SAME.
✏️ EXAM TIP: Always show all 5 steps clearly in exam. State formulas before substituting
values.

TOPIC 10: Circuit Breakers vs HRC Fuse & Series RLC Circuit (★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: With respect to circuit breakers: (a) Compare effectiveness of current limiting
circuit breaker with HRC fuse (6 marks) (b) A coil of 10Ω resistance and 0.15H inductance connected in
series with capacitor across 100V, 50Hz supply. Current and voltage are in phase — find current and
voltage drop across coil. (10 marks)
📋 Mark Division: CB vs Fuse comparison = 6 marks | Series RLC calculation = 10 marks
10.1 Current Limiting Circuit Breaker vs HRC Fuse
Feature Current Limiting CB HRC Fuse
Operation Mechanical trip + arc quenching Element melts and breaks
circuit
Resettable YES — can be reset after trip NO — must replace after
operation
Current limiting Limits peak fault current (fast Also limits current but slower
action)
Breaking capacity Very high (up to 100kA) Very high for HRC type
Cost Higher initial cost Lower cost, but replacements
needed
Protection type Overload + short circuit Mainly short circuit (fast types)
Indication Tripped position visible No clear visual indication of
operation
Maintenance Periodic inspection needed Simply replace when blown
10.2 Series RLC Circuit Calculation
Condition: Voltage and current are IN PHASE → Series Resonance condition
At resonance: XL = XC → Z = R (purely resistive)
Given: R = 10Ω, L = 0.15H, V = 100V, f = 50Hz
Step 1: Find XL
XL = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.15 = 47.12Ω
Step 2: At resonance XC = XL = 47.12Ω, find C
XC = 1/(2πfC) → C = 1/(2π × 50 × 47.12) = 67.5 μF
Step 3: Find circuit current (at resonance Z = R)
I = V/R = 100/10 = 10A
Step 4: Voltage drop across coil
Voltage across R: VR = IR = 10 × 10 = 100V
Voltage across L: VL = I × XL = 10 × 47.12 = 471.2V

Voltage across coil (R+jXL): Vcoil = I × √(R² + XL²) = 10 × √(100 + 2220) = 10 × 48.16 = 481.6V
✏️ EXAM TIP: At resonance: current is MAXIMUM, impedance is MINIMUM (=R), voltage
across L and C can be much larger than supply voltage — this is voltage magnification!

TOPIC 11: DC Motors — Torque, Speed Control & Shunt Motor
Calculations (★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) What design factor limits maximum torque of DC motor? (6 marks) (b) A
shunt motor runs no-load at 700 r/min, 440V supply, shunt resistance 2400Ω. Calculate additional
resistance to raise no-load speed to 1000 r/min. (10 marks)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: A 440V shunt motor takes armature current 30A at 700 rev/min. Armature
resistance 0.7Ω. Flux suddenly reduced 20%. Find: armature current momentarily, new steady speed
and current. Sketch graphs. (10 marks)
📋 Mark Division: Design factor = 6 | Calculation = 10 OR Effect description + graphs = 10
11.1 Factor Limiting Maximum Torque of DC Motor
Main limiting factor: ARMATURE CURRENT (hence COMMUTATION)
Explanation:
Torque T = K × φ × Ia (proportional to flux × armature current)
To increase torque, we increase Ia, but this is limited by:
82. Commutation limit: Excessive current causes sparking at commutator brushes → commutator
damage
83. Armature heating: I²R losses cause overheating of armature winding
84. Armature reaction: High current distorts main flux → reduced and unstable torque
85. Mechanical strength: High torque creates mechanical stress on shaft, coupling, gear
11.2 Back EMF and Speed Relationship
Back EMF: Eb = V - Ia×Ra
Speed: N ∝ Eb/φ = (V - Ia×Ra)/φ
For speed control: vary V (voltage control), φ (field/flux control), or Ra (armature resistance control)
11.3 Effect of Reducing Flux by 20%
Given: V = 440V, Ia = 30A, Ra = 0.7Ω, N1 = 700 RPM, flux reduced by 20%
Initial back EMF:
Eb1 = V - Ia×Ra = 440 - 30×0.7 = 440 - 21 = 419V
Momentarily after flux reduction (speed unchanged, so Eb unchanged):
New flux φ2 = 0.8φ1
New Eb still = 419V (speed hasn't changed yet)
New Ia = (V - Eb)/Ra = (440 - 419)/0.7 = 21/0.7 = 30A... BUT flux is less
Actually: Eb = K×φ×N, if φ reduces and N same → Eb reduces to 0.8×419 = 335.2V
Momentary Ia = (440 - 335.2)/0.7 = 104.8/0.7 = 149.7A (very high surge!)
New steady state (assuming same torque load, T = K×φ×Ia = constant):

K×φ2×Ia2 = K×φ1×Ia1 → 0.8×Ia2 = 1×30 → Ia2 = 37.5A
Eb2 = V - Ia2×Ra = 440 - 37.5×0.7 = 440 - 26.25 = 413.75V
N2/N1 = Eb2/Eb1 × φ1/φ2 = (413.75/419) × (1/0.8) = 0.9875 × 1.25 = 1234 RPM
✏️ EXAM TIP: For graph: show armature current spiking immediately then settling to new
value. Speed dips briefly then rises to new higher speed.

📌 EXAM QUESTION: Differentiate between half and full wave rectification. State where half wave
rectification may be used and purpose for which it is not well adapted. Sketch bridge connection by

📌 EXAM QUESTION: Diode half wave rectifier — 100Ω load, 100V AC rms source, diode resistance
5Ω during conduction. Calculate: (i) DC output voltage (ii) DC average load current.
📋 Mark Division: Comparison = 6 | Where used/not used = 4 | Bridge circuit sketch = 6 |
TOTAL = 16
12.1 Half Wave vs Full Wave Rectification
Feature Half Wave Full Wave Bridge
Diodes required 1 diode 4 diodes
Output waveform Pulsating DC (one half cycle) Pulsating DC (both half cycles)
DC output voltage Vdc = 0.318 × Vm Vdc = 0.637 × Vm
Ripple frequency Same as supply (50Hz) Twice supply (100Hz)
Ripple factor 1.21 (high ripple) 0.48 (lower ripple)
Efficiency 40.6% 81.2%
Transformer utilization Poor Good
Where Half Wave is Used:
• Simple, low-cost applications where ripple is acceptable
• Battery charging circuits (low current)
• Signal detection circuits
Where Half Wave is NOT Well Adapted:
• High power DC supplies — too much ripple
• Motor drives — pulsating torque
• Sensitive electronic equipment
12.2 Bridge Rectifier Calculation
Given: Load = 100Ω, Vrms = 100V, Rd = 5Ω
Step 1: Find peak voltage
Vm = Vrms × √2 = 100 × 1.414 = 141.4V
Step 2: Find DC output voltage (full wave bridge)
Vdc = (2×Vm/π) - 2×Vd_drop = 0.637×141.4 - 2×(voltage drop across 2 diodes in series)
For half wave: Vdc = Vm/π × [RL/(RL+Rd)] = 141.4/π × [100/105] = 45.0 × 0.952 = 42.84V
Step 3: Average load current

Idc = Vdc / RL = 42.84/100 = 0.428A

D1-D4, show current path for positive and negative half cycles separately.

TOPIC 13: AC Circuits — RMS, Form Factor & Parallel Alternators Load
(★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (a) Explain significance of root-mean-square value of AC waveform. Define form
factor (6 marks) (b) Total load 8000kW at 0.8 PF supplied by two alternators in parallel. One supplies
6000kW at 0.9 PF. Find KVA rating and power factor of other alternator. (10 marks)
📋 Mark Division: RMS + Form factor = 6 | Calculation = 10 | TOTAL = 16
13.1 RMS Value and Form Factor
RMS Value:
RMS (Root Mean Square) value of AC is equivalent to the DC value that produces the SAME heating
effect in a resistor.
For sinusoidal AC: Vrms = Vm/√2 = 0.707 × Vm
• This is why AC voltmeters measure RMS (e.g., 230V supply = 230V RMS)
• Importance: Used in all power calculations (P = V²/R, P = I²R)
Form Factor:
Form Factor = RMS value / Average value
For sinusoidal wave: FF = (Vm/√2) / (2Vm/π) = π/(2√2) = 1.11
• Form factor indicates the 'peakiness' of the waveform
• Higher form factor = more peaked waveform
13.2 Parallel Alternators — Load Sharing Calculation
Given: Total load = 8000kW at 0.8 PF, Alternator 1: P1 = 6000kW at 0.9 PF
Step 1: Find total KVA and KVAR
Total KVA = 8000/0.8 = 10,000 KVA
Total KVAR = 10,000 × sin(cos⁻¹0.8) = 10,000 × 0.6 = 6,000 KVAR
Step 2: Find KVA and KVAR of Alternator 1
KVA1 = 6000/0.9 = 6,667 KVA
KVAR1 = 6,667 × sin(cos⁻¹0.9) = 6,667 × 0.436 = 2,907 KVAR
Step 3: Find KW and KVAR of Alternator 2
P2 = Total P - P1 = 8000 - 6000 = 2000 kW
KVAR2 = Total KVAR - KVAR1 = 6000 - 2907 = 3093 KVAR
Step 4: Find KVA and PF of Alternator 2
KVA2 = √(P2² + KVAR2²) = √(2000² + 3093²) = √(4,000,000 + 9,566,249) = √13,566,249 = 3684 KVA
PF2 = P2/KVA2 = 2000/3684 = 0.543 (lagging)
✏️ EXAM TIP: Key: Active power (KW) adds directly. Reactive power (KVAR) adds directly.
KVA does NOT add directly — use phasor addition!

14.1 Proportional + Integral (P+I) Control
Proportional Control (P):
Output correction is proportional to the error signal. Error = Set point - Actual value.
• Advantage: Fast response to error
• Disadvantage: Leaves a permanent steady-state error (offset)
Integral Control (I):
Output correction is proportional to the integral (sum over time) of the error.
• Advantage: Eliminates steady-state error (offset)
• Disadvantage: Can cause oscillation if gain too high
P+I Combined:
Combines fast response (P) with zero steady-state error (I). Most common control mode in ship
systems.
Applications onboard:
• Boiler pressure/temperature control
• Engine speed governor
• Cargo tank level control
• HVAC temperature control
Block Diagram Components:
86. Setpoint input (+)
87. Comparator — produces error signal (setpoint - feedback)
88. P+I controller — processes error
89. Actuator — makes physical change
90. Process — the system being controlled
91. Sensor/Transducer — measures actual output
92. Feedback loop — returns measurement to comparator

Feature Series Resonance Parallel Resonance
Resonant frequency fr = 1/(2π√LC) fr ≈ 1/(2π√LC)

circuits

TOPIC 15: Electric Cable Insulation — Fire Hazards (★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: (A)(i) Discuss hazards and problems associated with electric cable insulation in
event of fire (4 marks) (ii) Suggest remedies (4 marks) (B) State how spread of fire may be reduced by
method used for installing electric cables (8 marks)
📋 Mark Division: Hazards = 4 | Remedies = 4 | Fire spread by cable installation = 8 | TOTAL
= 16
15.1 Hazards of Cable Insulation in Fire
Hazards:
• Toxic gas emission: PVC insulation releases hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas when burning —
highly toxic
• Smoke generation: Dense black smoke reduces visibility, hampers evacuation
• Fire propagation: Cables act as a 'wick' — fire travels along cable runs through bulkheads
• Loss of essential services: Fire damages control cables → loss of alarms, fire detection, comms
• Flashover: Overheated cables can cause flashover to adjacent cables
• Electric shock risk: Fire damages insulation → live conductors exposed
15.2 Remedies
• Use LSZH cables (Low Smoke Zero Halogen) — minimal toxic gas and smoke
• Fire-resistant cables for essential services (maintain circuit integrity for 90 min minimum)
• Regular insulation resistance testing (Megger testing)
• Avoid overloading cables — reduces heat generation
• Install smoke detectors near major cable runs
15.3 Reducing Fire Spread by Cable Installation Methods
Key Installation Methods:
93. Fire-stopping at bulkhead penetrations: Cables passing through bulkheads must be fitted with
approved fire-stopping materials (intumescent seals) that expand when heated to block fire
passage
94. Cable runs in separate zones: Essential service cables routed in different zones from non-
essential — limits total loss
95. Avoid cable bunching: Large bundles trap heat — space cables to allow cooling
96. Vertical cable runs protected: Fire travels upward through vertical cable drops — use fire
barriers at each deck level
97. Use of cable trays with fire barriers: Metal cable trays with fire-resistant coatings
98. Armored cables in high-risk areas: Steel Wire Armored (SWA) cables provide mechanical and
fire protection

99. Proper earthing: Prevents arcing from cable faults which could start fires
✏️ EXAM TIP: SOLAS requires: cables serving essential services must maintain circuit
integrity in fire. Specifically: fire pumps, emergency lighting, fire detection cables must be
fire-resistant type.

TOPIC 16: Insulated and Earthed Neutral Systems (★★★)
📌 EXAM QUESTION: With respect to insulated and earthed neutral systems used on board: (a)
Discuss advantages and disadvantages of both systems (8 marks) (b) What is earth fault and how do
you identify earth fault in 440V system? (4 marks) (c) Discuss consequences of earth fault in earthed
distribution system (4 marks)
📋 Mark Division: Advantages/Disadvantages = 8 | Earth fault identification = 4 |
Consequences = 4
16.1 Insulated Neutral System (IT System)
Advantages:
• First earth fault does NOT trip the supply — ship operations continue
• No dangerous touch voltage on first fault (person touching live conductor + earth not at risk as
no return path)
• Reduces risk of electrocution from single fault
• Used for 440V main power systems on ships
Disadvantages:
• Second earth fault creates a short circuit — danger
• Earth fault detection system needed (earth fault lamps)
• Sustained earth faults can stress insulation
16.2 Earthed Neutral System (TN System)
Advantages:
• Simple, well understood protection
• Earth faults immediately detected and cleared by fuses/MCBs
• Lower insulation stress on healthy conductors
Disadvantages:
• First earth fault causes immediate trip — loss of supply
• Higher risk of electric shock — fault current returns via earth
• Not preferred for ship's main power (essential services would trip)
16.3 Earth Fault Detection in 440V System
Earth Fault Lamps (most common ship method):
Three 240V lamps connected: one end to each phase, other end to earth. On healthy system: all three
lamps glow with equal (dim) brightness. On earth fault: faulted phase lamp goes DIM/OFF, other two
lamps glow BRIGHTER.
Earth Fault Relay:
Detects unbalanced current between phases and earth — triggers alarm without tripping the circuit.
16.4 Consequences of Earth Fault in Earthed System

• Immediate circuit breaker/fuse operation — loss of supply
• Dangerous touch voltages on equipment frames
• Step potential near fault location — electrocution risk
• Fire risk if fault current sustained and insufficient protection
• In 440V system: fault current can be hundreds of amperes — severe damage
✏️ EXAM TIP: Ships prefer INSULATED NEUTRAL for 440V distribution — first fault gives
alarm but does NOT interrupt supply. Essential for continuous ship operation.

17.1 Classification of Marine HV
System Voltage Range
Low Voltage (LV) AC Up to 1000V (1kV)
High Voltage (HV) AC Above 1000V (1kV) — typically 3.3kV, 6.6kV,
11kV on ships
Low Voltage DC Up to 1500V
High Voltage DC Above 1500V
Ships using HV systems: Large cruise ships, LNG carriers, drill ships, large container vessels
Benefits of HV: Reduced current for same power → smaller cables, less losses, smaller
switchgear
17.2 Insulation Testing Methods
Method 1 — Megger Test (Insulation Resistance Test):
• Apply DC test voltage (e.g., 5kV for HV equipment)
• Measure IR in MΩ — higher is better
• Minimum acceptable: 1 MΩ per kV of operating voltage
Method 2 — Polarization Index (PI) Test:
PI = Insulation Resistance at 10 minutes / Insulation Resistance at 1 minute
PI Value Condition of Insulation
Less than 1.0 Dangerous — do not energize
1.0 to 2.0 Questionable
2.0 to 4.0 Good
Above 4.0 Excellent
Why 3-Terminal Insulation Testers for HV:
• Guard terminal eliminates surface leakage current
• Only true insulation resistance measured (not surface contamination)

• Essential for accurate readings on HV equipment
✏️ EXAM TIP: PI test significance: distinguishes between DRY good insulation (PI high) and
WET/contaminated insulation (PI low, reading rises slowly). Crucial before energizing HV
equipment after maintenance.

What are Semiconductor Devices? (2 marks)
Semiconductor devices are electronic components made from semiconductor materials (silicon or
germanium) whose electrical conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators. Their
conductivity can be precisely controlled by doping with impurities (P-type and N-type) and by
applied voltage or light.
Advantages Over Thermionic (Valve) Devices (4 marks)
Thermionic Devices (Valves) Semiconductor Devices
Require heating filament — high power No heating required — operate at room
consumption temperature
Large and bulky Very small and compact
Fragile — glass envelope, vacuum Robust — solid state construction
High operating voltages (100s of volts) Low operating voltages (few volts)
Slow warm-up time Instant operation
Short lifespan — filament burns out Very long lifespan
Generate significant heat Low heat generation
Expensive Very inexpensive — mass produced
(a) Zener Diode — 3 marks
Working Principle:
A Zener diode is a specially doped P-N junction diode designed to operate in REVERSE BIAS at a
specific voltage called the Zener voltage (Vz). Normal diodes block reverse current, but a Zener
diode is designed to break down at a precise reverse voltage and maintain that voltage across its
terminals regardless of current variations.
• In forward bias: behaves like a normal diode — conducts at ~0.7V
• In reverse bias: blocks current until Zener voltage is reached
• At Zener voltage (Vz): breaks down — conducts in reverse — voltage across it remains
constant at Vz
• Current can increase greatly but voltage stays at Vz — this is the VOLTAGE REGULATION
property
Applications Onboard:

• VOLTAGE REGULATORS — maintains constant output voltage despite varying input or
load
• OVERVOLTAGE PROTECTION — protects sensitive circuits from voltage spikes
• VOLTAGE REFERENCE — provides stable reference voltage in measuring circuits
• CLIPPER CIRCUITS — clips voltage waveforms to Zener voltage level
(b) Transistor (BJT — Bipolar Junction Transistor) — 3 marks
Working Principle:
A transistor consists of three semiconductor layers: Emitter (E), Base (B) and Collector (C). In an
NPN transistor, a small base current controls a much larger collector-emitter current — this is the
AMPLIFICATION property.
• Small current into BASE controls large current from COLLECTOR to EMITTER
• Current gain (hFE or beta) = Ic / Ib — typically 50 to 500
• Three operating regions: Cutoff (off), Active (amplifying), Saturation (fully on)
• Used as SWITCH: Base current zero = transistor off (cutoff) | Base current sufficient =
transistor fully on (saturation)
• Used as AMPLIFIER: small AC signal at base produces large amplified signal at collector
Applications Onboard:
• AMPLIFIERS — in radio receivers, alarm systems, sensor signal conditioning
• SWITCHING — control relays, solenoids, alarms from small signal inputs
• OSCILLATORS — generate AC signals of specific frequency
• LOGIC CIRCUITS — in PLCs, alarm panels, control systems
• MOTOR CONTROL — in variable speed drives, soft starters
(c) Photocell (Photoelectric Device) — 3 marks
Working Principle:
A photocell (or photodiode/phototransistor) converts LIGHT ENERGY into ELECTRICAL ENERGY.
When light photons strike the semiconductor material, they knock electrons free from their bonds —
this is the PHOTOELECTRIC EFFECT — creating electron-hole pairs and generating a current.
• More light intensity = more electron-hole pairs = more current generated
• Photodiode: light creates reverse current proportional to light intensity
• Phototransistor: light acts as base current — amplifies the photocurrent
• LDR (Light Dependent Resistor): resistance DECREASES as light increases
Applications Onboard:
• FIRE DETECTION — photoelectric smoke detectors detect smoke by light scattering
• FLAME DETECTORS — UV/IR flame detectors in boiler burner management systems
• LIQUID LEVEL SENSING — optical level sensors in tanks
• NAVIGATION LIGHTS MONITORING — detect if navigation lights have failed
• CARGO MONITORING — optical sensors for cargo presence detection
• DAYLIGHT SENSORS — automatic switching of deck lighting
(d) Thyristor (SCR — Silicon Controlled Rectifier) — 4 marks

Working Principle:
A thyristor is a four-layer PNPN semiconductor device with three terminals: Anode (A), Cathode (K)
and Gate (G). It acts as a BISTABLE SWITCH — it can be triggered ON by a gate pulse and will
remain ON until the current falls below the holding current.
• FORWARD BLOCKED state: Anode positive, no gate pulse — thyristor blocks current (off)
• TRIGGERED ON: small gate pulse applied — thyristor switches on fully — conducts large
current from anode to cathode
• Once triggered ON, gate has no further control — thyristor stays on
• TURNS OFF only when anode current falls below holding current (natural or forced
commutation)
• Can handle very large currents and voltages — ideal for power control
• Half-controlled rectifier: SCRs control firing angle — varying DC output voltage
Applications Onboard:
• MOTOR SPEED CONTROL — variable voltage DC drives, soft starters
• BATTERY CHARGERS — controlled rectifier circuits for charging batteries
• AC VOLTAGE CONTROLLERS — dimmers, heater control
• SOFT STARTERS — control inrush current during motor starting using phase angle control
• STATIC CONVERTERS — convert AC to DC or control AC power
• UNINTERRUPTIBLE POWER SUPPLIES (UPS) — inverter circuits in UPS systems
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Semiconductor = conductivity between conductor and insulator — controllable by
doping and voltage
✓ Zener diode: operates in REVERSE BIAS — maintains constant voltage at Zener
voltage — used for voltage regulation
✓ Transistor: small base current controls large collector current — gain = Ic/Ib —
amplifier and switch
✓ Photocell: light creates electron-hole pairs — photoelectric effect — used in smoke
detectors, flame detectors
✓ Thyristor (SCR): 4-layer PNPN — gate pulse triggers it ON — stays ON until current
below holding current
✓ Thyristor application: motor speed control, soft starters, battery chargers
✓ All 4 devices: Zener = voltage regulator | Transistor = amplifier/switch | Photocell =
light sensor | SCR = power switch
MEMORY AID: Semiconductor Devices
Z-T-P-S: Zener (voltage regulation), Transistor (amplification/switching), Photocell (light
detection), SCR/Thyristor (power control)

2. DIESEL ELECTRIC PROPULSION SYSTEM
Asked in: 2019/JUL/Q3, 2019/OCT1/Q4, 2019/DEC/Q2, 2022/APR/Q2, 2023/NOV/Q1, 2024/JUN/Q2,
2025/JUN/Q2, 2025/DEC/Q1
EXAM QUESTION: Diesel electric propulsion is being chosen for increasingly wide variety
of vessels. a) Sketch a simple layout of such an installation (8). b) Explain the advantages
of selecting such a plant (8). — 16 marks
A) Sketch of Diesel Electric Propulsion Installation (8 marks)
Main Components:
• PRIME MOVERS — 3 to 6 diesel generator sets (medium speed engines) located anywhere
in ship — not necessarily aft
• MAIN GENERATORS — AC generators coupled to each diesel engine — generate electrical
power (typically 6.6 kV or 11 kV on large ships)
• MAIN SWITCHBOARD — distributes power from generators to all consumers including
propulsion
• PROPULSION TRANSFORMER — steps down voltage for propulsion drives if required
• VARIABLE FREQUENCY DRIVES (VFD) / POWER CONVERTERS — convert AC to
variable frequency AC or DC to control motor speed
• PROPULSION MOTORS — large electric motors (synchronous or induction) connected
directly to propeller shaft or through gearbox
• PROPELLER SHAFT AND PROPELLER — driven by propulsion motor
• CONTROL SYSTEM — integrated automation system controlling all generators, drives and
propulsion motors
Sketch Description:
Draw: Multiple diesel generator sets (3-4 shown) connected to main switchboard via bus bars. From
main switchboard, propulsion transformers feed into frequency converters/drives. Drives feed
propulsion motors. Motors connect to propeller shaft. Show service switchboard branching from
main switchboard for ship's service loads.
B) Advantages of Diesel Electric Propulsion (8 marks)
1. Flexibility of Generator Arrangement:
• Generator sets can be located ANYWHERE in the ship — not restricted to engine room aft
• Enables better ship design — more cargo space, better weight distribution, lower centre of
gravity
• Used on cruise ships, ferries, drilling ships, cable layers, ice breakers
2. Fuel Efficiency:
• Diesel generators operate at CONSTANT OPTIMAL SPEED (rpm) regardless of ship speed
• Only the NUMBER of generators running changes with load — not the speed of each
• Generators can be run at their most EFFICIENT LOAD POINT — significant fuel saving at
part load
• On conventional mechanical propulsion, engine speed must vary — less efficient at low
speeds

3. Redundancy and Reliability:
• Multiple generator sets — failure of one does not stop ship — others provide power
• REDUNDANT propulsion — on some ships two propulsion motors — one can fail and ship
still manoeuvres
• Dynamic positioning vessels REQUIRE this redundancy for safety
4. Excellent Manoeuvring:
• Electric motors provide MAXIMUM TORQUE at zero speed — ideal for manoeuvring in ports
• Speed control is smooth and precise — variable frequency drive gives infinite speed
variation
• Direction reversal is FAST — just reverse motor current — no mechanical reversing gear
needed
• No need for clutch or reversing gearbox — simpler mechanical transmission
5. Azimuth Thrusters / Pod Drives:
• Electric propulsion allows use of PODDED DRIVES (Azipods) — motor in pod below hull,
rotates 360 degrees
• Eliminates need for rudder — pod provides steering by rotation
• Dramatically improves manoeuvrability — ship can move in any direction
6. Reduced Noise and Vibration:
• Generators can be on ANTI-VIBRATION MOUNTS — vibration isolated from hull
• Electric motors run very smoothly — less vibration than direct mechanical drive
• Important for passenger comfort on cruise ships and noise-sensitive research vessels
7. Integrated Power System:
• ALL ship's power (propulsion + services) from SAME generators
• In light traffic or port — propulsion power available for cargo handling, hotel loads
• More efficient use of installed generator capacity
Disadvantages (briefly — for balance):
• Higher initial CAPITAL COST — converters, motors, cables are expensive
• Higher TRANSMISSION LOSSES — electrical conversion has losses (~5-8%)
• More complex ELECTRICAL SYSTEM — requires skilled ETO
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Diesel electric: diesel engines drive generators — generators power electric
propulsion motors
✓ Generators run at constant optimal speed — only number of running generators
changes with load
✓ Max torque at zero speed — ideal for port manoeuvring
✓ Pod drives enabled by electric propulsion — 360 degree rotation, no rudder needed
✓ Redundancy: multiple generators — one fails, ship continues
✓ Fuel efficient at PART LOAD — conventional propulsion wastes fuel at low speed

✓ Disadvantage: higher capital cost + electrical transmission losses

A) Typical Emergency Power Source — Cargo Ships (8 marks)
Location Requirements:

• Must be in a separate space from the main machinery space — fire or flooding in engine
room must not affect emergency power
• Located as high as practicable — protection from flooding
Emergency Generator:
• Self-contained diesel generator — independent of main engine room
• Capacity: sufficient to supply ALL required emergency services simultaneously
• Starting: must be capable of AUTO-START within 45 seconds of main power failure —

• Fuel: sufficient for MINIMUM 18 HOURS of operation at full emergency load
• Fuel supply: independent — not shared with main generators
• Cooling: self-contained — does not rely on main cooling systems
Emergency Battery:
• Provides power for FIRST 30 MINUTES before emergency generator starts and takes over
— or in case generator fails to start
• Batteries located in emergency switchboard room or dedicated battery room
• Automatically connected to emergency bus when main power fails — no manual intervention
• Must maintain supply for minimum 30 minutes for specified loads
Emergency Switchboard:

• Located adjacent to emergency generator — ABOVE BULKHEAD DECK
• Connected to main switchboard via emergency feeder — can receive power from main when

• Has PREFERENCE RELAY — automatically disconnects non-essential loads if emergency
generator overloaded
Transition from Main to Emergency Power:
• Main power fails — batteries immediately supply emergency loads

• Emergency generator auto-starts — reaches rated voltage and frequency
• After 45 seconds — emergency generator takes over from batteries
• Essential services restored in correct priority order

4. ALTERNATORS — POWER FACTOR, TRUE/APPARENT
POWER, PARALLEL OPERATION
Asked in: True/Apparent Power: 2018/FEB, 2018/DEC, 2019/FEB, 2025/JAN, 2025/AUG | Parallel: 2023/SEP,
2025/NOV | Reverse Power: 2021/JAN, 2022/FEB, 2024/MAR, 2024/JUL
A) True Power, Apparent Power and Power Factor (8 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Briefly explain true power, apparent power and power factor.
2025/AUG/Q4, 2025/JAN/Q4 — 8 marks
True Power (Active Power) — P:
• True power is the ACTUAL power consumed by the resistive component of a circuit and
converted into useful work (heat, mechanical work)
• Unit: WATTS (W) or Kilowatts (kW)
• Formula: P = V x I x cos(phi) — where cos(phi) is the power factor
• This is what the electricity meter measures — the power you actually pay for
• For purely resistive load: True power = Apparent power (power factor = 1)
Apparent Power — S:
• Apparent power is the TOTAL power supplied by the alternator — product of RMS voltage
and RMS current
• Unit: VOLT-AMPERES (VA) or Kilo-Volt-Amperes (kVA)
• Formula: S = V x I
• This is what the alternator must be RATED for — it must supply this total volt-amperes
• Apparent power includes both useful (true) power and reactive (wasted) power
Reactive Power — Q:
• Reactive power is exchanged between source and reactive components (inductors and
capacitors) — not consumed
• Unit: VOLT-AMPERES REACTIVE (VAR) or kVAR
• Inductive loads (motors, transformers) ABSORB reactive power — lagging power factor
• Capacitive loads SUPPLY reactive power — leading power factor
Power Factor (cos phi):
• Power factor = True Power / Apparent Power = P / S = cos(phi)
• Range: 0 to 1 — unity power factor (1.0) means all apparent power is true power
• LOW power factor: alternator must supply more current for same true power — wastes
capacity
• Typical shipboard power factor: 0.8 lagging — motors and transformers cause lagging PF
• POWER FACTOR CORRECTION: capacitors added to improve power factor — reduces
reactive current
Practical Importance for Marine Engineers:
• Alternator rated in kVA — maximum true power = kVA x power factor
• A 750 kVA alternator at 0.85 PF provides maximum 637.5 kW true power

• If PF falls to 0.70, same alternator provides only 525 kW — less useful power for same
machine size
• Poor power factor causes: higher current, more cable losses, possible alternator overheating
B) Two Alternators in Parallel — What Happens When Excitation Increased (8
marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Two alternators connected in parallel — what happens when we
increase the excitation of one machine? 2025/NOV/Q1 — 8 marks
When two alternators are running in parallel and the excitation (field current) of one alternator is
increased:
• EXCITATION controls the TERMINAL VOLTAGE and REACTIVE POWER (VAr) of the
alternator
• Increasing excitation does NOT directly change the load sharing of ACTIVE POWER (kW)
between machines — that is controlled by the prime mover (fuel/throttle)
What Happens Step by Step:
1. Increasing excitation increases the EMF of that alternator
2. With both machines connected to the same bus bars (fixed voltage), the machine with higher
excitation tries to push more current
3. The REACTIVE CURRENT (magnetising current) of the over-excited machine INCREASES
4. This machine now supplies MORE REACTIVE POWER (kVAR) to the system
5. The other machine's excitation is now relatively UNDER-EXCITED by comparison — it
absorbs reactive power
6. Result: the over-excited machine GENERATES reactive power | the under-excited machine
ABSORBS reactive power
7. Bus bar voltage may rise slightly if total excitation increased overall
In Practice:
• Over-excitation causes machine to operate at LEADING power factor — supplies reactive
power to other machine and loads
• Under-excitation causes machine to operate at LAGGING power factor — absorbs reactive
power
• To maintain correct load sharing — BOTH excitation AND throttle must be adjusted together
• Excitation too high: machine overheats due to excess current — risk of overload
C) Brushless Alternator — Operation and Rotating Diode Failure (16 marks)
Asked in: 2018/FEB-2025/AUG — very frequently asked — 16 marks
EXAM QUESTION: Explain with neat diagram operation of a brushless alternator. What
would likely happen if one rotating diode fails and becomes: a) An open circuit, b) A short
circuit. — 16 marks
Construction of Brushless Alternator:
• Main alternator — main stator (armature) and main rotor (field winding)

• Exciter — small AC generator with STATIONARY FIELD and ROTATING ARMATURE —
mounted on same shaft as main alternator
• Rotating rectifier assembly — full wave bridge rectifier using diodes — mounted on rotating
shaft
• AVR (Automatic Voltage Regulator) — controls exciter field current to maintain constant
terminal voltage
How It Works — Step by Step:
8. AVR senses terminal voltage of main alternator
9. AVR supplies DC current to EXCITER STATOR (field) — this is the only DC required from
external source
10. Exciter rotor (rotating armature) cuts exciter stator field — three-phase AC induced in exciter
rotor
11. This AC is rectified by ROTATING DIODES (mounted on shaft) — converted to DC
12. DC from rotating diodes supplied directly to MAIN ROTOR FIELD WINDING — no brushes
or slip rings needed
13. Main rotor field creates rotating magnetic field in main stator — main AC output generated
14. If terminal voltage drops — AVR increases exciter field current — more DC to main rotor —
more main output — voltage restored
Advantages of Brushless Design:
• NO BRUSHES OR SLIP RINGS — no carbon dust, no brush maintenance, no sparking
• Suitable for HAZARDOUS AREAS — no sparks from brushes
• Lower maintenance — major source of failures eliminated
• Higher reliability — no brush wear, no brush bounce
Rotating Diode Failure Effects:
a) Open Circuit Rotating Diode:
• One diode in the rotating bridge opens — that half-cycle of exciter output is lost
• DC supplied to main field becomes PULSATING (half-wave ripple instead of smooth DC)
• Main field current REDUCES — terminal voltage DROPS and becomes UNSTABLE
• Output voltage shows AC RIPPLE at exciter frequency — typically 3x shaft frequency
• AVR attempts to compensate — increases exciter field — but ripple remains
• Generator may still operate but with reduced output and unstable voltage
• Symptoms: AC ripple on DC bus, unstable output voltage, AVR hunting
b) Short Circuit Rotating Diode:
• One diode shorts — short circuit across that diode — creates path for reverse current
• Short circuit diode allows REVERSE CURRENT through the exciter winding at each half
cycle
• This OPPOSES and partially cancels the excitation current
• Net field current REDUCES significantly — terminal voltage DROPS sharply
• AVR tries to compensate by increasing exciter field — but short circuit limits effect
• The shorted diode may overheat rapidly — thermal failure of other components possible
• Severe case: voltage collapses, generator trips on undervoltage
• Symptoms: sudden voltage drop, AVR at maximum output, generator may trip

KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ True power (kW) = V x I x cos(phi) — actual useful power | Apparent power (kVA) =
V x I — total power supplied
✓ Power factor = kW / kVA = cos(phi) — always 0 to 1
✓ Increasing excitation: INCREASES reactive power (kVAR) — does NOT change kW
load sharing directly
✓ Brushless alternator: no brushes — exciter on same shaft — rotating diodes supply
main field
✓ AVR controls exciter field — senses terminal voltage — adjusts to maintain constant
voltage
✓ Open circuit diode: pulsating DC to main field — unstable voltage with AC ripple
✓ Short circuit diode: opposing current — sharp voltage drop — AVR at maximum —
possible trip
MEMORY AID: Brushless Alternator
AVR → Exciter field (stator) → Exciter armature (rotor) → Rotating diodes → Main field
(rotor) → Main output (stator)

5. REVERSE POWER PROTECTION FOR ALTERNATORS
Asked in: 2021/JAN/Q2, 2022/FEB/Q3, 2022/NOV/Q1, 2024/MAR/Q1, 2024/JUL/Q2
EXAM QUESTION: a) Explain why it is necessary to have reverse power protection for
alternators intended for parallel operation (6). b)(i) Sketch a reverse power trip (5). b)(ii)
Briefly explain the principle and how tripping is activated (5). — 16 marks
A) Why Reverse Power Protection is Necessary (6 marks)
When two or more alternators are running in parallel and the prime mover (diesel engine) of one
machine loses power or is throttled back too far, that alternator can become a SYNCHRONOUS
MOTOR — it draws power FROM the busbar instead of supplying power TO the busbar.
What Happens Without Protection:
• The alternator whose engine loses power starts to MOTOR — draws power from the
switchboard
• This OVERLOADS the remaining generators — they must now supply their own load PLUS
drive the motoring machine
• The motoring machine acts as a LOAD on the system — absorbs real power
• The diesel engine of the motoring machine is being DRAGGED — it may overspeed or be
damaged
• Risk of OVERLOAD TRIP on remaining generators — total blackout
For DC Generators Specifically:
• When a DC generator becomes motorised — it draws current from the bus
• This reverses the direction of current through the generator
• In a DC generator acting as a motor, the armature reaction and field can lead to RUNAWAY
if compound wound
• Risk of mechanical damage to engine
Why Protection is Needed:
• Prevents OVERLOADING of healthy generators
• Prevents BLACKOUT from cascade tripping
• Protects the DIESEL ENGINE from damage from being driven as a motor
• Required by SOLAS and classification society rules for parallel operation
B) Reverse Power Trip — Sketch and Principle (10 marks)
Sketch Description:
Draw: Alternator connected to busbar via circuit breaker. Current transformer (CT) in one phase
measures current. Voltage transformer (VT) measures voltage. Both CT and VT outputs fed to
REVERSE POWER RELAY (wattmetric relay). Relay output connected to trip coil of circuit breaker.
Show direction of normal current flow and reverse current flow arrows.
Principle of Operation:

• The reverse power relay is a WATTMETRIC relay — it measures the direction of REAL
POWER (watts) flow
• It uses both VOLTAGE (from VT) and CURRENT (from CT) to determine the phase
relationship
• When alternator is generating: current flows OUT from alternator to busbar — power is
POSITIVE
• When alternator is motoring: current flows IN to alternator from busbar — power is
NEGATIVE (REVERSE)
• The relay detects this phase reversal — power goes negative beyond the set threshold
How Tripping is Activated:
15. CT measures line current | VT measures line voltage — both connected to relay
16. Relay computes: P = V x I x cos(phi) — continuously
17. Normal operation: P is positive — relay is stable — no trip
18. Engine fuel reduces — alternator starts motoring — power flow reverses
19. P goes NEGATIVE — beyond set threshold (typically -3% to -8% of rated power for AC
alternators)
20. After TIME DELAY (to prevent nuisance tripping on transients) — relay energises trip coil
21. CIRCUIT BREAKER OPENS — faulty alternator disconnected from busbar
22. Alarm sounds — engineer alerted to investigate
Threshold Settings:
• AC alternators: typically 3-8% of rated kW in reverse before tripping
• DC generators: reverse current relay — trips when current reverses direction
• Time delay: typically 5-15 seconds — prevents nuisance trips during load swings
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Reverse power = alternator MOTORING — draws power from busbar instead of
supplying
✓ Cause: prime mover loses power or fuel reduced too much during parallel operation
✓ Effect without protection: overloads healthy generators, risk of total blackout
✓ Reverse power relay = wattmetric relay — measures direction of real power flow
✓ Trips when power goes negative beyond threshold (3-8% of rated power)
✓ Time delay prevents nuisance trips on normal load transients
✓ DC generators use REVERSE CURRENT RELAY — detects current direction
reversal
MEMORY AID: Reverse Power Protection
MOTOR = Motoring alternator draws power | Wattmetric relay detects negative power | Trips
circuit breaker after time delay

6. OVERCURRENT PROTECTION — 3 METHODS + INVERSE
TIME CHARACTERISTIC
Asked in: 2018/FEB, 2018/SEP, 2019/FEB, 2019/MAR, 2019/JUN, 2019/AUG, 2019/SEP, 2019/OCT1,
2019/OCT2, 2020/MAR, 2020/OCT, 2020/DEC, 2021/FEB, 2021/APR2, 2021/JUL2, 2021/OCT, 2021/DEC,
2022/JAN, 2022/JUN, 2024/SEP, 2025/JAN, 2025/AUG, 2025/OCT — VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED
EXAM QUESTION: a) Explain three methods of overcurrent protection for electrical circuit
(8). b) Explain with aid of diagram the meaning of the term inverse current time
characteristic (8). — 16 marks
A) Three Methods of Overcurrent Protection (8 marks)
Method 1 — FUSE:
• A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point metal (usually tin-lead alloy) enclosed in a cartridge
• When current EXCEEDS the fuse rating, the wire HEATS UP and MELTS — breaking the
circuit
• HRC (High Rupturing Capacity) fuses have sand-filled cartridge — arc quenched by sand
when fuse blows
• Advantage: simple, cheap, reliable, self-resetting not required — clear indication of operation
• Disadvantage: SINGLE USE — must be replaced after operation | Cannot be tested without
replacing | Risk of single-phasing if only one fuse blows in 3-phase circuit
• Used for: feeder protection, motor branch circuits, transformer primary protection
Method 2 — MINIATURE CIRCUIT BREAKER (MCB) / MOULDED CASE CIRCUIT
BREAKER (MCCB):
• An automatic switch that TRIPS when current exceeds set value — can be RESET manually
after fault is cleared
• THERMAL ELEMENT: bimetallic strip heats and bends with overload current — trips after
time delay proportional to overload (inverse time characteristic)
• MAGNETIC ELEMENT: electromagnet provides INSTANTANEOUS trip on heavy fault
current (short circuit)
• Advantage: resettable — no replacement needed | Adjustable trip setting | Can be used as
isolator | Tests possible
• Disadvantage: more expensive than fuse | May not be as fast as HRC fuse on heavy fault
• Used for: distribution boards, motor starters, final circuits
Method 3 — OVERCURRENT RELAY with CIRCUIT BREAKER:
• Current Transformer (CT) measures line current — provides scaled replica to overcurrent
relay
• Overcurrent relay continuously monitors current level
• When current exceeds set value — relay energises after time delay — sends trip signal to
circuit breaker
• Circuit breaker opens — isolates fault
• Advantage: VERY ACCURATE and ADJUSTABLE settings | Selectivity — can be
coordinated with other protection | Can trip very large currents safely | Remote indication
and recording
• Disadvantage: more complex and expensive | Requires CT and CB coordination
• Used for: main switchboard feeders, large motor circuits, alternator protection

B) Inverse Current Time Characteristic (8 marks)
Definition:
The inverse time characteristic is a protection characteristic where the TIME TAKEN TO TRIP is
INVERSELY PROPORTIONAL to the MAGNITUDE OF THE OVERCURRENT — that is, the
greater the overcurrent, the faster the relay trips.
The Characteristic Curve:
Sketch description: Draw axes — X axis = Current (as multiple of rated current, e.g. 1x to 10x), Y
axis = Time to trip (seconds, from 0.1 to 100 on log scale). Draw a curve that starts at top left (just
above rated current = slow trip, e.g. 100 seconds at 1.2x) and falls steeply towards bottom right
(heavy fault current = very fast trip, e.g. 0.1 seconds at 10x). Show the current setting (pickup point)
where relay starts to respond.
Why This Characteristic is Important:
• SMALL OVERLOADS (e.g. motor starting): allowed to persist for longer — motor may be
starting legitimately — tripping immediately would be nuisance
• MODERATE OVERLOADS: trip after intermediate time — time for operator to investigate
and shed load
• HEAVY FAULT CURRENT (short circuit): INSTANT trip — protects equipment from severe
damage
• This characteristic mirrors how equipment tolerates overcurrent — equipment can handle
small overloads for longer than severe faults

• Multiple relays in series can be coordinated — downstream relay trips faster than upstream

• This ISOLATES only the faulted section — healthy sections continue to operate
• Called GRADED PROTECTION or DISCRIMINATION

✓ This mirrors equipment thermal withstand — equipment can handle small overloads

7. PREFERENTIAL TRIPPING IN MARINE ELECTRICAL
DISTRIBUTION
Asked in: 2024/FEB/Q3, 2024/OCT/Q3 — 10+6 marks (16 total)
EXAM QUESTION: With reference to preferential tripping in a marine electrical distribution
system: a) With the aid of a sketch, describe a typical arrangement to provide three stages
of tripping giving instantaneous protection against short circuit (10). b) State why this
protection is required (6). — 16 marks
A) Three Stage Preferential Tripping Arrangement (10 marks)
What is Preferential Tripping:
Preferential tripping is a system where non-essential loads are automatically disconnected in a
predetermined order (preference) when the ship's generators are OVERLOADED — to protect
essential services and prevent total blackout.
Three Stages of Protection:
Stage 1 — Instantaneous Short Circuit Protection:
• Provided by INSTANTANEOUS OVERCURRENT RELAYS or magnetic trip on circuit
breakers
• Operates in MILLISECONDS — instantaneous response to short circuit fault
• Directly trips the faulted circuit breaker
• Does NOT wait for time delay — clears fault immediately to prevent damage to switchboard,
cables and equipment
• Set at high current (typically 8-12 times rated current) to discriminate from motor starting
currents
Stage 2 — First Preferential Trip (Non-Essential Loads):
• When generator overloads beyond first threshold — typically 10-15% above rated load
• FIRST PREFERENTIAL TRIP RELAY operates after SHORT TIME DELAY (e.g. 10-15
seconds)
• Automatically disconnects NON-ESSENTIAL LOADS in first priority group
• Examples: air conditioning, galley equipment, workshop machinery, entertainment systems,
cargo fans (non-critical)
• Load immediately reduced — generator overload relieved
• Alarm sounds — engineer alerted
Stage 3 — Second Preferential Trip (Semi-Essential Loads):
• If overload continues despite Stage 2 (or overload is greater) — second threshold reached
• SECOND PREFERENTIAL TRIP RELAY operates after LONGER TIME DELAY (e.g. 20-30
seconds from overload onset)
• Automatically disconnects SEMI-ESSENTIAL LOADS
• Examples: non-critical pumps, deck machinery, hotel loads, second auxiliary boiler
• Further load reduction — essential services protected
Essential Services — Never Tripped:

• Navigation lights | GMDSS | Fire detection | Emergency lighting | Steering gear | Bilge
pumps
• These are NEVER shed by preferential tripping — protected at all times
Sketch Description:
Draw main switchboard with generator connected. Show main bus bar. From bus bar, show three
categories of feeder circuit breakers: 1) Essential services (never tripped — bottom layer), 2) Semi-
essential (tripped by second preference relay), 3) Non-essential (tripped by first preference relay).
Show preference relays connected to overload sensing on generator. Show instantaneous short
circuit protection on each feeder breaker.
B) Why Preferential Tripping is Required (6 marks)
• PREVENTS TOTAL BLACKOUT — if generator overloads, uncontrolled tripping would
cause complete power failure — more dangerous than controlled load shedding
• MAINTAINS ESSENTIAL SERVICES — navigation, safety, fire protection never
compromised even during overload
• PROTECTS GENERATOR — sustained overload damages generator windings —
preferential tripping prevents this
• AUTOMATIC RESPONSE — faster than manual intervention — engineer cannot react
quickly enough to prevent damage
• DISCRIMINATING PROTECTION — only non-essential loads shed — ship continues to
operate safely
• REQUIRED BY SOLAS AND CLASS — mandatory for all merchant ships — part of
electrical installation requirements
• PREVENTS CASCADE FAILURE — without preference tripping, generator trip causes
blackout, emergency generator overloads, emergency generator trips — catastrophic
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Preferential tripping = automatic load shedding when generator overloads —
prevents blackout
✓ Stage 1: Instantaneous short circuit protection — milliseconds — clears faults
✓ Stage 2: First preference — non-essential loads tripped after 10-15 seconds overload
✓ Stage 3: Second preference — semi-essential loads tripped after 20-30 seconds
✓ Essential services (nav lights, fire, GMDSS) — NEVER tripped
✓ Purpose: prevent blackout, protect generator, maintain essential services
✓ Mandatory under SOLAS and classification society rules
MEMORY AID: Preferential Tripping
I-F-S-E: Instantaneous (short circuit), First preference (non-essential), Second preference
(semi-essential), Essential (never tripped)

B) Earth Fault and How to Identify in 440V System (4 marks)
What is an Earth Fault:
An earth fault occurs when a live conductor comes into contact with the metallic structure of the ship
(earth) due to insulation failure, damage, or moisture ingress. Current flows from the live conductor
through the fault path to earth.
How to Identify Earth Fault in 440V Insulated Neutral System:
• EARTH LAMPS: Three lamps connected from each phase to earth. Normally all three glow
at equal brightness. When earth fault occurs on one phase — that lamp DIMS or goes OUT
— the other two lamps become BRIGHTER
• INSULATION MONITORING DEVICE (IMD): Continuously monitors insulation resistance of
each phase to earth. Gives ALARM when resistance falls below set threshold (typically 50
kOhm). Digital display shows which phase has reduced insulation

• SYSTEMATIC TRACING: Trip feeders one at a time and observe earth lamps/IMD. When
the faulty feeder is isolated, earth lamps return to normal brightness — fault located to that
circuit
• MEGOHMMETER TEST: With circuit isolated, use megohmmeter to measure insulation
resistance of each conductor to earth
C) Consequences of Earth Fault in EARTHED Neutral System (4 marks)
• IMMEDIATE CIRCUIT DISCONNECTION — earth fault creates a short circuit (fault current
flows through earth path) — overcurrent protection trips the circuit breaker or blows fuse
immediately
• LOSS OF SUPPLY — the faulted circuit loses power — if this is an essential service circuit,
immediate loss of that service
• HIGH FAULT CURRENT — earth fault current can be very large — causes heat damage to
conductors, insulation, switchgear at fault point
• FIRE RISK — if fault current flows for any time before protection operates, heating may
ignite surrounding insulation or materials
• SHOCK RISK at fault location — before protection operates, fault point is at earth potential
but touch voltage risk exists
• Earthed system advantage: fault CLEARED quickly — less time for damage to accumulate

✓ Systematic tracing: trip feeders one by one, watch earth lamps return to normal
✓ Earthed neutral fault consequence: immediate trip, high fault current, fire risk at fault

✓ Two simultaneous earth faults in IT system = short circuit — very dangerous

EXAM QUESTION: Discuss criteria of classification of marine high voltage for AC and DC

Under IEC 60092 and classification society rules, voltages are classified as:
Classification AC Voltage DC Voltage
Low Voltage (LV) Up to 1000V AC Up to 1500V DC
High Voltage (HV) Above 1000V AC Above 1500V DC
Medium Voltage (typical 3.3 kV, 6.6 kV, 11 kV AC Common in large propulsion
shipboard HV) systems
• Typical shipboard HV systems: 3.3 kV (older ships), 6.6 kV (common), 11 kV (large cruise
and container ships)
• HV used for: main propulsion motors, large cargo pumps, bow thrusters on large vessels
• HV reduces current for same power — smaller cable cross-sections, lower losses
B) HV Distribution System Features (4 marks)
Sketch Description:
Draw: HV generators (3.3kV or 6.6kV) connected to HV main switchboard via HV circuit breakers
(vacuum or SF6 type). From HV switchboard — HV feeders to propulsion transformers/converters
