Key Features:
• VACUUM CIRCUIT BREAKERS (VCB) — used for HV switching — arc quenched in
vacuum
• SF6 CIRCUIT BREAKERS — sulphur hexafluoride gas quenches arc — used in very high
voltage systems
• EARTHING TRANSFORMERS — provide artificial neutral for protection purposes in
insulated HV systems
• PROTECTION RELAYS — differential, overcurrent, earth fault protection for HV equipment
• INTERLOCKS — prevent unsafe switching sequences — earthing switch cannot be closed
with circuit breaker closed
• RESTRICTED ACCESS — HV switchrooms require special permission to enter — safety
critical
• BUSBAR PROTECTION — differential protection monitors all currents into and out of busbar
C) Methods of Testing HV Insulation (4 marks)

1. Megohmmeter (Insulation Resistance) Test:
• Apply DC voltage (typically 500V, 1000V or 5000V) across insulation — measure resistance
in MOhm
• Simple test — quick result — indicates general insulation condition
• Limitation: single reading affected by temperature and moisture — not reliable for trending
alone
2. Polarisation Index (PI) Test — Most Important for HV:
• Measure insulation resistance at 1 minute and at 10 minutes under same DC test voltage
• PI = R (10 min) / R (1 min)
• PI > 2.0: good insulation — dry and clean
• PI 1.0 to 2.0: questionable — requires investigation
• PI < 1.0: POOR insulation — contaminated or damaged — do not energise
3. Dielectric Absorption (DA) Test:
• Similar to PI test — uses 30 second and 60 second readings — DA ratio = R60/R30
• Good insulation: ratio above 1.25
4. Hi-Pot (High Potential) Test:
• Apply MUCH HIGHER voltage than operating voltage — tests insulation integrity
• For new equipment: typically 2 x rated voltage + 1000V
• Pass: insulation withstands test voltage — no breakdown
• Destructive if insulation is borderline — may damage ageing insulation
D) Why 3-Terminal Insulation Testers are Used for HV (4 marks)
Standard 2-terminal megohmmeter measures total insulation resistance — but this INCLUDES
surface leakage currents across the insulation surface (due to moisture, dust, contamination) — not
just through-the-insulation resistance.
• 3-TERMINAL TESTERS have a GUARD terminal — the third terminal
• Guard terminal connected to any conducting surface layer on the insulation
• Surface leakage current is DIVERTED through the guard terminal — not measured by the
meter
• Only TRUE VOLUME RESISTANCE of insulation is measured — not surface leakage
• This gives accurate reading of actual insulation quality — not affected by surface
contamination
• Particularly important for HV insulation where surface tracking and creepage are significant
concerns
• Gives RELIABLE and REPEATABLE results — allows proper trending of insulation condition
E) Significance of PI Test
• PI test reveals MOISTURE and CONTAMINATION in insulation — not just overall resistance
• Dry, clean insulation shows RISING resistance over 10 minutes — PI > 2
• Wet or contaminated insulation shows FLAT or DECLINING resistance — PI < 2

• Simple IR test can give misleadingly high reading immediately but falls — PI reveals this
trend
• PI is STANDARD REQUIREMENT before energising HV equipment after overhaul or dry-
docking
• IEEE Std 43 and IEC 60034-27 recommend PI testing for HV rotating machines
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ HV = above 1000V AC or above 1500V DC in marine classification
✓ Common shipboard HV: 3.3 kV, 6.6 kV, 11 kV
✓ HV circuit breakers: Vacuum (VCB) or SF6 type — NOT air break
✓ PI = R(10min) / R(1min) — PI > 2.0 = good | PI < 1.0 = poor
✓ 3-terminal tester: guard terminal diverts surface leakage — measures VOLUME
resistance only
✓ Hi-pot test: applies 2 x rated voltage + 1000V — tests insulation integrity
✓ Earthing switch INTERLOCK: cannot close earthing switch with CB closed — safety
critical
MEMORY AID: PI Test
PI = R10/R1 — Greater than 2 = Good | 1 to 2 = Questionable | Less than 1 = Poor — Do
not energise

10. INDUCTION MOTORS — PRINCIPLE, SLIP, STAR-DELTA,
CRAWLING & COGGING
Asked in: 2018/FEB-2025/OCT — very frequently asked across multiple papers
A) Principle of Operation of Induction Motor (4 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Briefly explain the principle of operation of induction motors.
2024/DEC, 2025/OCT — 4 marks
An induction motor operates on the principle of ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION — the same
principle as a transformer. The motor has no electrical connection between stator and rotor.
23. THREE-PHASE AC supply to stator windings creates a ROTATING MAGNETIC FIELD —
rotates at synchronous speed Ns = 120f/P (where f = frequency, P = number of poles)
24. Rotating stator field CUTS the stationary rotor conductors — EMF induced in rotor by
Faraday's law
25. Rotor conductors are short-circuited (squirrel cage) — induced EMF drives current through
rotor
26. Current-carrying rotor conductors in stator magnetic field experience FORCE (Lenz's law) —
rotor rotates in direction of stator field
27. Rotor NEVER reaches synchronous speed — if it did, no relative motion between rotor and
field — no induced EMF — no current — no force — rotor would slow down
28. Rotor always runs at SLIGHTLY LESS than synchronous speed — the difference is SLIP
B) What is Slip? (4 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: What is slip for an induction motor? 2024/DEC, 2025/OCT — 4 marks
Slip is the difference between the synchronous speed of the rotating magnetic field and the actual
speed of the rotor, expressed as a fraction or percentage of synchronous speed.
• Formula: s = (Ns - Nr) / Ns x 100%
• Ns = synchronous speed = 120f/P | Nr = actual rotor speed
• At no load: slip is very small — typically 0.1% to 0.5%
• At full load: slip is typically 3% to 8% for squirrel cage motors
• At standstill (starting): slip = 1 (100%)
• Slip increases with load — more torque required = rotor slows more relative to field = more
slip = more induced EMF = more current = more torque
• Rotor current frequency = slip x supply frequency — at full load: fr = s x f
C) Star-Delta Starter — Circuit and Operation (8 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Draw a simple ladder logic diagram of star delta starting of an
induction motor. 2025/OCT/Q1, 2024/DEC/Q2 — 8 marks
Why Star-Delta Starter is Used:
• Direct-on-line (DOL) starting draws 5-7 times full load current — causes voltage dip on
switchboard
• Star-delta reduces starting current to approximately 1/3 of DOL starting current

• Also reduces starting torque to 1/3 — suitable for low-load start applications
How Star-Delta Starter Works:
29. START button pressed — MAIN CONTACTOR (KM) and STAR CONTACTOR (KY) close
simultaneously
30. Motor stator windings connected in STAR — each winding receives REDUCED voltage
(Vline/sqrt3)
31. Motor accelerates under reduced voltage — current is 1/3 of delta DOL current
32. After preset TIME DELAY (typically 5-10 seconds) — motor has accelerated
33. STAR CONTACTOR opens — brief moment with no contactor closed — motor coasts
34. DELTA CONTACTOR (KD) closes — motor windings now connected in DELTA — full line
voltage
35. Motor runs normally in delta configuration
Interlock Between Star and Delta:
• Star and delta contactors are ELECTRICALLY INTERLOCKED — cannot close
simultaneously
• Closing both simultaneously would SHORT CIRCUIT the windings — catastrophic damage
• Mechanical interlock also provided as backup
Ladder Logic Description:
Rung 1: START button (NO) + STOP button (NC) + KM contact (sealing) → KM coil (main
contactor)
Rung 2: KM contact (NO) + KD contact (NC interlock) + Timer (not yet timed out) → KY coil (star
contactor)
Rung 3: KM contact (NO) + Timer contact (timed out) + KY contact (NC interlock) → KD coil (delta
contactor)
Rung 4: KM contact (NO) → Timer coil (starts timing when main contactor closes)
D) Crawling and Cogging (6 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Explain the phenomenon of crawling and cogging in three phase
induction motors. 2025/JUN, 2025/OCT, 2019/JUL — 6 marks
Crawling:
• CRAWLING is the tendency of a squirrel cage induction motor to run steadily at a very low
speed — approximately 1/7th of synchronous speed — instead of accelerating to full speed
• CAUSE: The stator winding produces not only fundamental (1st harmonic) rotating field but
also higher harmonic fields — particularly the 7th harmonic
• The 7th harmonic field rotates at 1/7th of synchronous speed — if the rotor speed coincides
with this harmonic field speed, the motor can get stuck at this low speed
• Result: motor runs at 1/7 Ns continuously — draws high current — overheats — does not
accelerate
• PREVENTION: Careful design of rotor slot shape — skewing of rotor slots disrupts harmonic
fields
Cogging (or Magnetic Locking):

• COGGING is the tendency of induction motor rotor to REFUSE TO START even when full
voltage is applied — or to start jerkily
• CAUSE: When number of rotor slots equals number of stator slots (or a simple
multiple/submultiple), the rotor slots align with stator slots creating regions of MINIMUM
RELUCTANCE
• At these positions, the rotor is magnetically LOCKED — reluctance torque opposes rotation
• Result: motor fails to start from certain positions, or starts with jerky rotation
• PREVENTION: Number of rotor slots must NOT equal or be simple multiple of stator slots |
Rotor slots are SKEWED — slanted along the axis — this ensures continuous reluctance
change and smooth starting
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Induction motor: rotating stator field induces current in rotor — current in field creates
force — rotation
✓ Slip = (Ns - Nr)/Ns x 100% — typically 3-8% at full load
✓ Star-delta: starting current = 1/3 of DOL | starting torque = 1/3 of full voltage torque
✓ Star and delta contactors MUST be interlocked — simultaneous closure = short
circuit
✓ Crawling: motor runs at 1/7 synchronous speed due to 7th harmonic stator field
✓ Cogging: motor refuses to start — rotor slots align with stator slots — magnetic
locking
✓ Both prevented by SKEWING rotor slots
MEMORY AID: Slip Formula
s = (Ns - Nr)/Ns x 100% | Ns = 120f/P | At full load: 3-8% | At start: 100%

11. MOTOR STARTERS — DOL, STAR-DELTA, SOFT STARTER
Asked in: DOL: 2023/FEB, 2025/FEB, 2025/JUL | Soft start: 2023/JUL, 2024/APR, 2025/APR — 8+8 marks
A) Direct Online (DOL) Contactor Starter (8 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Sketch a circuit diagram of a push button direct online contactor
starter for a three phase incorporating overload and short circuit protection (8). Indicate
on a sketch the typical characteristic curves of current and torque against speed,
disadvantages of direct online start squirrel cage induction motor (8). — 16 marks
DOL Starter Circuit Description:
• MAIN CIRCUIT: Three-phase supply → Main fuses (HRC) for short circuit protection →
Overload relay (thermal) → Main contactor → Motor terminals
• CONTROL CIRCUIT: Start button (NO) → Stop button (NC) in series → Contactor coil |
Auxiliary contact of contactor (NO) in parallel with start button for HOLD-IN (sealing circuit)
• OVERLOAD PROTECTION: Bimetallic overload relay — trips control circuit if current
exceeds setting
• SHORT CIRCUIT PROTECTION: HRC fuses in main circuit — clears short circuit fault
• UNDERVOLTAGE PROTECTION: If supply fails, contactor de-energises — motor stops —
does not restart automatically when power returns — inherent protection
Torque-Speed and Current-Speed Characteristics:
Sketch description: Draw two curves on same graph (X axis = speed from 0 to Ns, Y axis = current
and torque). CURRENT curve: starts very HIGH at standstill (5-7 x FLC), falls as speed increases,
reaches normal running current near synchronous speed. TORQUE curve: starts moderate at
standstill, dips slightly (saddle), peaks around 70-80% synchronous speed (breakdown torque), then
falls to zero at synchronous speed.
Disadvantages of DOL Starting:
• HIGH STARTING CURRENT: 5-7 times full load current — causes VOLTAGE DIP on
switchboard — affects other loads
• HIGH MECHANICAL SHOCK: Full torque applied instantly — shock to drive train, couplings,
driven equipment
• HIGH STARTING TORQUE AT LOW SPEEDS: Not always suitable — risk of damage to
belt drives or centrifugal pumps
• SWITCHBOARD VOLTAGE DIP: Lights flicker, sensitive electronics may reset, other motors
may trip
• Only suitable for SMALL MOTORS where starting current can be tolerated by the supply
B) Soft Starter for Induction Motor (16 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: What is soft starting of an Induction Motor? Describe with a circuit
using thyristors used for soft starting. Discuss its advantages and disadvantages. — 16
marks | 2023/JUL, 2024/APR, 2025/APR
What is Soft Starting:

Soft starting is a method of starting an induction motor by GRADUALLY increasing the applied
voltage from a reduced value to full voltage — using thyristors (SCRs) to control the firing angle.
This limits the starting current and torque to acceptable values.
Circuit Description Using Thyristors:
• Three pairs of thyristors (SCRs) connected in ANTI-PARALLEL configuration — one pair per
phase
• Each pair consists of two thyristors connected back-to-back — allows both half-cycles of AC
to be controlled
• FIRING CONTROL CIRCUIT: continuously monitors motor current and controls the firing
angle (alpha) of each thyristor
• At START: firing angle is large — thyristors conduct for short portion of each cycle —
reduced voltage to motor
• As motor accelerates: firing angle PROGRESSIVELY REDUCED — more voltage passed —
current controlled at set ramp rate
• At FULL SPEED: thyristors fully conducting — full voltage applied — or bypass contactor
closes, bypassing thyristors
• BYPASS CONTACTOR: closed when motor reaches full speed — thyristors then taken out
of circuit to avoid thermal losses
Advantages of Soft Starter:
• CONTROLLED STARTING CURRENT: current limited to typically 2-3 x full load current —
no damaging current spike
• REDUCED VOLTAGE DIP: less impact on other consumers on same switchboard
• SMOOTH TORQUE: gradual acceleration — no mechanical shock to shaft, couplings,
gearboxes
• ADJUSTABLE RAMP: starting time and current limit adjustable to suit application
• MOTOR PROTECTION: built-in overload and phase failure protection
• REDUCED WEAR: less stress on mechanical components during starting
• ENERGY SAVING: can reduce voltage during light load running (not all soft starters)
Disadvantages of Soft Starter:
• COST: more expensive than DOL or star-delta starter
• HEAT GENERATION: thyristors generate heat — require cooling (heatsinks or forced air
cooling)
• HARMONIC DISTORTION: thyristor firing generates harmonics — can affect sensitive
equipment
• COMPLEXITY: more complex to maintain and fault-find than simple contactors
• REDUCED TORQUE AT START: may not provide enough torque for high-inertia or high-
load starts
• BYPASS CONTACTOR REQUIRED: thyristors are bypassed at full speed to avoid losses —
adds complexity
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ DOL starter: Start button → Contactor coil → Sealing contact holds in | Stop → de-
energises coil
✓ DOL disadvantage: 5-7x starting current — voltage dip — mechanical shock

✓ Soft starter: thyristors control firing angle — gradually increase voltage — limit
current to 2-3x FLC
✓ Anti-parallel thyristors: two SCRs back-to-back per phase — control both AC half
cycles
✓ Bypass contactor: closes at full speed — bypasses thyristors — reduces heat losses
✓ Soft starter advantage: controlled current, smooth torque, adjustable ramp
✓ Soft starter disadvantage: expensive, generates heat, harmonics, complex
MEMORY AID: Soft Starter vs DOL
DOL: simple, cheap, 5-7x Ifl, voltage dip | Soft: expensive, complex, 2-3x Ifl, smooth start

12. SYNCHRONOUS MOTORS — OPERATION, APPLICATION,
CAPACITOR FUNCTION
Asked in: 2019/AUG, 2019/OCT2, 2019/DEC, 2024/SEP, 2025/JAN — 16 marks
EXAM QUESTION: State the application of synchronous motors. Discuss how a
synchronous motor can function as a synchronous capacitor. Compare synchronous
motors with induction motor drives. — 16 marks
A) Principle of Operation (4 marks)
A synchronous motor is an AC motor that runs at EXACTLY synchronous speed — it does not have
slip. The rotor field (from DC excitation) locks onto the rotating stator field and is dragged around at
synchronous speed.
• Rotor carries DC field winding — fed via slip rings or brushless exciter
• Stator has three-phase AC winding — creates rotating magnetic field at Ns = 120f/P
• Rotor DC field locks onto stator rotating field — rotor rotates at EXACTLY synchronous
speed
• NOT self-starting — must be accelerated to near synchronous speed before DC excitation
applied
Starting Methods:
• DAMPER WINDINGS (amortisseur): squirrel cage bars embedded in rotor poles — acts as
induction motor during starting — once near synchronous speed, DC field switched on —
pulls into step
• VARIABLE FREQUENCY DRIVE: gradually increase frequency from 0 — motor accelerates
synchronously
• PONY MOTOR: separate small motor accelerates main motor to near synchronous speed
B) Applications of Synchronous Motors Onboard (4 marks)
• LARGE PUMPS: main sea water circulating pumps, cargo pumps on tankers — large,
constant speed loads
• COMPRESSORS: air conditioning and refrigeration compressors — constant speed required
• PROPULSION: electric propulsion systems on cruise ships and naval vessels
• POWER FACTOR CORRECTION: operating as synchronous capacitor (see below)
• PRECISION EQUIPMENT: equipment requiring exact constant speed — not affected by
load changes
• WINCHES AND HOISTS: where precise speed control is needed
C) Synchronous Motor as Synchronous Capacitor (4 marks)
When a synchronous motor is OVER-EXCITED (DC field current above normal), it draws LEADING
current from the supply — it behaves like a capacitor and SUPPLIES reactive power to the system.
• UNDER-EXCITED: motor draws LAGGING current (like an inductor) — absorbs reactive
power
• NORMALLY EXCITED: motor draws current at UNITY power factor — no reactive power
exchange
• OVER-EXCITED: motor draws LEADING current — GENERATES reactive power — acts as
capacitor

• By varying excitation, reactive power can be continuously and smoothly CONTROLLED
• Used for POWER FACTOR CORRECTION: improve overall system power factor of ship's
electrical system
• Advantage over static capacitors: continuously variable and REVERSIBLE — can supply or
absorb VAr
• Called SYNCHRONOUS CONDENSER or synchronous compensator in this application
D) Comparison: Synchronous Motor vs Induction Motor (4 marks)
Feature Synchronous Motor Induction Motor (Squirrel Cage)
Speed Exactly synchronous speed — Slightly less than synchronous —
constant has slip
Self-starting NOT self-starting — requires Self-starting — starts as induction
auxiliary means motor
Excitation Requires separate DC excitation No separate excitation needed
supply
Power factor Controllable — can be unity, Always lagging — 0.7 to 0.9
leading or lagging typically
Efficiency Higher at full load — no slip losses Slightly lower — slip losses exist
Cost Higher — more complex Lower — simpler, robust
construction construction
Maintenance Higher — slip rings (unless Lower — virtually no maintenance
brushless)
Application Large loads requiring constant General purpose — most common
speed and PF correction shipboard motor
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Synchronous motor runs at EXACTLY synchronous speed — no slip
✓ NOT self-starting — needs damper windings or VFD or pony motor
✓ Over-excited: draws LEADING current = acts as CAPACITOR = supplies reactive
power (kVAR)
✓ Under-excited: draws LAGGING current = acts as INDUCTOR = absorbs reactive
power
✓ Synchronous condenser: over-excited synchronous motor used purely for power
factor correction
✓ Comparison: synchronous = constant speed, controllable PF, expensive | induction =
self-start, cheap, robust
✓ Applications: large pumps, compressors, propulsion, power factor correction

13. DC MOTORS — CHARACTERISTICS, BACK EMF, DC
GENERATOR MOTORISATION
Asked in: DC motor characteristics: 2024/OCT/Q2 | DC generator motorisation: 2023/JAN, 2024/MAR,
2024/NOV — 16 marks
A) Characteristics of DC Motor (4 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Describe the characteristics of a DC motor. Explain advantages for
deck machinery. Describe control system for the motor. 2024/OCT/Q2 — 4+4+8
Shunt Motor Characteristics:
• SPEED: nearly constant from no load to full load — slight droop due to armature resistance
voltage drop
• TORQUE: proportional to armature current — linear relationship
• STARTING: low starting torque — needs external resistance to limit starting current
• Speed control: vary armature voltage (below base speed) or field weakening (above base
speed)
Series Motor Characteristics:
• SPEED: varies greatly with load — high speed at light load, low speed at heavy load
• TORQUE: proportional to SQUARE of current at low currents — very high starting torque
• NEVER run on no load — speed becomes dangerously high (runaway)
• Ideal for: traction, cranes, winches — high starting torque loads
Advantages for Deck Machinery (Winches, Windlass):
• DC series motor provides HIGH TORQUE at LOW SPEED — ideal for heavy lift and
anchoring
• Speed easily controlled by varying armature voltage — smooth and precise
• Regenerative braking possible — motor acts as generator — energy returned to supply
• Robust construction — handles shock loads well
B) Back EMF — Definition and Derivation (6 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: What is back emf? Derive the relation for the back emf and the supplied
voltage in terms of armature resistance. 2024/APR, 2023/OCT, 2025/APR — 6 marks
When a DC motor armature rotates in the magnetic field, it generates an EMF by Lenz's law — this
induced EMF OPPOSES the applied voltage and is called BACK EMF (Eb).
• Eb = PHINZN/60A — where PHI = flux per pole, N = speed, Z = total conductors, P = poles,
A = parallel paths
• Eb is proportional to SPEED and FLUX — faster rotation = higher back EMF
• At standstill: Eb = 0 — full supply voltage drives current through armature resistance
• As motor accelerates: Eb increases — net voltage across armature resistance decreases —
current reduces
• At full speed: Eb is just below supply voltage — only small current flows for no-load losses

Voltage Equation:
V = Eb + Ia x Ra
Where: V = supply voltage | Eb = back EMF | Ia = armature current | Ra = armature resistance
Therefore: Ia = (V - Eb) / Ra
• Starting (Eb = 0): Ia = V/Ra — VERY LARGE CURRENT — this is why starter resistance is
needed
• Running (Eb near V): Ia = small — normal running current
• Back EMF is a SELF-REGULATING mechanism — if load increases, speed drops, Eb
drops, Ia increases, torque increases — automatically compensates
C) Which Device Prevents DC Generator from Becoming Motorised (16 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Which of the following devices will prevent a DC generator from
becoming motorized? (i) Over current relay (4) (ii) Motorization trip (4) (iii) Reverse power
relay (4) (iv) Reverse current relay (4). Give detailed explanations as to why the remaining
options were not considered (8). — 2023/JAN, 2024/MAR, 2024/NOV
Answer: REVERSE CURRENT RELAY prevents DC generator from motorising
(i) Over Current Relay — NOT suitable (4 marks):
• Overcurrent relay trips when current EXCEEDS a set value
• When a DC generator becomes motorised, it DRAWS current from the bus instead of
supplying it
• The current drawn by a motorised generator may not exceed the overcurrent relay setting —
it depends on load
• Overcurrent relay cannot detect the DIRECTION of current flow — only the magnitude
• Therefore it CANNOT reliably detect motorisation — it is NOT the correct device
(ii) Motorisation Trip — NOT a standard protection device (4 marks):
• Motorisation trip is a general term — not a specific standalone relay
• In practice, motorisation protection IS achieved, but through the REVERSE CURRENT
RELAY — the motor trip function is the RESULT of the reverse current relay operation
• There is no specific discrete device called only a motorisation trip — it is the function, not the
device
• Therefore this description is imprecise — the correct device is the reverse current relay
(iii) Reverse Power Relay — Used for AC generators, NOT DC (4 marks):
• Reverse power relay (wattmetric relay) detects reversal of REAL POWER FLOW —
designed for AC alternators
• For AC systems: measures V x I x cos(phi) — detects when power direction reverses
• For DC generators: power reversal detection is simpler — just current direction
• A reverse power relay requires AC voltage and current phasors to compute power — NOT
applicable to DC systems
• Therefore the REVERSE POWER RELAY is for AC generators — NOT the correct device
for DC generators

(iv) Reverse Current Relay — CORRECT device (4 marks):
• The REVERSE CURRENT RELAY detects when the direction of current through the DC
generator REVERSES
• Normal operation: generator supplies current TO the busbar — current flows OUT of positive
terminal
• Motorising: generator draws current FROM the busbar — current flows INTO positive
terminal — DIRECTION REVERSES
• Reverse current relay uses a directional current sensing element (polarised electromagnet or
rectifier circuit)
• When current direction reverses beyond threshold — relay trips the generator circuit breaker
• Threshold typically set at 5-8% of rated current in reverse direction — time delay to prevent
nuisance trips
• After tripping, the generator is isolated — engine can be stopped or investigated
• CONCLUSION: Reverse current relay is the ONLY device that correctly detects motorisation
in DC generators by sensing current reversal
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ DC shunt motor: nearly constant speed, proportional torque, good for general use
✓ DC series motor: high starting torque, speed varies with load, NEVER run unloaded
✓ Back EMF: Eb = V - Ia.Ra | As speed increases, Eb increases, Ia decreases
automatically
✓ Back EMF is self-regulating: load increases → speed drops → Eb drops → Ia
increases → torque increases
✓ DC generator motorisation: detected by REVERSE CURRENT RELAY — detects
current direction reversal
✓ NOT overcurrent relay (cannot detect direction) | NOT reverse power relay (for AC
only)
✓ Reverse current relay threshold: typically 5-8% of rated current in reverse
MEMORY AID: DC Generator Protection
Reverse CURRENT relay (DC) = detects current direction reversal | Reverse POWER relay
(AC) = detects power flow reversal

14. TRANSFORMERS — LOSSES, EFFICIENCY, LIQUID-
COOLED HAZARDS, 3-PHASE
Asked in: Liquid-cooled hazards: 2023/FEB, 2023/APR, 2023/JUL, 2023/SEP, 2023/NOV, 2024/JUL,
2024/OCT, 2025/FEB, 2025/SEP, 2025/NOV — VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED
A) Potential Hazards of Liquid-Cooled Transformers (6 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: Explain the potential hazards if liquid-cooled transformers are used. —
2023/FEB onwards, 6 marks almost every paper
Liquid-cooled transformers use oil (mineral or synthetic) for both cooling and insulation. While
effective, they introduce several significant hazards onboard ship:
• Hazard 1 — FIRE HAZARD — Transformer oil is FLAMMABLE — if the transformer
overheats or has an internal fault (arc), the oil can ignite. The fire can be difficult to
extinguish — oil fires require foam or CO2. In an engine room environment, an oil
transformer fire can rapidly escalate.
• Hazard 2 — EXPLOSION RISK — Internal arcing or severe overheating causes oil to
VAPORISE rapidly. The sudden expansion of oil vapour can RUPTURE the transformer tank
— explosion of the tank can cause structural damage and propel burning oil fragments
throughout the space.
• Hazard 3 — OIL SPILL POLLUTION — Transformer oil is an ENVIRONMENTAL
POLLUTANT under MARPOL Annex I. Any leakage or rupture releases oil that can
contaminate bilges, enter the sea, and cause pollution offences.
• Hazard 4 — TOXIC FUMES — Older transformers may contain PCB (polychlorinated
biphenyl) oil — known carcinogen. Even modern transformer oil, when burned, produces
toxic combustion products including carbon monoxide, acrolein and other harmful gases.
• Hazard 5 — ELECTRICAL HAZARD — Oil-cooled transformers operate at HIGH
VOLTAGE. Oil provides insulation — if oil quality degrades (moisture ingress,
contamination) insulation breaks down — risk of electric shock to personnel and equipment
damage.
• Hazard 6 — MOISTURE INGRESS — Oil is HYGROSCOPIC — absorbs moisture from
atmosphere. Moisture reduces insulation quality, promotes partial discharge, and
accelerates insulation deterioration.
Precautions and Alternatives:
• DRY-TYPE TRANSFORMERS (resin-encapsulated) — preferred for shipboard use — no oil
— no fire risk — no pollution risk — suitable for enclosed spaces
• If oil-type used: install in FIRE RESISTANT ENCLOSURE | Provide OIL CONTAINMENT
TRAY (bund) | Install BUCHHOLZ RELAY (detects gas from internal faults) | Regular OIL
SAMPLING AND TESTING
B) Transformer Losses — Types and Factors Affecting (3 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: What are the losses in transformers? Mention various factors which
affect these losses. — Part of frequently asked question
Iron Losses (Core Losses) — CONSTANT:

• HYSTERESIS LOSS: Energy lost in magnetising and demagnetising the core material each
cycle — proportional to frequency and flux density (Bmax^1.6)
• EDDY CURRENT LOSS: Circulating currents induced in the laminated core — proportional
to frequency squared and flux density squared
• Minimised by: using SILICON STEEL core (high resistivity) and THIN LAMINATIONS (0.3-
0.5 mm)
• Iron losses are CONSTANT — do not depend on load current — present whenever
transformer is energised
Copper Losses (I^2R Losses) — VARIABLE:
• Heat dissipated in primary and secondary winding resistances
• Copper losses = I1^2 x R1 + I2^2 x R2
• VARIABLE — proportional to SQUARE OF LOAD CURRENT — increase with load
• Minimised by: using large cross-section conductors (lower resistance)
Factors Affecting Losses:
• FREQUENCY: higher frequency increases both hysteresis and eddy current losses
• FLUX DENSITY: higher flux density increases core losses — determined by applied voltage
• LOAD CURRENT: higher load increases copper losses proportionally to I^2
• TEMPERATURE: higher temperature increases resistance — more copper losses
• CORE MATERIAL: silicon steel has lower losses than plain iron
• LAMINATION THICKNESS: thinner laminations reduce eddy current losses
C) 3-Phase Transformers — Parallel Operation and Bank vs Unit (16 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: With reference to 3-phase transformers: a) Essential and desirable
conditions for parallel operation (5). b) Advantages of transformer bank of three 1-phase
transformers over unit 3-phase transformer (5). c) Efficiency calculation at half load 0.8 PF
(6). — 2025/JAN, 2025/AUG
Essential Conditions for Parallel Operation of 3-Phase Transformers:
• Essential 1 — SAME VOLTAGE RATIO: both transformers must have same turns ratio —
equal primary and secondary voltages. If different — circulating current will flow between the
transformers even at no load.
• Essential 2 — SAME POLARITY: both transformers must have same polarity — angular
displacement between primary and secondary must be the same. Incorrect polarity causes
large circulating currents.
• Essential 3 — SAME PHASE SEQUENCE: the phase rotation of both must be identical.
Wrong phase sequence causes large fault currents and equipment damage.
• Essential 4 — SAME VECTOR GROUP: both transformers must have same vector group
(e.g. both Dyn11 or both YNyn0). Different vector groups cause phase displacement — large
circulating currents.
Desirable Conditions:
• SAME PERCENTAGE IMPEDANCE: transformers with same per-unit impedance share load
proportionally to their ratings. Different impedances cause unequal load sharing — smaller
impedance transformer takes more load.
• SAME KVA RATING: for most efficient utilisation — equal ratings share load equally.

• SAME FREQUENCY: obvious but important — must both be on same supply.
Advantages of Three Single-Phase Transformer Bank Over Unit 3-Phase
Transformer:
• SPARE: one single-phase transformer of the bank can be carried as a spare — unit 3-phase
transformer spare is the entire unit (very expensive and heavy)
• If one transformer FAILS: the bank can continue with remaining two in open-delta (V-
connection) at 57.7% capacity — unit 3-phase transformer is completely out of service on
failure
• TRANSPORTATION: single-phase units are smaller and lighter — easier to transport to ship
through narrow passages and hatches
• MAINTENANCE: individual units can be serviced one at a time — bank can continue
operating at reduced capacity
• REPAIR: single units can be sent ashore for repair — more workshop options available
Advantages of Unit 3-Phase Transformer:
• SMALLER OVERALL SIZE AND WEIGHT: single unit is more compact than three separate
units
• LOWER COST: single unit generally less expensive than three single-phase units of
equivalent total rating
• SIMPLER CONNECTIONS: only one set of connections required
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Liquid-cooled transformer hazards: FIRE (oil burns), EXPLOSION (vapour),
POLLUTION (MARPOL), TOXIC FUMES, ELECTRICAL, MOISTURE
✓ Preferred onboard: DRY-TYPE (resin encapsulated) — no oil hazards
✓ Iron losses (constant) = hysteresis + eddy current | Copper losses (variable) = I^2R
✓ Essential parallel conditions: same voltage ratio, same polarity, same phase
sequence, same vector group
✓ Bank advantage: spare single unit, V-connection operation on failure, easier transport
✓ Iron losses constant (always present) | Copper losses vary as load^2
✓ Buchholz relay: detects gas/oil movement from internal arcing — warns before
catastrophic failure
MEMORY AID: Transformer Parallel Conditions
V-P-PS-VG: Voltage ratio (same), Polarity (same), Phase Sequence (same), Vector Group
(same)

15. RECTIFIERS — HALF WAVE, FULL WAVE, BRIDGE, PEAK
Asked in: 2024/OCT/Q1, 2025/FEB/Q3, 2025/JUL/Q3 — 16 marks
EXAM QUESTION: Differentiate between half and full wave rectification. State where half
wave rectification may be used and purpose for which it is not well adapted. Sketch a
bridge connection by which full wave rectification may be obtained. — 16 marks
A) Half Wave Rectifier (4 marks)
A half wave rectifier uses a SINGLE DIODE to pass only ONE HALF CYCLE of the AC input —
either the positive or negative half cycle.
• CIRCUIT: Single diode in series with load resistor across AC supply
• OPERATION: Positive half cycle — diode forward biased — conducts — current flows
through load. Negative half cycle — diode reverse biased — blocks — no current
• OUTPUT: Pulsating DC — only positive half cycles appear at output — large gaps between
pulses
• DC OUTPUT VOLTAGE (average): Vdc = Vm / pi = 0.318 x Vm — where Vm = peak AC
voltage
• RIPPLE: very high — 121% ripple factor — requires large capacitor filter to smooth
Where Half Wave Used:
• Signal detection circuits — AM radio demodulation
• Battery chargers where smooth DC not critical
• Signal rectification in instruments and meters
Where NOT Well Adapted:
• NOT suitable for POWER SUPPLIES requiring smooth DC — excessive ripple
• NOT suitable for HIGH POWER applications — only uses half of AC waveform — inefficient
(transformer utilisation factor 0.287)
• NOT suitable for motor drives — pulsating current causes torque ripple
B) Full Wave Rectifier — Bridge Connection (8 marks)
A BRIDGE RECTIFIER uses FOUR DIODES arranged in a bridge configuration to rectify BOTH
HALF CYCLES of AC — producing smoother DC output.
Bridge Circuit Description:
Draw a diamond/square arrangement of four diodes (D1, D2, D3, D4). Label the four corners: top
(A+), bottom (A-), left (AC input +) and right (AC input -). Diodes arranged so that: D1 top-left to top,
D2 top-right to top, D3 bottom to bottom-left, D4 bottom to bottom-right. Show load connected
between top (positive) and bottom (negative) output. Show AC input across left and right corners.
Operation:
• POSITIVE HALF CYCLE: Current flows through D1 → load → D4 — load sees positive
voltage
• NEGATIVE HALF CYCLE: Current flows through D2 → load → D3 — load STILL sees
positive voltage
• Both half cycles produce current in SAME direction through load — full wave rectification

• DC OUTPUT VOLTAGE: Vdc = 2Vm/pi = 0.637 x Vm — twice the half wave output
• RIPPLE: much lower — 48% ripple factor — easier to filter
• RIPPLE FREQUENCY: 2 x supply frequency — 100Hz for 50Hz supply — easier to filter
than 50Hz
C) Comparison Table (4 marks)
Feature Half Wave Full Wave (Bridge)
Diodes required 1 4
Output frequency Same as supply (50Hz) Twice supply (100Hz)
DC output voltage (avg) 0.318 x Vm 0.637 x Vm
Ripple factor 121% — very high 48% — much lower
Transformer utilisation 28.7% — very inefficient 81.2% — much better
Filter required Very large filter needed Smaller filter needed
Efficiency 40.6% 81.2%
Applications Low power, signal detection Power supplies, battery
chargers, drives
D) Peak Rectifier (4 marks)
EXAM QUESTION: By means of schematic circuit diagram illustrate the peak rectifier. If
supply voltage is v(t) = Vm Sin(wt), what is the voltage across the load resistor? —
2023/OCT, 2025/APR
A peak rectifier (or peak detector/clamper circuit) captures and holds the PEAK VALUE of the AC
input voltage.
• CIRCUIT: Diode in series + capacitor in parallel with load resistor
• OPERATION: During positive half cycle, diode conducts and charges capacitor to peak
voltage Vm
• When AC falls below capacitor voltage: diode reverse biased — capacitor HOLDS charge —
maintains output near Vm
• OUTPUT VOLTAGE: approximately equal to PEAK voltage Vm — much higher than
average rectifier output
• If v(t) = Vm sin(wt) then Vload ≈ Vm (peak voltage, with small ripple if capacitor is large)
• APPLICATIONS: Power supplies needing high DC voltage from AC | Amplitude detection in
communications | Voltage multiplier circuits
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Half wave: 1 diode, 0.318Vm average, 121% ripple, 50Hz ripple — inefficient
✓ Full wave bridge: 4 diodes, 0.637Vm average, 48% ripple, 100Hz ripple — efficient
✓ Bridge: both half cycles used — current always in same direction through load
✓ Peak rectifier: diode + capacitor — output = Vm (peak voltage) — capacitor holds
charge
✓ Half wave: NOT suitable for power supplies or motors — excessive ripple
✓ Full wave ripple frequency = 2 x supply frequency — easier to filter

✓ Ripple factor: half wave 121% | full wave 48% — lower is better
MEMORY AID: Rectifier Output Voltages
Half wave: Vdc = 0.318 x Vm | Full wave bridge: Vdc = 0.637 x Vm | Peak rectifier: Vdc ≈ Vm

16. PLC — PROGRAMMABLE LOGIC CONTROLLERS
Asked in: 2020/FEB, 2021/JAN, 2021/FEB, 2022/FEB, 2025/MAR — 8+4+4 marks
EXAM QUESTION: With respect to PLCs used onboard ships: a) Draw and explain the
block diagram of a PLC (8). b) Name the onboard ship equipment where PLCs are used (4).
c) What are the advantages of PLC controllers over other types of controllers? (4). — 16
marks
A) Block Diagram of PLC (8 marks)
Main Sections of a PLC:
1. Input Section (Input Module):
• Receives signals from FIELD DEVICES — sensors, switches, transmitters, limit switches,
push buttons
• Converts signals to logic levels (24VDC or 5VDC) for CPU processing
• ISOLATES field signals from CPU using optocouplers — protection from surges
• Monitors: discrete inputs (on/off switches) and analogue inputs (temperature, pressure, flow
signals)
2. CPU (Central Processing Unit):
• The BRAIN of the PLC — executes the control program
• Continuously scans program in a repeating SCAN CYCLE: Read inputs → Execute program
→ Update outputs
• Contains: processor, memory (program and data storage), internal timers and counters
• Program stored in FLASH MEMORY — retained when power is off
• Scan cycle time: typically 1-100 milliseconds
3. Memory:
• PROGRAM MEMORY: stores the user control program (ladder logic, function block diagram)
• DATA MEMORY: stores input/output status, timer values, counter values, internal variables
• Battery-backed RAM: retains data during power failure
4. Output Section (Output Module):
• Receives logic signals from CPU — converts to OUTPUT SIGNALS for field devices
• Drives: contactors, solenoid valves, motor starters, alarm indicators, displays
• Output types: relay outputs (can switch AC or DC), transistor outputs (DC only, fast), triac
outputs (AC)
• ISOLATED from CPU — protects processor from load switching transients
5. Power Supply:
• Converts incoming supply (24VDC or 230VAC) to regulated voltages for all modules
• Provides backup battery for memory retention
6. Programming Device / HMI:

• PC or handheld terminal used to write, upload and modify program
• HMI (Human Machine Interface) — touchscreen display for operator monitoring and control
• Communication via USB, Ethernet, RS232/485
B) Onboard Ship Equipment Using PLCs (4 marks)
• CARGO HANDLING SYSTEMS: container ship cranes, tanker cargo pump control, bulk
carrier conveyor systems
• BALLAST WATER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM: automatic control of ballast pumps and valves
• ENGINE ROOM AUTOMATION (UMS): monitoring and control of main engine, boilers,
pumps, separators
• FIRE DETECTION AND CONTROL: fire detection panels, deluge system control
• DYNAMIC POSITIONING SYSTEM: automatic position control using GPS, gyro, wind
sensors
• REFRIGERATION CONTROL: reefer container temperature control, refrigerated cargo hold
control
• SEWAGE TREATMENT PLANT: automatic control of treatment process
• HVAC SYSTEM: heating, ventilation and air conditioning control
• STEERING GEAR CONTROL: autopilot and steering control systems
C) Advantages of PLCs Over Other Controllers (4 marks)
Advantage Explanation
Flexibility Program can be CHANGED without rewiring — simply reprogram. Relay
logic requires complete rewiring for any logic change.
Reliability No moving parts in logic — more reliable than relay panels. Mean time
between failures (MTBF) very high — years of continuous operation.
Fault diagnosis Built-in FAULT DETECTION — monitors its own operation, inputs and
outputs. LED indicators show status of each I/O — quick fault finding.
Compact size One PLC replaces hundreds of relays, timers, counters — massive space
saving in control panels.
Easy maintenance Modular design — faulty module simply swapped. No need to trace wiring
in complex relay panels.
Data logging PLC can LOG data — alarms, events, process values — stored for
analysis and reporting.
Communication Can connect to SCADA, DCS, HMI systems — data sharing across the
ship network.
Cost effective Lower lifetime cost — reduced wiring, faster installation, less maintenance,
longer life.
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ PLC sections: Input → CPU (scan cycle) → Memory → Output | Plus Power supply
and HMI
✓ Scan cycle: Read inputs → Execute program → Update outputs — repeated
continuously
✓ Input module: isolates field signals via optocouplers — protects CPU
✓ Output types: relay (AC/DC), transistor (DC fast), triac (AC)

✓ Key advantage: REPROGRAMMABLE — logic changes without rewiring
✓ Used onboard: cargo, ballast, UMS, fire detection, DP, refrigeration, steering
✓ PLC vs relays: more reliable, compact, diagnosable, flexible, data logging
MEMORY AID: PLC Scan Cycle

17. UMS — UNATTENDED MACHINERY SPACES
Asked in: 2023/APR/Q7, 2025/SEP/Q7 — 7+7+6 marks (20 marks in some papers)
EXAM QUESTION: UMS monitoring and control system giving false alarms and incorrect
data printouts. State possible causes if: i) Localised to a particular area of engine
operation ii) General to the engine room. State action as Electrical Engineer. Explain
procedure to locate and rectify a general fault in the UMS system. — 2023/APR, 2025/SEP
A) Possible Causes of False Alarms — Localised to Particular Area (7 marks)
If false alarms are localised to ONE particular area or system:
• FAULTY SENSOR: The sensor (temperature, pressure, level, flow) in that area has failed —
drifted out of calibration or developed an internal fault — gives incorrect reading
• DAMAGED SIGNAL CABLE: Cable from sensor to alarm panel in that area has developed a
fault — short circuit, open circuit, moisture ingress, mechanical damage causing intermittent
signal
• LOOSE CONNECTION: Terminal connections at sensor, junction box or panel have become
loose — causing intermittent or spurious signals
• SENSOR CONTAMINATION: Sensor is physically blocked or contaminated — pressure
transmitter blocked with sludge, temperature sensor with scale — gives wrong reading
• INCORRECT ALARM SETPOINT: Alarm setpoint for that specific sensor has been changed
inadvertently or drifted — alarm activates at wrong value
• VIBRATION: Excessive vibration in that area causing micro-fractures in sensor wiring or
loose connectors
• LOCAL EARTHING FAULT: Earth fault in that area introducing noise into signal cables —
causing spurious readings
B) Possible Causes — General to Engine Room (7 marks)
If false alarms and incorrect data are GENERAL throughout the engine room:
• POWER SUPPLY FAILURE/INSTABILITY: Unstable power supply to UMS (24VDC or
110VAC) — voltage fluctuations affect all sensors and processing simultaneously
• COMMON EARTH FAULT: Earth fault in common power supply or signal ground —
introduces noise across all channels simultaneously
• CPU/PROCESSOR FAULT: Failure of the central processing unit or data acquisition card —
affects all processing and output
• COMMUNICATION BUS FAULT: Fault in the fieldbus or data communication network
(Modbus, PROFIBUS etc.) — data from all sensors corrupted or lost
• POWER SURGE: Lightning strike or switching surge has damaged the input cards —
multiple channels affected
• ENVIRONMENTAL: Excessive heat or humidity in UMS control room affecting all electronics
• SOFTWARE FAULT: Software corruption or watchdog failure causing erratic system
behaviour
• BATTERY FAILURE: Backup battery failure causing memory corruption — system resets to
incorrect state
C) Action as Electrical Engineer (7 marks)
Immediate Actions:

36. INFORM MASTER and Chief Engineer immediately — may need to post an engine room
watch (cancel UMS)
37. ACTIVATE MANUAL WATCH: If UMS reliability is in doubt — post continuous watch in
engine room as per SOLAS requirements for UMS ships
38. CHECK POWER SUPPLY: Verify UMS power supply voltages are correct and stable —
check fuses, isolators
39. IDENTIFY FAULT SCOPE: Determine if fault is localised or general — check alarm panel for
which zones/channels are affected
40. CHECK RECENT MAINTENANCE: Any recent work done that may have disturbed cables or
connections?
41. BACKUP MONITORING: Ensure all critical parameters being manually monitored during
investigation
Investigation Procedure:
42. CHECK UMS DIAGNOSTIC DISPLAY: Modern UMS systems have built-in diagnostics —
check error logs and fault indicators
43. ISOLATE SUSPECT AREA: If localised — isolate that sensor/circuit and observe if general
alarms clear
44. CHECK SIGNAL CABLES: Measure cable insulation resistance — check for open circuits or
shorts
45. VERIFY SENSORS: Check sensor calibration — measure actual physical parameter
independently (thermometer, pressure gauge) and compare
46. CHECK EARTH CONTINUITY: Test all earth connections — look for earth loops or broken
earths
47. POWER SUPPLY CHECK: Measure all supply voltages — check ripple and stability with
oscilloscope
D) Procedure to Locate and Rectify General UMS Fault (6 marks)
48. DIVIDE THE SYSTEM: Systematically divide UMS into sections — power supply, input
cards, processor, output cards, communication, display
49. START WITH POWER: Check all supply voltages and fuses — most common cause of
general failures
50. CHECK COMMUNICATION BUS: Use diagnostic tools to test communication between
nodes — identify any nodes not responding
51. ISOLATE SUSPECT MODULE: If a card or module suspected — isolate and replace with
spare if available — observe if fault clears
52. SENSOR VERIFICATION: Cross-check sensor readings against independent measurement
53. SOFTWARE: Perform controlled SYSTEM RESTART if hardware checks are satisfactory —
may clear software glitch
54. DOCUMENT ALL FINDINGS: Record all measurements, parts replaced, tests done — for
future reference
55. RETURN TO UMS: Once fault found and rectified — verify system is reading correctly
across ALL parameters before withdrawing manual watch

2025/NOV/Q5 — 6+10 marks
EXAM QUESTION: a) Sketch an arrangement showing the principal of a proportional plus
integral (P+I) control loop (6). b) Compare the series and parallel resonance circuits (10).
— 16 marks (P+I part is 6 marks)
A) Proportional Plus Integral (P+I) Control — 6 marks
What is Control Error:
• ERROR (e) = Set Point (SP) - Process Variable (PV) — the difference between desired and
actual value
• Controller's job: drive error to ZERO — maintain process at set point
Proportional Control (P):
• Output proportional to current error: Output = Kp x e
• PROBLEM: Proportional control alone leaves a STEADY STATE ERROR (offset) — cannot
eliminate it completely
• As error reduces, controller output reduces — before reaching zero error, output is
insufficient to hold process at set point
Integral Control (I):
• Output proportional to the INTEGRAL (sum over time) of the error
• Output = Ki x integral of e.dt
• Integral action continues to increase output as long as ANY error exists — however small
• ELIMINATES STEADY STATE ERROR — only stops integrating when error = ZERO
• Disadvantage: INTEGRAL WINDUP — if error persists for long time, integral term grows
very large — causes overshoot when error finally reduces
P+I Combined Action:
• Total output = Kp x e + Ki x integral(e.dt)
• Proportional: provides immediate response proportional to current error
• Integral: eliminates steady state error — drives error to zero over time
• Together: fast initial response (P) + accurate steady state (I)
Sketch Description:
Draw block diagram: Set Point (SP) input → Summing junction (subtract PV) → Error signal (e) →
P+I controller block (showing two parallel paths: Kp multiplier and Ki integrator) → Summed output
→ Process (plant) → Output = Process Variable (PV) → feedback arrow back to summing junction
Applications Onboard:
• TEMPERATURE CONTROL: boiler temperature, HVAC, refrigeration
• PRESSURE CONTROL: boiler pressure, air pressure regulators
• SPEED CONTROL: generator AVR, engine speed governors
• LEVEL CONTROL: boiler water level, tank level control

KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Error = Set Point - Process Variable | Controller drives error to zero
✓ P control: fast response but LEAVES steady state error (offset)
✓ I control: eliminates steady state error but can cause integral windup and overshoot
✓ P+I combined: fast response (P) + zero steady state error (I)
✓ Integral windup: error persists long time — integral grows large — causes overshoot
when error clears
✓ Applications: temperature, pressure, level, speed control onboard
✓ Output = Kp.e + Ki.integral(e)
MEMORY AID: P+I Control
P = proportional to current error (fast response) | I = proportional to accumulated error
(eliminates offset) | P+I = best of both

Introduction to SOLAS
SOLAS — Safety of Life at Sea — is the most important international treaty dealing with the safety
of merchant ships. It was first adopted in 1914 following the Titanic disaster of 1912, and has been
revised several times since. The current version is SOLAS 1974 with amendments adopted through
IMO (International Maritime Organization).
SOLAS sets minimum standards for the construction, equipment and operation of ships, compatible
with their safety. Flag States are responsible for ensuring that ships flying their flag comply with
these requirements. Ships are issued with certificates as proof of compliance.
Full Name: International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea
Adopted: 1974 (replacing earlier 1929 and 1948 versions) — continuously amended

Asked in: 2018/FEB, 2018/AUG, 2018/SEP, 2018/OCT, 2018/NOV, 2018/DEC, 2019/JAN, 2019/FEB, 2019/MAR,

Regulation: SOLAS Chapter III Reg 19 | IMO Resolution A.1050(27) — Revised
Recommendations for Entering Enclosed Spaces Aboard Ships (2011) | Code of Safe
Working Practices (COSWP) Chapter 15
Introduction — Why Enclosed Spaces are Dangerous
Enclosed spaces on ships represent one of the most serious and persistent causes of fatalities at
sea. Despite decades of safety regulations and training, seafarers continue to die in enclosed
spaces every year. The tragedy is that many deaths occur because well-intentioned crew members
enter a space to rescue a colleague without taking proper precautions — and become casualties
themselves.
The International Maritime Organization, through Resolution A.1050(27), has issued detailed
recommendations for entering enclosed spaces. SOLAS Chapter III Regulation 19 requires ships to
carry equipment for testing the atmosphere of enclosed spaces before entry. The Code of Safe
Working Practices (COSWP) provides the practical guidance for implementation.
Understanding enclosed space safety is not just an exam requirement — it is essential knowledge
that can save lives, including your own.
A) Definition of Enclosed Space
Under IMO Resolution A.1050(27), an enclosed space is defined as a space which has any of the
following characteristics:
• Limited openings for entry and exit
• Inadequate ventilation — natural ventilation is insufficient to maintain safe atmospheric
conditions
• Not designed for continuous worker occupancy — the space is entered occasionally for
maintenance, inspection or cargo work rather than as a workplace
The key point is that a space does NOT need to be sealed or confined to be classified as an
enclosed space. Even a space with an open hatch can be an enclosed space if it has inadequate
natural ventilation.
B) Examples of Enclosed Spaces Onboard
Category Examples Primary Hazard
Cargo spaces Cargo holds, cargo tanks (tankers), Oxygen depletion from cargo oxidation,
ballast tanks, void spaces, inert gas, chemical vapours
cofferdams
Machinery spaces Double bottom tanks, duct keels, Accumulation of gases from machinery,
pipe tunnels, engine room bilge poor ventilation
spaces, shaft tunnels

Deck spaces Fore peak, after peak, bosun's store, Accumulation of fumes, poor ventilation

C) Hazards Associated with Enclosed Spaces — Detailed
1. Oxygen Deficiency — Most Common Fatal Hazard:
Normal atmospheric air contains approximately 20.9% oxygen. When oxygen concentration falls
below safe levels, the human body cannot function properly. Oxygen deficiency can occur without
any visible warning — the air may look and smell perfectly normal but be immediately life-
threatening.
• Below 19.5%: Mildly impaired judgment, increased breathing rate — first warning level
• Below 16%: Headache, dizziness, rapid fatigue — ability to perform tasks greatly reduced
• Below 14%: Extreme fatigue, coordination problems, intermittent respiration — may lose
consciousness
• Below 10%: Nausea, vomiting, rapid loss of consciousness — death within minutes
• Below 6%: Spasmodic breathing, convulsions, death in seconds
CAUSE: Oxygen is consumed by: rusting of steel (oxidation), biological decomposition of organic
matter in cargo residues, bacterial action, burning of fuel, reaction of certain cargoes with moisture.
2. Oxygen Enrichment:
• Above 23.5%: Oxygen enrichment — greatly increased fire and explosion risk
• Enriched atmosphere causes materials that would not normally burn to ignite — even
clothing can catch fire
• Caused by: leaking oxygen equipment, oxygen purging operations
3. Toxic Gases:
• Hydrogen Sulphide (H2S): Produced by decay of organic matter in sewage, fish cargo,
vegetable matter. Heavier than air — settles in bottom of spaces. DANGEROUS: smells like
rotten eggs at low concentrations but SMELL DISAPPEARS at high concentrations — victim
cannot detect lethal levels. TLV: 1 ppm short-term exposure limit
• Carbon Monoxide (CO): Produced by incomplete combustion — engine exhausts, burning
materials. Colourless and ODOURLESS — completely undetectable by senses. Binds to
haemoglobin preventing oxygen transport. TLV: 35 ppm TWA
• Carbon Dioxide (CO2): Produced by biological processes, inert gas systems, fire. Colourless
and odourless. Displaces oxygen. Dangerous above 5%.
• Hydrocarbon Vapours: From cargo residues, fuel oil. Flammable and can displace oxygen.
• Sulphur Dioxide (SO2): From burning sulphur-containing fuels. Irritant to eyes, nose and
respiratory system.
4. Flammable and Explosive Atmospheres:
• Hydrocarbon vapours from oil cargo or fuel residues can form EXPLOSIVE MIXTURES with
air
• Lower Explosive Limit (LEL): below this concentration mixture is too lean to ignite
• Upper Explosive Limit (UEL): above this concentration mixture is too rich to ignite
• Between LEL and UEL: EXPLOSIVE — any spark or flame causes explosion
• A space can be simultaneously oxygen-deficient AND contain explosive vapours

5. Inert Gas Atmosphere:
• Cargo tanks on tankers may contain inert gas (CO2 or nitrogen) used to prevent explosion
during cargo operations
• Inert gas atmosphere contains virtually NO OXYGEN — immediately fatal
• Tank must be thoroughly ventilated and gas-freed before entry

E) Full Entry Procedure — Step by Step
The following procedure must be followed every time an enclosed space is entered, without
exception. There are no shortcuts — cutting corners in enclosed space entry has killed experienced
seafarers.
1. Step 1: OBTAIN PERMIT TO WORK: A formal written permit must be issued and signed by
the responsible officer (Chief Officer for deck spaces, Chief Engineer for machinery spaces).
The permit specifies the space, work to be done, duration, persons involved, precautions
and emergency arrangements. No entry without a signed permit.
2. Step 2: ATMOSPHERE TESTING: Test the atmosphere with a CALIBRATED, APPROVED
gas detector before entry and continuously during work. Test must be done by a competent
person. Test for: O2 (19.5–23.5%), flammable gas (<1% LEL), toxic gases (H2S <1ppm, CO
<35ppm). Test at different levels — top, middle and bottom of space — as different gases
have different densities.
3. Step 3: VENTILATION: Thoroughly ventilate the space using forced ventilation before entry.
Natural ventilation is insufficient for most enclosed spaces. Minimum ventilation period
before entry: as recommended by the risk assessment — typically at least 30 minutes of
forced ventilation for small spaces, longer for large tanks. Continue forced ventilation during
work.
4. Step 4: ISOLATE ALL HAZARDOUS SOURCES: Apply Lock Out Tag Out (LOTO) to all
pipelines, valves and mechanical equipment that could introduce hazardous substances or
cause injury. Blank flanges on all pipelines entering the space. Isolate electrical equipment in
the space. Ensure no steam, water, gas or chemicals can enter.
5. Step 5: COMMUNICATION SYSTEM: Establish reliable means of communication between
the person inside the space and the standby person outside. Telephone, radio or voice
communication. Test before entry. Agree distress signals.
6. Step 6: STANDBY PERSON: A trained standby person must be stationed at the entrance
AT ALL TIMES while anyone is inside. The standby person maintains contact, monitors the

atmosphere at the entrance and is the first responder if something goes wrong. The standby
person must NOT enter the space to attempt rescue.
7. Step 7: RESCUE EQUIPMENT READY: Before anyone enters, all rescue equipment must
be positioned at the entrance ready for immediate use: BA set (Breathing Apparatus), lifeline
and harness, rescue tripod or mechanical advantage system, first aid kit, resuscitation
equipment, communication equipment.
8. Step 8: BRIEF ALL PERSONNEL: Brief all persons who will enter the space and the
standby person: nature of hazards, emergency signals and procedure, escape routes,
communication protocol.
9. Step 9: ENTER WITH APPROPRIATE EQUIPMENT: Enter with personal gas detector,
communications, torch. In atmospheres that may deteriorate: wear BA set. Wear appropriate
PPE — chemical suit if required.
10. Step 10: CONTINUOUS MONITORING: Monitor atmosphere CONTINUOUSLY during work
using personal gas detector. If alarm activates — LEAVE IMMEDIATELY via predetermined
escape route. Do not investigate — exit first.
F) Standby Person — Duties and Restrictions
The standby person has a critical and difficult role. They must remain at the entrance at all times,
maintain contact with the entrant, and in the event of an emergency, summon help while resisting
the powerful instinct to rush in and help their colleague. Many fatalities have occurred precisely
because the standby person entered without BA to help and became a second casualty.
• Station at entrance and DO NOT LEAVE under any circumstances while someone is inside
• Maintain CONTINUOUS COMMUNICATION with entrant — if communication is lost, treat as
emergency
• Monitor atmosphere at the entrance level
• Hold lifeline if entrant is using one
• Control the permit — ensure no unauthorised persons enter
• Know the emergency procedure — including who to call and how to summon rescue team
• CRITICAL: NEVER enter the space to attempt rescue — raise the alarm and wait for a
properly equipped rescue team. Even experienced people can be overcome instantly in a
dangerous atmosphere. The number one rule: DO NOT become a second casualty.
G) Emergency Rescue from Enclosed Space — Full Procedure
If a person collapses or becomes unresponsive in an enclosed space, the correct procedure is
immediate escalation to a full emergency response — NOT a single person rushing in to help.
11. RAISE ALARM IMMEDIATELY — shout, press alarm button, contact bridge or engine room.
Do not waste time trying to revive casualty from the entrance.
12. CALL MASTER — activate ship's emergency response plan
13. ALERT MEDICAL OFFICER or person with first aid training
14. RESCUE TEAM ASSEMBLES — minimum two persons, both equipped with BA sets,
lifelines, torch, first aid equipment
15. Rescue team DONS BA SETS BEFORE ENTERING — do not enter without BA regardless
of how urgent the situation seems
16. Rescuers use LIFELINES connected to a fixed point outside — so they can be pulled out if
they become incapacitated
17. CASUALTY DRAGGED OUT — do not attempt to carry in a confined space — dragging is
faster and requires less space and effort

18. Do NOT remove casualty's BA set if they are wearing one — do not interrupt their air supply
19. Pass casualty to MEDICAL TEAM waiting outside — immediately commence first aid and
CPR if required
20. Do NOT re-enter the space until atmosphere has been retested and confirmed safe

✓ Definition: Limited openings + inadequate ventilation + not designed for continuous
occupancy
✓ Safe O2: 19.5% to 23.5% — below 19.5% DANGER, above 23.5% FIRE RISK
✓ H2S: smell disappears at lethal concentrations — most treacherous toxic gas —
cannot detect by smell
✓ PERMIT TO WORK is mandatory — no exceptions — signed by responsible officer
✓ STANDBY PERSON at entrance AT ALL TIMES — NEVER enters to rescue alone
✓ Rescue team: minimum TWO persons, BOTH in BA sets, with lifelines
✓ DRAG casualty out — do not carry — do not remove their BA set
✓ Test atmosphere at MULTIPLE LEVELS — different gases have different densities
MEMORY AID: Entry Procedure
P-A-V-I-C-S-R-B-E-M: Permit, Atmosphere test, Ventilate, Isolate, Communication, Standby

2. LIFE-SAVING APPLIANCES — LIFEBOATS, DAVITS AND
DRILLS
Asked in: Free fall: 2023/SEP, 2023/DEC, 2025/FEB, 2025/APR, 2025/AUG | Gravity davit: 2024/SEP,
2025/OCT | Drills: Multiple years
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter III — Life-Saving Appliances and Arrangements | LSA Code
(Life-Saving Appliances Code) | MSC/Circ.1392 — Revised guidelines for maintenance and
inspection of safety equipment
Introduction — SOLAS Chapter III
SOLAS Chapter III deals with life-saving appliances and arrangements required on ships. It
specifies the types, quantities, standards and maintenance requirements for all survival craft, rescue
boats, personal life-saving appliances and related equipment. The LSA Code provides the detailed
technical standards for these appliances.
The fundamental philosophy of SOLAS Chapter III is to provide sufficient means for all persons
onboard to abandon ship safely and to survive until rescued, even in the worst foreseeable
conditions. Different ship types have different requirements — passenger ships have the most
stringent requirements, while cargo ships have slightly different arrangements.
Chapter III covers: Survival craft (lifeboats, liferafts), rescue boats, line-throwing appliances,
personal life-saving appliances (lifejackets, immersion suits, lifebuoys), general emergency alarm,
muster stations, LSA maintenance and inspection
Key principle: All persons onboard must be able to reach and embark survival craft within 10
minutes of alarm
A) Gravity Davit Arrangement — Introduction
A gravity davit is a mechanical system for stowing, handling and launching a lifeboat. The term
'gravity' refers to the fact that gravity acts on the davit arms to swing them outboard when released
— no powered mechanism is needed for the outboard swing. Once the davit arms are in the
outboard position, the falls (wire ropes) and winch are used to lower the lifeboat to the water.
Gravity davits are the most common lifeboat launching arrangement on cargo ships. They are
reliable, mechanically simple and allow launching even when the ship has a moderate list. SOLAS
requires them to be able to launch the lifeboat even when the ship has a list of up to 20 degrees.
Asked in: 2024/SEP/Q8, 2025/OCT/Q8 — 16 marks (8+8)
EXAM QUESTION: Q: a) Sketch the arrangement showing the lifeboat both in the housed
position and at maximum point of outboard travel (8). b) Describe the lowering and raising
of lifeboat stating safety features and requirement as per SOLAS 74 with respect to time
for hoisting (8).
Components of Gravity Davit:
• Davit arms — curved steel arms pivoted at the bottom, mounted on ship's side. When gripes
are released, arms swing outboard under gravity
• Tricing pendants — ropes/wires that hold the lifeboat tight against the ship's side in the
stowed position. Released before lowering.
• Gripes — steel wires with quick-release hooks that secure the lifeboat in the davit cradle.
First to be released during lowering.

• Cradle — curved steel cradle on deck that supports the lifeboat weight when stowed
• Falls (wire ropes) — wire ropes running from the winch drum, over sheaves at the davit
head, to the lifeboat hooks. Carry the weight during lowering and hoisting.
• Winch with centrifugal brake — motor-driven winch for hoisting. Centrifugal brake controls
speed of descent during lowering — prevents free fall.
• Limit switches — stop the winch motor at correct upper and lower positions to prevent
overwinding or over-lowering
• Bowsing tackle — additional line to pull the boat towards the ship's side for embarkation
• Painter — line connecting bow of lifeboat to ship — keeps boat alongside during
embarkation, released before moving away
• On-load release hooks — can release falls while load (weight of boat + persons) is on the
hooks — releases at water level
• Hydrostatic interlock — prevents accidental on-load release at height — only allows release
when boat is waterborne
Lowering Procedure — Step by Step:
21. MUSTER ALARM: Seven or more short blasts followed by one long blast on ship's whistle
and general alarm. All crew muster at their assigned lifeboat station.
22. PREPARE LIFEBOAT: Remove any boat covers. Check engine, fuel, water. Ensure painter
is secured to ship.
23. RELEASE GRIPES: Quick-release the gripes holding boat in cradle.
24. SWING OUTBOARD: Release tricing pendants — davit arms swing outboard under gravity
with boat suspended on falls.
25. EMBARKATION: When boat is at embarkation deck level — crew board via embarkation
ladder or directly. Officer last to board after accounting for all persons.
26. LOWER USING FALLS: Winch operator lowers using centrifugal brake — controlled, steady
descent.
27. WATER LEVEL: When lifeboat touches water — on-load release hooks activated — falls
released. Painter still attached.
28. CAST OFF PAINTER: Release painter — boat free from ship. Start engine. Move clear of
ship.
Hoisting — SOLAS Requirements:
• Hoisting time: lifeboat must be capable of being hoisted from water to stowed position in
MAXIMUM 30 MINUTES with full complement onboard
• Falls must have sufficient strength to support weight of fully loaded lifeboat
• Limit switches prevent overwinding at top of travel
• Winch must be capable of operating from both local and remote positions
Safety Features of Gravity Davit:
• Centrifugal brake: speed-sensitive brake on winch drum — as lowering speed increases,
brake applies — prevents uncontrolled free fall — most important safety feature
• Hydrostatic interlock on on-load release: prevents accidental release of falls at height — only
operates when boat is waterborne
• Limit switches: prevent overwinding of falls during hoisting
• Hand brake: manual backup in case of power failure
• Anti-reeve device: prevents falls from jumping off sheaves

B) Free Fall Lifeboat — Introduction
A free fall lifeboat is a fundamentally different concept from the conventional davit-launched lifeboat.
Instead of being lowered by falls and davits, the free fall lifeboat is positioned on an inclined ramp at
the stern of the ship. When released, it slides down the ramp and enters the water as a projectile —
the crew inside experience significant deceleration forces during water entry. The lifeboat hull is
specially designed to withstand these forces.
Free fall lifeboats are mandatory on bulk carriers and oil tankers built after certain dates. The
rationale is that in a catastrophic event (structural failure, rapid flooding), a conventional lifeboat
may not be launchable — the free fall lifeboat can be released quickly even as the ship is sinking or
capsizing.

3. SAFETY OF NAVIGATION — BNWAS, LRIT AND VDR
Asked in: 2019/JAN, 2019/APR, 2019/JUL, 2019/DEC, 2021/MAR, 2021/NOV, 2022/APR, 2022/JUN, 2023/SEP,
2025/FEB, 2025/JUN, 2025/JUL, 2025/OCT — asked in almost every paper
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter V — Safety of Navigation | Reg 19 (navigational systems and
equipment) | Reg 19-1 (LRIT) | Reg 19-2 (BNWAS) | Reg 20 (VDR) | Reg 20-1 (S-VDR)
Introduction — SOLAS Chapter V
SOLAS Chapter V deals with Safety of Navigation — the requirements for navigational equipment,
watchkeeping and safety procedures to ensure ships can navigate safely at all times. Chapter V
applies to ALL ships on ALL voyages — it is one of the few SOLAS chapters that applies even to
small vessels and domestic voyages.
Three of the most important and frequently examined items from Chapter V are BNWAS (Bridge
Navigational Watch Alarm System), LRIT (Long Range Identification and Tracking) and VDR/S-VDR
(Voyage Data Recorder). These systems were introduced in response to accidents and incidents
that revealed the need for better monitoring of bridge watchkeeping and improved ability to
investigate marine casualties.
A) BNWAS — Bridge Navigational Watch Alarm System
Asked in: 6 marks in most papers
EXAM QUESTION: Q: Briefly discuss with respect to safety of navigation — a) Bridge
Navigation Watchkeeping Alarm System (BNWAS) (6 marks)
Background — Why BNWAS was Introduced:
Several serious maritime accidents occurred due to the officer on watch becoming incapacitated —
through medical emergency, falling asleep, or being distracted — without any alarm being raised.
The BNWAS was developed to detect such incapacitation and escalate an alarm to wake the officer
or summon assistance before the situation becomes critical.
Purpose:
BNWAS is designed to monitor the alertness of the officer of the watch (OOW) during bridge
watchkeeping. It continuously requires the OOW to prove they are conscious and alert by
acknowledging a periodic signal. Failure to acknowledge escalates through a series of alarms.
How BNWAS Works — Three Stage Escalation:
29. Stage 0: DORMANT PERIOD: System has a set dormant period (typically 3-12 minutes,
adjustable) during which no acknowledgement is required. The OOW can move around the
bridge freely during this period.
30. Stage 1: STAGE 1 ALARM — Bridge Alarm: After the dormant period, the system emits an
audible and/or visual signal on the bridge. The OOW must acknowledge this within a set
time (typically 15 seconds to 3 minutes). Acknowledgement can be by pressing a button,
moving helm controls, operating radar or chart table buttons.
31. Stage 2: STAGE 2 ALARM — Officer/Master Cabins: If Stage 1 is not acknowledged, the
alarm escalates to sound in designated cabins — typically Master, Chief Officer and at least
one other officer. These persons can then investigate and respond to the bridge.

32. Stage 3: STAGE 3 ALARM — General Alarm: If Stage 2 is also not acknowledged within the
set time, the BNWAS activates the ship's general alarm — alerting all crew to the potential
incapacitation of the bridge watch.
Acknowledgement Methods:
• Pressing dedicated acknowledgement button(s) at various positions on the bridge
• Operating helm controls — moving the wheel
• Operating radar controls
• Operating ECDIS controls
• Movement detection — some systems use infrared presence detection
SOLAS Requirements:
• Mandatory for: all ships 150 GT and above on international voyages — phased
implementation from 2011
• Must be in CONTINUOUS OPERATION during all sea watches — cannot be turned off
during watchkeeping
• Only the MASTER can switch the system to standby or off — the OOW cannot disable it
• Must have three-stage alarm escalation as described above
• Must be fail-safe — power failure should activate an alarm, not silently disable the system
• Must be approved by Administration or recognised organisation
• Cannot be disabled by the watch officer — must be done by Master
B) LRIT — Long Range Identification and Tracking
Asked in: 5 marks in most papers
EXAM QUESTION: Q: Long Range Identification and Tracking of ships (LRIT) — 5 marks
Background — Why LRIT was Introduced:
Following the terrorist attacks of September 2001, IMO recognised the need for coastal states and
flag states to be able to track ships at long range — far beyond the range of AIS (Automatic
Identification System) which is only effective to about 40-70 nm. LRIT provides a global tracking
system accessible by flag states, coastal states and port states.
Purpose:
LRIT provides automatic, mandatory position reporting from ships to shore authorities. Unlike AIS
which broadcasts to all ships and shore stations in range, LRIT transmits to an LRIT Data Centre via
satellite — the data is then made available only to authorised parties (flag state, coastal state, port
state) who have a legitimate reason to track that vessel.
How LRIT Works:
• Ship's LRIT system (typically an Inmarsat-C terminal with LRIT software) automatically polls
its GPS position
• Position, ship identity (IMO number) and date/time transmitted to LRIT Data Centre via
SATELLITE every 6 HOURS automatically
• LRIT Data Centre stores position data and makes it available to authorised users

• In emergencies: search and rescue authorities can request POLLING ON DEMAND —
position transmitted as frequently as every 15 minutes

ships at all times ships are where they should be
Coastal State Positions of ships within 1000 Monitor ships approaching their waters
nm of coastline — maritime safety and security

hours before scheduled arrival security assessment
at port

every 15 minutes pinpoint ship's location in emergency
SOLAS Requirements:
• Mandatory for: all ships on international voyages — passenger ships, cargo ships 300 GT
and above, mobile offshore drilling units
• System must be operational 24 hours a day, 7 days a week
• Ship cannot turn off LRIT without flag state authorisation — system must always transmit
• Ships must maintain LRIT equipment in working order — failure to transmit is a violation
• Implemented under SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 19-1
C) VDR and S-VDR — Voyage Data Recorder
Asked in: 5 marks in most papers
EXAM QUESTION: Q: Voyage Simplified Voyage Recorder (VDR/S-VDR) — 5 marks
Background — Why VDR was Introduced:
Before the mandatory introduction of VDRs, the investigation of marine casualties was extremely
difficult. When a ship sank or suffered a major accident, there was often no reliable record of what
happened in the minutes and hours before the accident — the bridge log could be lost, witnesses
might give conflicting accounts, and the causes of many accidents remained unknown. The VDR
was introduced to provide an objective, tamper-proof record of events — analogous to the flight
data recorder (black box) on aircraft.
Purpose:
The VDR records data from ship's systems and stores it in a protected capsule. In the event of an
accident, the capsule can be recovered and the data used to reconstruct the events leading up to
the accident. This enables accurate accident investigation, identifies root causes and helps prevent
similar accidents in future.
