4. STEERING GEAR — TESTS, DRILLS AND REQUIREMENTS
Asked in: 2023/JAN/Q9, 2024/NOV/Q9 — 6+5+5 marks (16 total)
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-1 Reg 26, 29 — Steering gear requirements and testing |
SOLAS Chapter V Reg 26 — Steering gear: testing and drills
Introduction — Why Steering Gear Safety Matters
Loss of steering control is one of the most dangerous situations a ship can face. An uncontrolled
ship can collide with other vessels, run aground, or cause environmental damage. SOLAS Chapter
II-1 specifies detailed requirements for the design and construction of steering gear — including
redundancy, power requirements and emergency arrangements. Chapter V specifies testing and
drill requirements to ensure the steering gear is always in good working order and crew are trained
to respond to steering failures.
The requirement for testing within 12 hours before departure is particularly important — many
steering gear failures could have been caught before departure if proper tests were conducted.
EXAM QUESTION: Q: With reference to the 1978 SOLAS protocol which outlines
mandatory requirements for steering gear tests and drills: a) Describe the test procedure
to be carried out within 12 hours before departure on a sea voyage (6). b) Describe the
emergency steering drills that must take place at least every 3 months (5). c) State how
often the tests in (a) and the drill in (b) should be carried out for ships which regularly
engage on voyages of short duration (5). — 16 marks | 2023/JAN/Q9, 2024/NOV/Q9
A) Test Procedure Within 12 Hours Before Departure (6 marks)
SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 26.1 requires the following checks to be carried out on every ship
before departure on every voyage. These checks must be completed within 12 hours before
departure and the results entered in the official logbook.
33. CHECK MAIN STEERING GEAR: Operate the main steering gear from the bridge. Order
helm hard over to port — verify rudder responds correctly and indicator on bridge matches
actual rudder position. Order helm hard over to starboard — verify same. Order helm to
midships — verify.
34. CHECK AUXILIARY STEERING GEAR: Switch to auxiliary steering gear. Operate from
bridge. Verify functions correctly and provides adequate control of rudder.
35. CHECK REMOTE STEERING FROM BRIDGE WINGS: Test steering control from both port
and starboard bridge wing positions. Verify control is transferred correctly and rudder
responds.
36. CHECK RUDDER ANGLE INDICATOR: Compare indicator reading at bridge with indicator
in steering gear room and actual rudder position. All three must agree at hard over positions
and midships.
37. CHECK RATE OF TURN INDICATOR: Verify functioning if fitted.
38. CHECK COMMUNICATION between bridge and steering gear room: Test all communication
systems — telephone, telegraph and any backup communication. Must be reliable two-way
communication.
39. CHECK EMERGENCY LIGHTING in steering gear room: Verify emergency lighting is
operational — important if main power fails during steering emergency.
40. CHECK HYDRAULIC OIL LEVEL: Verify oil level in hydraulic system is correct. Look for any
signs of leakage.

41. CHECK OVERRIDE CONTROLS: Verify override and bypass controls are operational and
correctly marked.
42. RECORD IN LOGBOOK: All checks, times and results recorded in official bridge logbook.
Signed by officer conducting checks.
B) Emergency Steering Drills — Every 3 Months (5 marks)
SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 26.4 requires emergency steering drills to be conducted at least
every THREE MONTHS. The purpose is to ensure all relevant officers and crew are trained to
operate the steering gear from alternative control positions in the event of loss of bridge steering
control.
43. NOTIFICATION: Master or Chief Officer notifies relevant personnel — navigating officers,
engineer officers who may operate steering gear, any crew members involved.
44. TRANSFER TO STEERING GEAR ROOM: Transfer steering control from the bridge to
LOCAL CONTROL in the steering gear room. This simulates the main failure mode — loss
of bridge control.
45. COMMUNICATION ESTABLISHED: Establish communication between bridge and steering
gear room. Officer on bridge gives helm orders by telephone or radio. Engineer or officer in
steering gear room executes orders manually on the steering gear.
46. STEERING FROM LOCAL CONTROL: Conduct steering using the local control in the
steering gear room — typically by operating hydraulic controls directly. Practice giving and
executing helm orders.
47. PRACTICE CHANGEOVER PROCEDURES: Practice changeover from main to auxiliary
steering gear, from electric to manual operation, and from bridge to aft steering — any
combination required by the muster list.
48. ALL OFFICERS AND RELEVANT CREW PARTICIPATE: The drill must include all officers
and any crew members with steering gear duties on the muster list.
49. RECORD IN LOGBOOK: Drill recorded in official logbook — date, time, participants,
observations, any deficiencies found.
C) Tests and Drills for Short Duration Voyages (5 marks)
SOLAS recognises that for ships regularly engaged in voyages of short duration — where departure
and arrival happen frequently (such as ferries, coastal vessels) — the requirement to test within 12
hours before every single departure would be excessive and impractical.
• For ships on short voyages: the pre-departure test described in (A) may be conducted AT
LEAST ONCE PER WEEK instead of before every departure
• 'Short duration' is not precisely defined in SOLAS — it is generally taken to mean voyages
where multiple departures occur within a 12-hour period
• The weekly test must be as comprehensive as the pre-departure test
• Even on short voyage ships — if there is a gap of 12 hours or more between voyages, the
full test must be done before departure
• Emergency steering drills: every 3 months — same requirement applies regardless of
voyage duration
• All tests and drills must still be recorded in the official logbook
SOLAS Construction Requirements for Steering Gear:
• Main steering gear: must put rudder from 35 degrees one side to 30 degrees other side in
NOT MORE THAN 28 SECONDS at maximum ahead service speed

• Auxiliary steering gear: must be capable of steering the ship in an emergency
• Power-operated steering gear: must have at least TWO INDEPENDENT power units
• If one power unit fails: the other must be capable of automatic starting and restoring steering
within 45 seconds
• High water level alarm in steering gear room — detects flooding
• Steering gear room: accessible from weather deck without going through interior spaces
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Pre-departure test: within 12 HOURS before departure — check main, auxiliary,
bridge wings, rudder indicators, communications
✓ Emergency steering drill: every 3 MONTHS minimum — transfer to steering gear
room local control
✓ Short voyage ships: weekly test acceptable instead of before every departure
✓ Main steering gear: 35 to 30 degrees in 28 SECONDS at max service speed —
SOLAS requirement
✓ Two independent power units required for power-operated steering
✓ Automatic restart of second unit within 45 seconds if first fails
✓ All tests and drills MUST be recorded in official logbook — PSC can check

5. ESSENTIAL ELECTRICAL SERVICES AND FIRE RESISTANT
CABLES
Asked in: 2025/FEB/Q1, 2025/JUL/Q1 — 5+5+6 marks (16 total)
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-1 Reg 41, 42, 43, 44 — Emergency electrical power |
SOLAS Chapter II-2 — Fire resistant cables for essential services | IEC 60092 Series —
Electrical installations in ships
Introduction — Why Essential Services Must Survive Fire
On a ship, fire is one of the most serious emergencies possible. Unlike on land where you can
simply run away from a burning building, at sea the crew must remain on the ship to fight the fire,
maintain critical safety systems, communicate with shore authorities and if necessary organise an
orderly abandonment. For all these activities to be possible, certain electrical services must remain
operational EVEN when there is a fire.
SOLAS Chapter II-1 specifies which electrical services are 'essential' and must remain operational
under fire conditions. Chapter II-2 specifies the requirements for cables supplying these services —
they must be fire resistant so that the cables themselves do not fail and disconnect the services
when they are most needed.
EXAM QUESTION: Q: a) State essential electrical services on board that are able to be
operable under fire conditions (5). b) Explain how electric cables for the essential services
in part (a) pass through bulkheads whilst maintaining gas tight and watertight integrity (5).
c) State the requirements for the cables which supply electrically driven emergency fire
pumps (6). — 16 marks
A) Essential Electrical Services — Must Remain Under Fire Conditions (5
marks)
Navigation Services:
• Navigation lights — required to indicate ship's position to other vessels especially at night
• All navigational aids — radar, ECDIS, GPS, echo sounder, gyrocompass — needed to
maintain situational awareness
• Daylight signalling lamp and whistle — distress signalling
Communication Services:
• GMDSS equipment — VHF radio (Channel 16 distress), MF/HF radio, EPIRB, SART —
essential for distress communication
• Internal communications — public address system for emergency announcements, bridge
telephones, engine room telegraph
• Ship-to-shore communication
Safety and Firefighting Services:
• Fire detection and alarm system — must continue to detect fire and activate alarms even in
fire conditions
• Emergency fire pump — electrically driven emergency fire pump must remain operational
• Sprinkler system pump — on ships fitted with automatic sprinklers

• Fixed firefighting system controls — CO2, foam, inert gas system activation panels
• Fire door control and indicators — closing fire doors and monitoring their status
Flooding and Damage Control:
• Emergency bilge pump — to combat flooding
• Watertight door indicators and controls — showing and operating watertight doors
• Bilge level alarms — warning of flooding in any compartment
Lifesaving:
• Emergency lighting — throughout accommodation, corridors, stairways, muster stations,
lifeboat embarkation areas, machinery spaces
• Lifeboat launching equipment — if electrically operated
• General alarm system — to warn all persons onboard
B) How Essential Service Cables Pass Through Bulkheads (5 marks)
Fire divisions (A-class and B-class bulkheads) are the ship's primary structural defence against fire
spreading from one compartment to another. These divisions are designed to maintain their integrity
(prevent fire, smoke, heat and gas from passing through) for specified periods. However, essential
service cables must pass through these bulkheads to connect equipment in different compartments.
If the cable transit is not properly sealed, the cable penetration becomes a weak point — fire, smoke
and hot gases can penetrate through the gap around the cable.
Requirements for Cable Transits Through Fire Divisions:
50. APPROVED CABLE TRANSIT SYSTEMS: Cables must pass through specially designed
and approved cable transit fittings — not simply through holes in the bulkhead. These fittings
are designed to maintain the fire rating of the bulkhead.
51. INTUMESCENT MATERIAL: The most common sealing method. The transit fitting is packed
with intumescent material — a substance that expands rapidly when exposed to heat. When
fire heats the material, it expands to fill any gaps around cables — providing a fire, smoke
and gas-tight seal that can withstand fire for the rated period (30 or 60 minutes for A-class).
52. CERAMIC WOOL / MINERAL WOOL: Used in combination with or instead of intumescent
material. High temperature resistant — maintains integrity at temperatures where
intumescent material may fail.
53. MAINTAIN SAME FIRE RATING: The transit fitting must maintain the SAME fire rating as
the bulkhead it passes through. An A-60 bulkhead requires an A-60 rated transit. Using a
lower-rated transit would create a weak point.
54. WATERTIGHT AND GAS-TIGHT INTEGRITY: In addition to fire resistance, cable transits
through watertight bulkheads must maintain WATERTIGHT INTEGRITY — no water can
pass through even under pressure. Through gas-tight bulkheads, the transit must be gas-
tight.
55. MINIMISE PENETRATIONS: SOLAS requires that penetrations through fire divisions be
kept to the ABSOLUTE MINIMUM — each penetration is a potential weak point. Cables
should be grouped and passed through as few transits as possible.
56. RECORD ON FIRE CONTROL PLAN: All cable transits through fire divisions must be
recorded on the ship's fire control plan — so firefighters know the locations of all
penetrations.
57. REGULAR INSPECTION: Cable transits must be regularly inspected — check that sealing
material has not been damaged, that cables have not been added or removed leaving gaps,
and that the transit is still correctly rated.

C) Requirements for Cables Supplying Emergency Fire Pumps (6 marks)
The emergency fire pump is a critical safety system — it provides water for firefighting when the
main fire pump is unavailable (typically because the engine room where the main pump is located is
on fire). For the emergency fire pump to be available when most needed — during a fire — its
electrical supply cable must have special properties.
• Requirement 1 — FIRE RESISTANT CABLES: The cables supplying the emergency fire
pump must be FIRE RESISTANT — they must maintain their electrical integrity and continue
to supply power even when exposed to fire. This is different from fire retardant cables which
simply do not spread flame but will eventually fail if on fire.
• Requirement 2 — SEPARATE ROUTING: The cables must be routed SEPARATELY from
the cables supplying the main fire pump and other machinery space equipment. This
ensures that a single fire event cannot destroy both the main and emergency fire pump
supplies simultaneously. The routing must keep the emergency fire pump cables away from
the engine room and any other high fire risk area.
• Requirement 3 — ROUTE AWAY FROM HIGH-RISK AREAS: Cables must be routed away
from areas likely to be involved in fire — engine room, galley, paint store. Preferred routing is
through accessible deck spaces and accommodation areas which have lower fire risk.
• Requirement 4 — CLEARLY IDENTIFIED: Emergency fire pump cables must be clearly
and distinctively marked throughout their length so they can be identified during
maintenance and inspection.
• Requirement 5 — INDEPENDENCE FROM MAIN MACHINERY SPACE: The emergency
fire pump and its electrical supply must be completely independent of the main machinery
space — the pump must be operable even if the engine room is completely inaccessible due
to fire.
• Requirement 6 — POWERED FROM EMERGENCY SWITCHBOARD: The emergency fire
pump must be powered from the EMERGENCY SWITCHBOARD — so it receives power
from the emergency generator if main power fails.
• Requirement 7 — EMERGENCY SWITCHBOARD LOCATION: The emergency
switchboard and emergency generator are located ABOVE THE BULKHEAD DECK outside
the engine room — ensuring they remain accessible even when the engine room is involved
in fire.

6. SHORE ELECTRICAL SUPPLY CONNECTION
Asked in: 2023/FEB/Q1, 2023/APR/Q3, 2023/JUN/Q3, 2025/SEP/Q3, 2025/NOV/Q3 — 8+8 marks (16 total)
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-1 Reg 11 — Shore connection | IEC 60092-502 — Electrical
installations in ships: tankers — special features | IEC 60309 — Plugs, socket-outlets and
couplers for industrial purposes (international shore connection standard)
Introduction — Shore Electrical Supply on Ships
When a ship is in port, the main diesel generators onboard can be shut down and the ship's
electrical power supplied from a shore connection. This provides significant benefits — it reduces
fuel consumption, eliminates exhaust emissions in port (increasingly important in ports with strict
environmental regulations), reduces noise and vibration, and allows generators to be serviced
without causing a blackout.
However, connecting shore power is not simply plugging in a cable. The shore supply must be
compatible with the ship's electrical system — same voltage, same frequency and same phase
sequence. Failure to verify these before connecting can cause serious damage to electrical
equipment and create safety hazards. SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 11 specifies requirements for
the shore connection arrangement.
EXAM QUESTION: Q: With reference to the provision of a shore electrical supply to a ship:
a) Sketch an arrangement for taking AC shore supply and checks to be carried out prior
taking shore connection (8). b) Describe the methods of safely connecting the
arrangement sketched in (a) to the shore supply (8). — 16 marks
A) Arrangement and Pre-Connection Checks (8 marks)
Components of Shore Connection Arrangement (Sketch Description):
• Shore power cable — heavy duty flexible cable from shore socket to ship. Rating must be
sufficient for full ship load.
• International shore connection socket/inlet — standardised flange fitting on ship's side. IEC
60309 standard connection.
• Shore connection box on deck — contains the ship-side connection point, protective cover,
cable support.
• Isolation switch/circuit breaker on ship side — allows shore supply to be isolated without
disconnecting cable.
• Voltmeter — shows incoming shore voltage before connection to main switchboard.
• Frequency meter — shows shore supply frequency.
• Phase sequence indicator — confirms phase rotation matches ship's system.
• Synchroscope or synchronising panel — for parallel operation with ship's generators.
• Shore supply circuit breaker on main switchboard — the final switch that connects shore
power to ship's bus bars.
• Reverse power relay — prevents ship's power from feeding back to shore grid accidentally.
• Earth connection — safety earth from shore to ship's hull.
Checks Before Taking Shore Connection:
58. Check 1: VERIFY SHORE VOLTAGE: Check that the shore supply voltage matches the
ship's system voltage. Common mismatches: 380V shore / 440V ship or 440V shore / 380V

ship. Even small voltage differences can cause problems. Check using voltmeter at shore
connection box before proceeding.
59. Check 2: VERIFY SHORE FREQUENCY: Confirm shore supply frequency matches ship's
system. 50 Hz (Europe, India, most of Asia) vs 60 Hz (USA, Japan). Running 50 Hz
equipment on 60 Hz supply causes motors to run faster than designed — overheating and
mechanical damage. Running 60 Hz equipment on 50 Hz causes motors to run slower —
reduced ventilation, overheating.
60. Check 3: CHECK PHASE SEQUENCE: Verify the phase rotation (A-B-C sequence) of the
shore supply matches the ship's system. Incorrect phase sequence causes all three-phase
motors to run in REVERSE direction — dangerous for pumps, compressors, fans. Use
phase sequence indicator or small test motor.
61. Check 4: INSPECT CABLE CONDITION: Check the shore cable for physical damage —
cuts, abrasion, crushing, bare conductors. Check cable rating is appropriate for load. Check
all connectors and plugs are undamaged and correctly rated.
62. Check 5: ENSURE EARTH CONNECTION: Verify that the earth (protective conductor)
connection will be made — check earth continuity of cable. The earth MUST be connected
before any live conductors are energised.
63. Check 6: CHECK SHIP'S GENERATOR STATUS: Decide whether ship's generators will be
shut down (transfer to shore only) or run in parallel with shore. If shutting down, ensure no
essential services will be interrupted. If paralleling, prepare synchronising equipment.
64. Check 7: CHECK REVERSE POWER RELAY: Ensure reverse power relay is set and
operational — will trip shore supply circuit breaker if any power backfeeds to shore.
B) Safe Connection Procedure (8 marks)
Procedure for Transfer to Shore Power (Shutting Down Ship's Generators):
65. PREPARE SHIP: Reduce ship's generator load to minimum. Ensure all non-essential loads
are shed. Inform engine room.
66. CONNECT EARTH FIRST: Connect the earth conductor between shore supply and ship's
hull BEFORE making any live connections. This prevents static charge buildup and ensures
personnel protection.
67. CONNECT CABLE: Connect the shore power cable — earth conductor first, then live
conductors. Ensure all connections are tight — loose connections cause arcing and
overheating.
68. VERIFY PARAMETERS: At shore connection box, measure and confirm: voltage correct,
frequency correct, phase sequence correct.
69. CLOSE SHORE ISOLATING SWITCH: Close the isolating switch on the ship's shore
connection box — shore voltage now appears at ship-side circuit breaker but not yet
connected to bus bars.
70. PARALLEL WITH GENERATORS (if applicable): If running generators in parallel during
transfer — use synchroscope to match shore voltage, frequency and phase angle to running
generator before closing shore circuit breaker.
71. CLOSE SHORE CIRCUIT BREAKER ON SWITCHBOARD: Close the shore supply circuit
breaker on the main switchboard — shore power now connected to bus bars.
72. TRANSFER LOAD: Gradually increase load on shore supply while reducing generator load
— or in one step if not paralleling.
73. OPEN GENERATOR CIRCUIT BREAKER: Once load transferred, open generator circuit
breaker and shut down generator.
74. MONITOR: Monitor shore supply voltage, frequency and current continuously — shore
power can vary or be interrupted without warning.
Important Safety Points:

• NEVER connect shore supply without first verifying voltage, frequency and phase sequence
— mismatches cause equipment damage and safety hazards
• EARTH FIRST — always connect earth conductor before live conductors — disconnect live
conductors before earth
• Phase sequence error causes ALL motors to reverse — including bilge pumps, fire pumps
— serious safety risk
• Post WARNING SIGNS clearly visible: 'SHORE POWER CONNECTED — DO NOT START
GENERATORS' — prevents accidental parallel connection
• Maintain a WATCH on shore supply throughout port stay — shore power can fail without
warning
• When disconnecting: reverse the procedure — restore generator supply, transfer load, then
disconnect shore
• KEEP RECORDS: Log all connections and disconnections with times in machinery logbook
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Always verify THREE things before connecting: Voltage, Frequency, Phase
sequence
✓ EARTH FIRST — connect earth before live, disconnect live before earth
✓ Phase sequence error: ALL motors run in REVERSE — dangerous
✓ Reverse power relay: prevents ship's generators accidentally supplying shore grid
✓ Post WARNING SIGNS: shore power connected — do not start generators
✓ Monitor continuously in port — shore power can fail without warning
✓ IEC 60309 — standard international shore connection plug and socket specification
MEMORY AID: Shore Connection Checks
V-F-P-C-E-Warning: Voltage, Frequency, Phase sequence, Cable condition, Earth first,
Warning signs posted

7. PORT STATE CONTROL (PSC)
Asked in: 2024/JAN/Q7, 2024/MAR/Q7, 2025/MAR/Q7 — 8+8 marks (16 total)
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter I Reg 19 — Control of ships by port states | Paris MOU, Tokyo
MOU, Indian Ocean MOU, Black Sea MOU — Regional PSC agreements | IMO Res.
A.1120(30) — Procedures for Port State Control, 2017
Introduction — Port State Control
Port State Control (PSC) is the inspection regime that allows any country (port state) to inspect
foreign ships calling at its ports to ensure they meet international maritime safety, environmental
and labour standards. PSC acts as the last line of defence against substandard ships that may have
evaded the oversight of their flag state.
The concept of PSC arises from the fact that while flag states are responsible for ensuring their
ships meet international standards, not all flag states exercise effective oversight. Ships may be
registered in countries with minimal maritime administration. PSC allows the port country to enforce
standards on ships visiting its ports, regardless of flag state.
PSC inspections are conducted by PSC Officers (PSCOs) — trained marine surveyors employed by
port state maritime authorities. They board ships in port and conduct inspections of various aspects
of the ship's safety, equipment, documentation and manning.

8. CLASSIFICATION SOCIETY — ROLE, ESP AND CONDITION
OF CLASS
Asked in: 2024/JAN/Q7 — 6+5+5 marks (16 total)
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter I — Surveys and Certificates | IMO Resolution A.739(18) —
Guidelines for the authorisation of organisations acting on behalf of the Administration | IACS
— International Association of Classification Societies
Introduction — What is a Classification Society
A classification society is a non-governmental, non-profit (in most cases) technical organisation that
establishes and maintains technical standards for the construction and operation of ships, and
carries out surveys to verify that ships meet these standards. Classification is voluntary —
shipowners choose to have their vessels classed — but in practice, unclassed ships cannot obtain
insurance, flag state certificates or trading rights.
Classification societies also act as Recognised Organisations (ROs) on behalf of flag states — they
carry out statutory surveys and issue SOLAS and MARPOL certificates on behalf of flag state
administrations that do not have the technical capacity to do this themselves. This makes them
central to the entire framework of maritime safety certification.
The major classification societies are members of IACS — the International Association of
Classification Societies — which sets common standards and quality requirements for member
societies.
EXAM QUESTION: Q: Write short notes on: a) Role of Classification Society acting as
Recognised Organisation (6). b) Enhanced Survey Programme (ESP) and its applicability
(5). c) Condition of Class (COC) (5). — 2024/JAN/Q7
A) Role of Classification Society as Recognised Organisation (RO) (6 marks)
What is a Recognised Organisation:
Under SOLAS Chapter I Regulation 6, flag states can authorise classification societies to act on
their behalf — to carry out surveys and issue certificates. These authorised societies are called
Recognised Organisations (ROs). The flag state remains responsible for the ships in its register, but
delegates the technical work to the RO.
Core Functions of a Classification Society:
75. Function 1: DEVELOP RULES AND STANDARDS: Classification societies develop
comprehensive technical rules for ship design, construction and equipment. These rules
cover hull structure, stability, machinery, electrical systems, fire protection and all other
aspects of ship safety. Rules are based on research, operating experience and engineering
best practice.
76. Function 2: SURVEY DURING CONSTRUCTION: Classification surveyors oversee the
construction of ships to verify they are built in accordance with the classification rules. Key
construction stages are inspected: keel laying, frame erection, launching, machinery
installation, testing before delivery.
77. Function 3: ISSUE CLASS CERTIFICATE: When a ship is found to meet all classification
requirements, the society issues a CLASS CERTIFICATE. This confirms the ship is built and
maintained to the society's standards. The class certificate is renewed through periodic
surveys.

78. Function 4: PERIODIC CLASS SURVEYS: Classification societies conduct ongoing
surveys throughout the ship's life — annual surveys, intermediate surveys and special (five-
yearly) surveys. These verify the ship maintains its class condition — hull, machinery and
equipment continue to meet the standards.
79. Function 5: STATUTORY SURVEYS AS RO: Acting as RO for flag states, classification
societies conduct the statutory surveys required by SOLAS, MARPOL and Load Lines
conventions — and issue the corresponding certificates (SOLAS safety certificates, IOPP
certificate, Load Line certificate) on behalf of the flag state.
80. Function 6: TECHNICAL EXPERTISE AND ADVICE: Classification societies provide
technical advice to shipowners, designers and flag states on all aspects of ship design,
construction and operation. This expertise draws on the society's extensive experience
surveying thousands of ships.
Major IACS Member Classification Societies:
• Lloyd's Register (LR) — United Kingdom | Bureau Veritas (BV) — France | DNV (Det Norske
Veritas) — Norway
• American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) — USA | ClassNK (Nippon Kaiji Kyokai) — Japan
• RINA (Registro Italiano Navale) — Italy | ClassKR (Korean Register) — South Korea
• Indian Register of Shipping (IRS) — India | China Classification Society (CCS) — China
B) Enhanced Survey Programme (ESP) (5 marks)
Introduction:
The Enhanced Survey Programme was introduced by IACS in response to a series of catastrophic
structural failures of ageing bulk carriers and oil tankers in the late 1980s and early 1990s, which
resulted in significant loss of life. The investigation found that corrosion of hull structure in critical
areas — particularly cargo holds and ballast tanks — had gone undetected through standard
surveys. ESP introduced more rigorous and systematic inspection of these areas in older vessels.
Applies to: Bulk carriers and oil tankers that are over 10 YEARS OLD at their class renewal (5-
yearly) survey
Authority: IACS Unified Requirement Z10 (bulk carriers) and Z10.1 (oil tankers)
What ESP Involves — Additional Requirements Over Standard Survey:
• THICKNESS MEASUREMENTS: Comprehensive measurement of hull plating, frames and
longitudinals in all cargo holds and ballast tanks. Measurements taken at representative
locations and compared against original thickness to determine corrosion rates. Areas with
excessive corrosion identified for renewal or monitoring.
• CLOSE-UP SURVEYS of CRITICAL STRUCTURAL AREAS: Surveyors physically enter
tanks and holds to inspect structure at close range — not just visual inspection from a
distance. Particular attention to: upper wing tanks, lower wing tanks, frames, hopper tanks,
web frames.
• COATING CONDITION ASSESSMENT: Systematic inspection of protective coatings in
ballast tanks and cargo holds. Coating breakdown is the primary cause of accelerated
corrosion. Condition rated: Good, Fair, Poor. Poor coating triggers more frequent surveys.
• SURVEY STATUS REPORT: A comprehensive report maintained for each vessel showing
all survey findings, thickness measurements and recommendations. Available to port states
and other interested parties on request.
• SURVEY PLANNING MEETING: Before ESP survey, a meeting between ship's officers and
surveyor to plan the survey, identify areas of concern, review previous findings.

• REPORTING AND RECORDS: All ESP findings, including photographs, thickness
measurements and coating assessments, formally documented and retained in the ship's
class records.
C) Condition of Class (COC) (5 marks)
Introduction:
A Condition of Class is a qualification attached to a ship's class certificate requiring the shipowner to
carry out specific work or submit additional information within a specified time limit. It is used when a
surveyor finds something that requires attention but does not immediately threaten the ship's safety
to the extent of requiring immediate suspension of class.
When a COC is Raised:
• A deficiency, damage or deterioration is found during a survey that needs rectification, but
the ship is not in immediate danger
• Outstanding maintenance items identified during survey that could lead to safety issues if not
addressed
• A component or structure has deteriorated to a level requiring repair before the next periodic
survey
• Information is required by the classification society — e.g. stability calculations, structural
analysis
Effect of a Condition of Class:
• The ship RETAINS CLASS but with the condition attached — the class certificate remains
valid
• The ship can continue to trade but MUST complete the required work by the stated deadline
• The COC is recorded in the classification society's register — visible to insurers, charterers,
port states
• PSC inspectors are notified of outstanding COCs — likely to trigger a more detailed
inspection
• If the COC is not cleared by the deadline: CLASS IS SUSPENDED — the class certificate
becomes invalid
• Class suspension means: statutory certificates issued by the society (SOLAS, MARPOL)
also become invalid — ship cannot legally trade
• To restore class: the required work must be completed and verified by a surveyor — then
class suspension is lifted
Difference Between COC and Recommendation:
• COC: mandatory — must be completed by deadline or class is suspended
• Recommendation: advisory — surveyor suggests improvement but no deadline, no class
consequence if not done
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Classification society: sets rules + surveys construction + issues class certificate +
statutory surveys as RO
✓ RO = Recognised Organisation — authorised by flag state to issue SOLAS,
MARPOL certificates

✓ ESP: bulk carriers and tankers over 10 YEARS OLD — thickness measurements,
close-up surveys, coating inspection
✓ ESP introduced after bulk carrier structural failures — fatal accidents due to

✓ COC: deficiency found — ship can trade but MUST rectify by deadline
✓ COC not cleared = CLASS SUSPENDED = statutory certificates invalid = cannot
trade

1. ENCLOSED SPACES — ENTRY PROCEDURES & HAZARDS
Asked in: 2018/FEB, 2018/AUG, 2018/SEP, 2018/OCT, 2018/NOV, 2018/DEC, 2019/JAN, 2019/FEB, 2019/MAR,
2019/APR, 2019/JUN, 2019/JUL, 2019/SEP, 2019/OCT, 2020/MAR, 2021/JAN, 2021/MAR, 2021/JUL, 2021/NOV,
2021/DEC, 2022/JAN, 2022/FEB, 2022/APR, 2022/JUN, 2023/DEC, 2025/JUN — MOST FREQUENTLY ASKED
TOPIC
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter III Reg 19 | IMO Resolution A.1050(27) — Revised
recommendations for entering enclosed spaces | Code of Safe Working Practices (COSWP)
A) Definition of Enclosed Space
An enclosed space is a space that has limited openings for entry and exit, inadequate ventilation,
and is not designed for continuous worker occupancy — and which may have or develop a
hazardous atmosphere.
B) Examples of Enclosed Spaces Onboard
Category Examples
Cargo spaces Cargo holds, cargo tanks, ballast tanks, void spaces
Machinery spaces Double bottom tanks, cofferdams, duct keels, pipe tunnels
Service spaces Chain lockers, store rooms, paint lockers, pump rooms
Deck spaces Fore peak, after peak, emergency generator room (if poorly
ventilated)
C) Hazards of Enclosed Spaces
• Oxygen deficiency — oxygen below 19.5% causes dizziness, unconsciousness, death.
Normal air = 20.9% O2
• Oxygen enrichment — above 23.5% O2 increases fire and explosion risk dramatically
• Toxic gases — H2S (hydrogen sulphide), CO (carbon monoxide), SO2, hydrocarbon
vapours
• Flammable gases — methane, hydrocarbon vapours — explosion risk
• Inert gas atmosphere — CO2 or nitrogen used to preserve cargo — immediately fatal
• Biological activity — rotting cargo consumes oxygen and produces toxic gases
• Chemical reactions — cargo reacting with steel, moisture, or residues producing gas
• Residual cargo — chemical vapours from previous cargo even if tanks appear clean
• Poor visibility — limited lighting, smoke, or dust
• Physical hazards — falls, restricted movement, entrapment
D) Checks Before Entry — Atmosphere Testing
The atmosphere MUST be tested before entry and continuously monitored during work:
Parameter Safe Range Action if Outside Range
Oxygen (O2) 19.5% to 23.5% Do NOT enter — ventilate and retest
Flammable gas (LEL) Below 1% LEL Do NOT enter — ventilate and retest

Toxic gases (H2S) Below 1 ppm (short Do NOT enter — ventilate and retest
exposure)
CO Below 35 ppm TWA Do NOT enter — ventilate and retest
E) Safety Precautions Before Entry — Full Procedure
1. Obtain PERMIT TO WORK — signed by responsible officer (Chief Officer or Chief Engineer)
2. ATMOSPHERE TESTING — test with calibrated gas detector for O2, flammable gas, toxic
gases
3. VENTILATION — thoroughly ventilate the space for minimum 24 hours before entry where
possible
4. ISOLATE all pipelines, valves, mechanical equipment — Lock Out Tag Out (LOTO)
5. COMMUNICATION — establish reliable communication system between entrant and
standby person
6. STANDBY PERSON — trained person stationed at entrance AT ALL TIMES — never left
unattended
7. RESCUE EQUIPMENT ready at entrance — BA set, lifeline, rescue harness, first aid kit
8. PERSONNEL BRIEFING — all entrants briefed on hazards, procedures, emergency signals
9. ENTRY — minimum two persons (one entrant, one standby) — never enter alone
10. CONTINUOUS MONITORING — atmosphere tested continuously during work with personal
gas detector

A) Gravity Davit Arrangement
Asked in: 2024/SEP/Q8, 2025/OCT/Q8 — 16 marks (8+8)
Components:
• Davit arms — curved steel arms that swing outboard when released
• Tricing pendants — hold lifeboat against ship's side in stowed position
• Gripes — secure lifeboat in housed position
• Falls (wire ropes) — support lifeboat during lowering and hoisting

• Limit switches — stop winch at correct positions
• Bowsing tackle — pulls boat to embarkation position

Lowering Procedure:
20. Sound alarm — crew muster at lifeboat station
21. Release gripes — boat free to swing outboard
22. Release tricing pendants — boat swings to outboard position
23. Board the lifeboat — crew embark via embarkation ladder
24. Release painter — boat free from ship
25. Lower using falls — centrifugal brake controls speed
26. At water — release fall hooks — boat free
27. Start engine — move clear of ship
Raising (Hoisting) — SOLAS Requirements:
• Hoisting time: lifeboat must be hoisted from water to stowed position in MAXIMUM 30
MINUTES with full complement
• Falls must be capable of raising lifeboat with full complement
• Limit switches prevent overwinding
Safety Features of Gravity Davit:
• Centrifugal brake — automatically controls lowering speed, prevents free fall
• Limit switches — stop winch at correct upper and lower positions
• On-load release — can release falls at water level with load on
• Off-load release — backup release when no load on falls
• Gripes with quick release — fast release in emergency

How BNWAS Works:
28. System requires officer on watch to acknowledge a signal at regular intervals
29. If officer does not acknowledge within set time — STAGE 1 ALARM sounds on bridge
(audible)
30. If still not acknowledged — STAGE 2 ALARM sounds in designated cabins (Master, Officers)
31. If still no response — STAGE 3 ALARM — general alarm throughout ship
Acknowledgement Methods:

• Moving the helm or engine controls (automatic detection of movement)
• Pressing button at chart table or radar
SOLAS Requirements for BNWAS:

• Must be in operation during all sea watches
• Cannot be switched off by officer on watch — only Master can disable

Asked in: 2023/FEB/Q1, 2023/APR/Q3, 2023/JUN/Q3, 2025/SEP/Q3, 2025/NOV/Q3 — 8+8 marks (16 total)
Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-1 Reg 11 — Shore connection | IEC 60092-502 — Electrical
installations in ships
A) Arrangement for Taking AC Shore Supply — Sketch Description
Components of Shore Connection Arrangement:
• International Shore Connection socket — standard flange connection
• Shore supply cable — flexible heavy duty cable from shore to ship
• Ship's shore connection box — mounted on ship's deck
• Isolating switch/circuit breaker — on ship side
• Voltmeter — to verify shore voltage before connecting
• Synchroscope or synchronising panel — to match frequency and phase before paralleling
• Ship's main switchboard — where shore supply is connected
• Reverse power relay — prevents backfeed to shore
B) Checks Before Taking Shore Connection
53. Verify SHORE SUPPLY VOLTAGE matches ship's system voltage — typically 440V or
6.6kV
54. Verify SHORE SUPPLY FREQUENCY matches — 50Hz or 60Hz
55. Check PHASE SEQUENCE — must match ship's system (ABC sequence)
56. Inspect CABLE condition — no damage, correct rating for current
57. Ensure shore EARTH CONNECTION is made before energising
58. Check ship's MAIN BREAKER is OPEN — generators not running in parallel with shore
during connection
59. Verify POLARITY is correct
60. Check ISOLATION of ship's generators before connecting shore supply
C) Safe Connection Procedure
61. STOP all ship's generators OR prepare for synchronisation
62. Connect shore cable to SHIP'S SHORE CONNECTION BOX — check tightness
63. Earth connection made FIRST before live conductors
64. Check voltage and frequency on incoming shore supply
65. Close ship's SHORE SUPPLY BREAKER
66. If paralleling with generators — SYNCHRONISE first (match voltage, frequency, phase
angle)
67. Transfer load to shore supply — close shore breaker, open generator breaker
68. Monitor voltage and current — ensure within limits
69. Secure cable — prevent tripping hazard
D) Important Safety Points
• NEVER connect shore supply without checking voltage and frequency — mismatch causes
equipment damage

• Earth first, live last — always connect earth before energising
• Phase sequence check — reversed phases cause motors to run backwards
• Reverse power relay must be enabled — prevents ship's power feeding back to shore grid
• Post warning signs — SHORE SUPPLY CONNECTED — so generators not started
accidentally
• Maintain watch on shore supply throughout — shore power can be interrupted without
warning

Earth connection
✓ EARTH FIRST before live conductors — always

✓ Reverse power relay: prevents backfeed to shore grid

Definition: A condition attached to the class certificate requiring the shipowner to carry out specific

• Emergency procedures — step by step actions for each type of emergency

This is the most important part of Clause 5 — Master's Overriding Authority:

What Overriding Authority Means
• Master can OVERRULE company instructions if safety or environment is at risk
• No commercial pressure from company can override Master's safety decisions

BRIEF ANSWER — Annex I Key Facts
• Applies to: All ships of 400 GT and above; oil tankers 150 GT and above
• Key document: IOPP Certificate (International Oil Pollution Prevention Certificate)
• ORB: Oil Record Book — Part I (machinery spaces), Part II (cargo/ballast for tankers)
• Discharge limit: 15 ppm for machinery space bilge water (with OWS + OCM)
• Special areas: Zero discharge — Mediterranean, Baltic, Black Sea, Red Sea, Antarctic, etc.
• Oil tankers: 30 litres per nautical mile limit for clean ballast discharge
DETAILED ANSWER
A. IOPP Certificate — Supplement Record (7 marks):
The IOPP Certificate is issued to ships over 400 GT. The supplement (record of construction and
equipment) contains:
• Ship particulars — name, flag, GT, IMO number, type
• Machinery space details — capacity and type of OWS (Oil Water Separator), capacity of
bilge holding tank
• Oil Discharge Monitoring and Control (ODMC) system details
• For tankers — crude oil washing equipment, inert gas system, segregated/dedicated clean
ballast tanks
• Slop tank capacity and arrangements
• Details of oil discharge monitoring equipment for cargo/ballast
• Retention of oil on board capacity
• For bulk carriers — arrangements to prevent oil contamination of ballast water
B. Engine Room Provisions under MARPOL Annex I — Large Ocean-going Vessels (7
marks):
• Oil Water Separator (OWS): Required on all ships 400 GT and above; must reduce oil
content to 15 ppm
• Oil Content Meter (OCM): Continuous monitoring; automatic shutoff if exceeds 15 ppm
• Bilge holding tank: To retain oily bilge water for discharge at port reception facilities
• Oil Record Book Part I: Must record every operation involving bilge water, fuel oil, lubricating
oil
• Standard Discharge Connection: For transfer of oily residues to reception facilities
• Sludge tank: For retention of sludge from purifiers/separators; minimum capacity = 1% of
fuel oil bunker capacity
• 15 ppm alarm and automatic stopping device on the OWS overboard discharge
• The OWS must be type approved and certified
C. Oil Spill During Bunkering — Procedure (16 marks):
Immediate Actions:
• Stop bunkering immediately — close all valves
• Alert Master and Chief Engineer
• Sound the general alarm if major spill
• Deploy absorbent booms/pads around the spill area on deck

• Prevent oil from entering sea — close freeboard openings, scuppers, sea chest
• Use oil dispersants only with port authority approval
Notification Requirements:
• Notify port authority / coast guard immediately
• Notify flag state administration
• Notify shipowner / company DPA (Designated Person Ashore)
• Complete Oil Record Book entry for the incident
Post-Incident Actions:
• Make entry in the Official Log Book
• Prepare SOPEP (Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan) incident report
• Cooperate fully with port authority investigation
• Resume bunkering only with port authority permission after root cause is fixed
• Review SOPEP procedures to prevent recurrence
D. Oil/Water Separator — Sketch Description (8 marks):
• First stage: Gravity separation — coarse oil particles rise to top, collected in oil collection
chamber
• Second stage: Coalescing filter — fine oil droplets coalesce on filter material, rise and collect
• 15 ppm monitor continuously measures oil content of effluent
• If reading exceeds 15 ppm: automatic 3-way valve diverts flow back to bilge tank, overboard
valve closes
• If reading is below 15 ppm: 3-way valve opens overboard discharge
• All operations must be recorded in Oil Record Book Part I
• Effect of temperature: Higher temperature reduces oil viscosity, improves separation
• Effect of density: Greater density difference between oil and water = better separation
E. Oil Monitoring System for Ballast/Bilge Discharges (8+4+4 marks):
• Inputs recorded: flow rate, total quantity discharged, ship position (GPS), date/time,
overboard/bilge tank valve status, oil content reading (ppm)
• The system generates an automatic printout that forms part of the ORB
• Difficulties: Sensor fouling by emulsified oil, temperature fluctuations causing false readings,
calibration drift, electrical interference, maintenance requirements in harsh marine
environment
F. Pump Room Bottom Protection (6 marks):
• Required under MARPOL Annex I for oil tankers
• Double bottom under pump room to contain any oil leaked from pump glands/pipes
• Bilge suction system in pump room to recover any leakage
• Bilge level alarms fitted
• Pump room must be gas-tight from the rest of the ship
• Fire detection system in pump room
G. IBC Code — Chemical Tankers (4 marks):
• IBC = International Bulk Chemical Code
• Applies to: Chemical tankers carrying noxious liquid substances in bulk
• Certificates issued: Certificate of Fitness for Carriage of Dangerous Chemicals in Bulk (CoF)
• Issued to: Chemical tankers (Type I, II, III based on cargo hazard level)

• Type I: Maximum environmental/safety hazard — most stringent requirements
• Type II: Significant hazard — moderate requirements
• Type III: Sufficient hazard — least stringent
💡 EXAM TIP: For engine room provisions, always mention OWS, OCM, ORB, sludge tank, and 15
ppm limit. These are the five key items examiners look for.

2. MARPOL Annex II — Noxious Liquid Substances (NLS)
[ 16 MARKS (8+8) ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 With respect to MARPOL 73/78, Annex-II, Noxious liquid chemicals are divided into
categories. a) State the number of categories, and what does each category signify. (8)
b) State the requirement of procedures and Arrangements Manual, and what information
is available. (8) [Feb 2025, Sep 2023, Feb 2024]
Q2 As per Annex II of MARPOL. Describe categories in which substances are divided. (8)
Give conditions under which they can be discharged outside special areas. (8) [Dec
2024, Feb 2023]
BRIEF ANSWER — Annex II Key Facts
• Applies to: Chemical tankers carrying NLS in bulk
• 4 categories: X, Y, Z, OS (Other Substances)
• Key document: NLS Certificate (Noxious Liquid Substances Certificate)
• P&A Manual: Procedures and Arrangements Manual — mandatory document
• Cargo Record Book: Must record all NLS cargo/ballast operations
DETAILED ANSWER
A. Four Categories of NLS (8 marks):
Category Description & Discharge Conditions
Category X Greatest hazard to marine environment or human health. DISCHARGE
PROHIBITED at sea. Must be discharged to port reception facilities
only.
Category Y Hazard to marine environment or human health. Discharge only
allowed: >12 nm from land, >25 m water depth, ship underway >7
knots, max 1 cubic metre per nautical mile, tank washed and washings
to reception facility first.
Category Z Minor hazard. Discharge allowed: >12 nm from land, >25 m depth, ship
underway >7 knots.
OS (Other Substances) Assessed as presenting no hazard. Unregulated — may be discharged
at sea without restrictions. Listed in Appendix III of Annex II.
Key Points for All Categories:
• Tank prewash required for Cat X, Y before departure from unloading port
• Prewash residues must be discharged to port reception facility
• Ship must be fitted with Cargo Record Book (CRB) — record all loading, discharge, cleaning
operations
• All operations must be done as per the P&A Manual
• In special areas (Baltic, Black Sea, Antarctic): Cat X, Y, Z — NO discharge allowed
B. Procedures and Arrangements (P&A) Manual (8 marks):
• Mandatory document required on all NLS tankers
• Approved by the flag state administration

• Must be carried on board at all times
The P&A Manual must contain:
• Ship's particulars and the NLS cargo systems description
• Description of cargo pumping, stripping and ventilation systems
• Tank cleaning procedures for each cargo type
• Prewash procedures and requirements by category
• Procedures for discharge to sea and to reception facilities
• Methods to determine water content of slops before discharge
• List of all approved NLS cargoes the ship is certified to carry
• Procedure for completing the Cargo Record Book
• Emergency procedures for cargo spills
💡 EXAM TIP: The 8+8 mark split is very common. First 8 = categories with conditions. Second 8 =
P&A Manual contents. Learn both equally well.

3. MARPOL Annex IV — Prevention of Pollution by Sewage
[ 16 MARKS (8+8) — VERY FREQUENTLY ASKED ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 With reference to MARPOL Annex IV: a) Draw a biological sewage treatment plant and
explain the principle of operation. (8) b) Periodical maintenance and checks and tests
required to be done to verify the effectiveness of the above system. (8) [Dec 2025, Jun
2025, Nov 2023, Mar 2024, Jul 2019, Apr 2019, Oct 2019, Dec 2019, Jan 2021, Mar
2021, Dec 2021, Jul 2022]
BRIEF ANSWER — Annex IV Key Facts
• Applies to: Ships of 400 GT and above; ships certified to carry 15 or more persons
• Sewage = waste from WCs, urinals, medical premises, drainage from spaces with live
animals
• Discharge requirements: 3 nm if treated; 12 nm if untreated; comminuted/disinfected — 3 nm
• Equipment options: Sewage treatment plant (STP) OR holding tank OR
comminuting/disinfecting system
• Special areas: No discharge — Baltic Sea is a MARPOL Annex IV Special Area (PSSA)
DETAILED ANSWER
A. Biological Sewage Treatment Plant — Principle of Operation (8 marks):
A biological STP uses aerobic bacteria to break down organic matter in sewage. The process has
three stages:
Stage 1 — Aeration Chamber (Biological Treatment):
• Raw sewage enters the aeration chamber
• Air blower supplies continuous air to maintain aerobic conditions
• Aerobic bacteria digest and break down organic matter (BOD reduction)
• Sewage is agitated to keep bacteria in contact with organic matter
Stage 2 — Settlement/Clarification Chamber:
• Treated effluent flows into the settlement tank
• Sludge (bacteria and solids) settles to the bottom
• Settled sludge is recirculated back to the aeration chamber to maintain bacterial population
• Excess sludge is periodically removed
Stage 3 — Chlorination/Disinfection Chamber:
• Clarified effluent passes through a chlorinator
• Chlorine tablets or sodium hypochlorite kills remaining pathogens
• Effluent is then discharged overboard (if within discharge requirements)
• Discharged effluent must meet coliform count: less than 250 faecal coliforms per 100 mL
• BOD must not exceed 25 mg/L; suspended solids not exceed 35 mg/L
NOTE FOR EXAM — Diagram description:
• Draw three connected chambers: Aeration → Settlement → Chlorination
• Show: Air blower connected to aeration chamber, sludge return line from settlement to
aeration, chlorinator in final chamber, overboard discharge with valve

• Label: Raw sewage inlet, air inlet, sludge recycle, chlorine dosing, effluent outlet
B. Periodic Maintenance and Tests (8 marks):
Daily Checks:
• Check air blower operation — confirm air supply to aeration chamber
• Check effluent colour — should be clear/light yellow, not dark or foul-smelling
• Check chlorinator — ensure adequate chlorine tablet supply in dosing chamber
• Check for leaks from all joints and connections
• Record in maintenance log
Weekly Checks:
• Test effluent for chlorine residual — should be 0.2–0.5 ppm
• Check sludge level in settlement tank — desludge if required
• Inspect blower air filter — clean if dirty
• Check float switches and alarm systems
Monthly Checks:
• Full inspection of all chambers — open inspection hatches
• Check aeration diffusers — clean or replace if clogged
• Test all alarms: high level alarm, blower failure alarm
• Test the automatic bypass valve operation
• Chemical test of effluent quality (BOD, suspended solids, coliform count)
Annual Checks:
• Drydock inspection — empty and clean all tanks
• Inspect anodes and coating inside tanks
• Recertification inspection by flag state or class society surveyor
• Test the entire system under simulated working conditions
Effectiveness Verification Tests:
• Coliform count test — samples to shore laboratory
• BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) test
• Suspended solids test
• Residual chlorine test — daily
• pH test of effluent
💡 EXAM TIP: This question appears in almost EVERY exam paper. Memorize the three-stage
process (Aeration → Settlement → Chlorination) and the maintenance schedule by
daily/weekly/monthly/annual. The drawing is worth marks — even a simple labelled sketch helps.

4. MARPOL Annex V — Prevention of Pollution by Garbage
[ 16 MARKS (8+8) ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 With reference to Annex V of MARPOL 73/78 that deals with the prevention of pollution of
the sea by garbage: a) Define the following terms: i) Garbage ii) Nearest land iii) Special
areas. (8) b) State the regulations governing the disposal of garbage outside special
areas. (8) [Oct 2024, Mar 2023]
BRIEF ANSWER — Annex V Key Facts
• Applies to: ALL ships of any size
• Garbage Management Plan: Required on ships 100 GT and above, and ships certified to
carry 15+ persons
• Garbage Record Book: Required on ships 400 GT and above
• Placards: Required on all ships; displayed in all areas where garbage generated
• Most important change: Annex V 2013 — PROHIBITION of discharge of ALL garbage at sea
EXCEPT food waste
DETAILED ANSWER
A. Key Definitions (8 marks):
i) Garbage:
• All kinds of victual, domestic and operational waste — excluding fresh fish — generated
during the normal operation of the ship
• Includes: food waste, plastics, paper, rags, glass, metal, bottles, crockery, fishing gear, and
all other similar refuse
• Does NOT include: fresh fish, sewage (Annex IV), oil (Annex I), NLS (Annex II), radioactive
waste
ii) Nearest Land:
• 'From the nearest land' means from the nearest baseline from which the territorial sea of the
territory is established
• Exception: For certain parts of Australia — 'from the nearest land' means from a line drawn
12 nm seaward from the coast (to protect the Great Barrier Reef)
• This definition is important because discharge distances are measured from 'nearest land'
iii) Special Areas:
• Areas where Annex V applies most strictly — NO discharge of ANY garbage (except food
waste, under conditions)
• Special Areas under Annex V include: Mediterranean Sea, Baltic Sea, Black Sea, Red Sea,
Gulfs Area (Persian Gulf/Gulf of Oman), North Sea, Antarctic Area, Wider Caribbean Region
• In Special Areas: Only food waste may be discharged — more than 12 nm from nearest
land, ship underway, passed through comminuter/grinder (particles less than 25mm)
B. Garbage Disposal Regulations OUTSIDE Special Areas (8 marks):
Type of Garbage Discharge Conditions Outside Special Areas

Plastics (all types) PROHIBITED — NO discharge at sea anywhere
Fishing gear (synthetic) PROHIBITED — NO discharge at sea anywhere
Cooking oil PROHIBITED — NO discharge at sea anywhere
Garbage mixed with prohibited PROHIBITED — treated as most restrictive category
substances
Food waste (not ground) Beyond 12 nm from nearest land, ship underway
Food waste Beyond 3 nm from nearest land, ship underway
(ground/comminuted <25mm)
Cargo residues (non- Beyond 12 nm from nearest land, ship underway
hazardous)
Cleaning agents/additives (in Beyond 12 nm from nearest land, ship underway
wash water)
Animal carcasses As far from land as possible, preferably beyond 12 nm
Operational waste (paper, rags, Beyond 12 nm from nearest land, ship underway
glass, metal)
Other Requirements:
• Garbage Management Plan: Must describe how garbage is collected, stored, processed,
and disposed of
• Garbage Record Book: Every discharge or incineration must be recorded with date, position,
category, estimated amount
• GRB must be kept for 2 years after last entry
• Placards: In English and working language of crew; displayed in galley, mess rooms, deck
areas
• Reception facilities: Port must provide adequate reception facilities for garbage
• Incineration: Permitted at sea for garbage except: plastics, PVC, heavy metals, PCBs,
products of crude oil, and garbage containing more than traces of heavy metals
💡 EXAM TIP: The table of disposal conditions is very commonly tested. Memorize: ALL plastics
PROHIBITED. Food waste 3 nm (ground) or 12 nm (unground). Special areas = only food waste >12
nm comminuted.

5. MARPOL Annex VI — Prevention of Air Pollution from Ships
[ 8+8 MARKS ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 a) Briefly describe the environmental impact of NOx and SOx and allowable limitations as
per Annex VI of MARPOL in emissions control areas and outside emission control areas.
(8) b) Briefly describe methods to control NOx emission. (8) [Aug 2024]
BRIEF ANSWER — Annex VI Key Facts
• Applies to: All ships with diesel engines over 130 kW
• Key certificate: IAPP Certificate (International Air Pollution Prevention Certificate)
• Regulates: SOx, NOx, ODS (ozone depleting substances), VOCs, shipboard incineration,
fuel oil quality
• ECAs: Emission Control Areas — strictest limits apply
• ECAs declared: Baltic Sea, North Sea, North America, US Caribbean Sea
DETAILED ANSWER
A. Environmental Impact and Limits for NOx and SOx (8 marks):
SOx (Sulphur Oxides) — Environmental Impact:
• Causes acid rain — damages forests, freshwater ecosystems, buildings
• Contributes to respiratory diseases in humans — asthma, bronchitis
• Forms fine particulate matter (PM2.5) — health hazard
• Damages marine ecosystems through ocean acidification
SOx Limits under Annex VI:
Area Sulphur Limit (% m/m)
Outside ECAs (Global) 0.50% since 1 January 2020 (IMO 2020 Global Sulphur Cap)
Inside ECAs 0.10% since 1 January 2015
Previous global limit 3.50% (before 2020)
Compliance Methods for SOx:
• Use low sulphur fuel oil (LSFO or ULSFO — ultra low sulphur)
• Install exhaust gas cleaning system (scrubbers) — open loop, closed loop, or hybrid
• Use alternative fuels: LNG (natural gas), methanol, hydrogen
NOx (Nitrogen Oxides) — Environmental Impact:
• Contributes to smog formation and photochemical reactions
• Causes acid rain and eutrophication of water bodies
• Health impacts: respiratory disease, lung inflammation
• Contributes to ozone depletion in lower atmosphere
NOx Limits under Annex VI (Tier System):
Tier Ships Built After NOx Limit (g/kWh) at n < 130 rpm

Tier I 1 January 2000 17.0 g/kWh
Tier II 1 January 2011 14.4 g/kWh (globally)
Tier III 1 January 2016 3.4 g/kWh (in NOx ECAs only)
B. Methods to Control NOx Emissions (8 marks):
1. Engine Internal Modifications (Primary Methods):
• Injection timing retardation: Retarding fuel injection reduces peak combustion temperature,
reducing NOx formation
• Charge air cooling: Cooling intake air reduces combustion temperature
• Fuel valve nozzle optimization: Better atomization reduces local high-temperature zones
• Miller Cycle: Early intake valve closing reduces effective compression ratio and peak
temperature
• Emulsified fuel: Water-in-fuel emulsion reduces combustion temperature
2. Exhaust After-treatment (Secondary Methods):
• SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction): Urea (AdBlue) is injected into exhaust gases; reacts
with NOx over a catalyst to produce N2 and H2O — most effective, achieves Tier III
compliance
• EGR (Exhaust Gas Recirculation): A portion of exhaust gas is recirculated back into the
combustion air — reduces O2 concentration and peak temperature, reducing NOx
• Water injection: Direct injection of water into combustion chamber reduces peak temperature
3. Alternative Fuels:
• LNG (Liquefied Natural Gas): Naturally low NOx emissions due to lower combustion
temperatures
• Methanol and hydrogen: Very low or zero NOx emissions
💡 EXAM TIP: For the 8-mark NOx control question, give at least 4 methods. SCR and EGR are the
most important — explain both briefly. The Tier system (I/II/III) is often expected in the limits answer.

6. Ballast Water Management Convention (BWM)
[ 16 MARKS ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 What is meant by 'Control and Management of Ships ballast water and sediments'? Why
is this term so significant with reference to shipping in recent times? (16) [Feb 2024]
BRIEF ANSWER — BWM Key Facts
• Convention: International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships Ballast
Water and Sediments, 2004 (BWM Convention)
• Entered into force: 8 September 2017
• Applies to: All ships in international trade that carry ballast water
• Certificate: International Ballast Water Management Certificate (IBWMC)
• BWM Plan: Required on all ships
• BWM Record Book: Required on all ships
DETAILED ANSWER
Why Ballast Water Management is Significant (8 marks):
• Ships take on ballast water at one port and discharge it at another port in a different
country/ocean
• Ballast water contains millions of microorganisms, larvae, bacteria, algae, and invasive
species
• When discharged, these invasive aquatic species can colonise new environments, causing
ecological damage
• Famous example: Zebra mussels from Eastern Europe invaded Great Lakes of North
America via ballast water — caused billions of dollars in damage
• Other examples: Toxic algae (red tide), cholera bacteria, Japanese starfish in Australian
waters
• Economic impacts: Damage to fisheries, water treatment plants, power plant cooling
systems, aquaculture
• Once an invasive species is established, it is nearly impossible to eradicate
Standards under BWM Convention:
• Standard D-1 (Ballast Water Exchange): Exchange ballast water in open ocean (>200 nm
from land, >200m depth). At least 95% volumetric exchange required. Was transitional —
being phased out
• Standard D-2 (Performance Standard): Treat ballast water to reduce organisms to: less than
10 viable organisms per m3 (>50 microns); less than 10 per mL (10-50 microns); less than 1
CFU per 100 mL of Vibrio cholerae; less than 250 CFU/100mL of E. coli; less than 100
CFU/100mL of intestinal Enterococci
Ballast Water Treatment Systems:
• UV (Ultraviolet) treatment: UV light destroys DNA of organisms — most common system
• Electrolysis: Generates sodium hypochlorite from seawater to kill organisms
• Chemical treatment: Biocides added to ballast water
• Filtration + UV: Combined filtration and UV treatment
• Ozone treatment: Ozone gas injected into ballast water

Ship Requirements:
• Ballast Water Management Plan (BWMP): Describes ship's ballast system, treatment
system, procedures
• Ballast Water Record Book (BWRB): Records all ballast operations — uptake, exchange,
treatment, discharge
• Ballast Water Reporting Form: Filed with port state on arrival
• IBWMC: Valid 5 years with intermediate surveys
💡 EXAM TIP: For 16 marks, explain: why it matters (ecological threat), the two standards (D-1 and
D-2), treatment methods, and ship documentation requirements. This covers all aspects.

1. Structure of MLC 2006 — Convention Titles
[ 10 MARKS ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 With reference to Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) answer the following: a) Explain the
structure of the convention with titles. (10) [Jan 2025, Aug 2025]
Q2 With reference to MLC, briefly discuss DMLC Part I and Part II covering welfare
measures for seafarers. (8) [Mar 2025, Jan 2025, Aug 2025]
BRIEF ANSWER (Quick Recall)
MLC 2006 has 3 main parts: Articles, Regulations, and the Code (Standards A + Guidelines B). It is
organized under 5 Titles:
• Title 1 — Minimum Requirements for Seafarers to Work on a Ship
• Title 2 — Conditions of Employment
• Title 3 — Accommodation, Recreational Facilities, Food and Catering
• Title 4 — Health Protection, Medical Care, Welfare and Social Security
• Title 5 — Compliance and Enforcement

DETAILED ANSWER (Full 10-Mark Response)
The Maritime Labour Convention 2006 (MLC 2006) is often called the 'fourth pillar' of international
maritime law alongside SOLAS, MARPOL, and STCW. It consolidates 68 earlier ILO maritime
labour instruments into a single document.
Structure of MLC 2006:
• Articles — General principles and obligations
• Regulations — Mandatory requirements (brief)
• Code — Standard A (mandatory details) and Guideline B (non-mandatory
recommendations)
TITLE 1 — Minimum Requirements for Seafarers to Work on a Ship:
• Regulation 1.1: Minimum Age — No person under 16 years. No under-18 for night work or
hazardous work
• Regulation 1.2: Medical Certificate — Valid medical certificate confirming fitness
• Regulation 1.3: Training and Qualifications — Must hold required certificates/qualifications
• Regulation 1.4: Recruitment and Placement — Regulate seafarer recruitment services
TITLE 2 — Conditions of Employment:
• Regulation 2.1: Seafarers' Employment Agreements (SEA) — Written, signed agreement
• Regulation 2.2: Wages — Paid monthly, no unauthorized deductions
• Regulation 2.3: Hours of Work and Rest — Max 14 hrs work/24 hrs; Max 72 hrs work/7 days.
Min 10 hrs rest/24 hrs; Min 77 hrs rest/7 days
• Regulation 2.4: Entitlement to Leave — Min 2.5 calendar days per month of service
• Regulation 2.5: Repatriation — At shipowner's expense on contract expiry, medical grounds,
or ship loss
• Regulation 2.6: Seafarer Compensation for Ship's Loss or Foundering
• Regulation 2.7: Manning Levels — Safe and efficient manning
• Regulation 2.8: Career and Skill Development
TITLE 3 — Accommodation, Recreational Facilities, Food and Catering:
• Regulation 3.1: Accommodation and Recreational Facilities — Minimum space
requirements, noise/vibration limits, sanitation, ventilation, lighting
• Regulation 3.2: Food and Catering — Adequate food and drinking water; qualified cook
required
TITLE 4 — Health Protection, Medical Care, Welfare and Social Security:
• Regulation 4.1: Medical Care on Board and Ashore — Seafarers entitled to free medical
care
• Regulation 4.2: Shipowners' Liability — Covered for illness/injury for up to 16 weeks
• Regulation 4.3: Health and Safety Protection and Accident Prevention
• Regulation 4.4: Access to Shore-based Welfare Facilities
• Regulation 4.5: Social Security — Member states provide coverage
TITLE 5 — Compliance and Enforcement:
• Regulation 5.1: Flag State Responsibilities — Inspection, certification, DMLC
• Regulation 5.2: Port State Responsibilities — Inspection of foreign ships in port

• Regulation 5.3: Labour-supplying Responsibilities — Countries supplying seafarers
💡 EXAM TIP: For a 10-mark answer, name all 5 Titles with at least 2–3 key regulations under each.
Use headings to organize.
2. DMLC Part I and Part II — Welfare Measures
[ 8 MARKS ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 With reference to Maritime Labour Convention (MLC): Briefly, discuss DMLC Part I and
Part II covering welfare measures for seafarers. (8) [Aug 2025, Jan 2025, Mar 2025]
Q2 With reference to MLC 2006, briefly discuss DMLC Part I and II covering welfare
measures for seafarers. (8) [Aug 2024, Jan 2024]
BRIEF ANSWER (Quick Recall)
DMLC = Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance. Two-part document:
• Part I: Issued by flag state — lists national laws implementing MLC 2006
• Part II: Prepared by shipowner — shows how they comply with those laws on that specific
ship
DETAILED ANSWER (Full 8-Mark Response)
The DMLC is a document accompanying the Maritime Labour Certificate (MLC Certificate). Ships of
500 GT or more on international voyages must carry both.
DMLC Part I — Flag State Document:
• Issued by the flag state (e.g., DG Shipping for Indian vessels)
• Lists national requirements implementing the 14 areas covered by MLC 2006
• The 14 areas include: minimum age, medical certificate, qualifications, SEA, use of licensed
recruitment, hours of work/rest, manning levels, accommodation, food & catering, health &
safety, medical care, complaints procedures, wage payments, repatriation
• Not ship-specific — applicable to all ships of that flag
DMLC Part II — Shipowner Document:
• Prepared by the shipowner/operator
• Describes the specific measures taken on that ship to comply with the national requirements
in Part I
• Must be approved by the flag state or recognized organization
• Ship-specific — tailored to each vessel
• Must be kept on board and available for inspection by port state control
Welfare Measures Covered:
• Seafarers must be provided proper food, safe accommodation, and recreational facilities
• Access to shore-based welfare facilities in port

• Complaint procedures — both onboard and ashore
• Adequate medical care at no cost to seafarer
• Repatriation rights guaranteed
💡 EXAM TIP: Distinguish clearly: Part I = government document, Part II = shipowner document.
Examiners love this distinction.
3. Grievance Redressal Mechanism for Indian Flagged Vessels
[ 8 MARKS ]
📝 EXAM QUESTIONS — from DieselShip Question Bank
Q1 With reference to MLC: Briefly discuss the grievance redressal mechanism for seafarers
of Indian flagged vessel. (8) [Mar 2025]
Q2 With reference to Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) 2006, briefly discuss the following:
a) Minimum requirements for seafarers working on a ship. b) Conditions of employment.
c) Accommodation and recreational facilities. d) Health protection, welfare, and social
security protection. (16) [Oct 2024]
BRIEF ANSWER (Quick Recall)
• Every ship must have onboard complaint procedure
• Seafarer can complain to master, then shipowner, then flag state
• Seafarer can also report to port state during port call
• Protection against victimization guaranteed
DETAILED ANSWER (Full 8-Mark Response)
MLC 2006 Regulation 5.1.5 requires every ship to have a fair, effective, and well-documented
onboard complaint procedure.
Onboard Complaint Procedure:
• Step 1: Seafarer raises complaint with immediate superior or the Master
• Step 2: If not resolved, complaint is forwarded to the shipowner
• Step 3: Seafarer may also report to competent authority of the flag state
• The complaint procedure must be posted in a conspicuous place onboard
• The seafarer must receive a written response within a reasonable time
For Indian Flagged Vessels — Specific Provisions:
• Governed by the Merchant Shipping (Maritime Labour Convention) Rules, 2016
• The Directorate General of Shipping (DG Shipping) is the competent authority
• Seafarers can file complaints to DG Shipping via the designated Maritime Labour Inspector
• The shipping company must have a documented grievance redressal system as part of
DMLC Part II
• Trade unions and seafarer organizations may also assist in resolution

Port State Complaint:
• If a seafarer is in a foreign port, they may report to the port state authority
• Port State Control (PSC) officers can inspect and investigate the complaint
• If serious, PSC may detain the ship until rectified
Protection Against Victimization:
• Seafarers must be protected from dismissal or other reprisals for filing a complaint
• This is a mandatory requirement under MLC 2006 Standard A5.1.5
💡 EXAM TIP: Mention all 3 levels: onboard → shipowner → flag state/DG Shipping. Also mention
port state option for extra marks.
4. The 16-Mark Combo Question (4 parts × 4 marks each)
[ 16 MARKS — 4 PARTS ]
This question type asks about 4 sub-topics from MLC: Minimum Requirements, Conditions of
Employment, Accommodation, Health & Welfare. Each part is 4 marks.
4a. Minimum Requirements for Seafarers to Work (4 marks)
• Minimum Age: No person under 16 years shall work on a ship. Under 18 cannot do night
work (2300–0500 hrs) or hazardous work
• Medical Certificate: Valid certificate from approved medical practitioner confirming fitness for
shipboard duties
• Qualifications: Must hold STCW certificates or other required qualifications for their
rank/duties
• Recruitment: Must use only ILO-compliant licensed recruitment agencies
4b. Conditions of Employment (4 marks)
• SEA: Written contract signed before joining; must contain wages, leave, repatriation terms
• Wages: Paid monthly at minimum to a nominated bank account; ITF/IMO minimum wages
apply
• Hours of Work/Rest: Max 14 hrs work per 24 hrs; max 72 hrs per week. Min 10 hrs rest per
24 hrs; min 77 hrs per week
• Annual Leave: Minimum 2.5 calendar days per month of service
• Repatriation: Shipowner's expense — on contract expiry, illness, ship loss, or other valid
reasons
4c. Accommodation and Recreational Facilities (4 marks)
• Adequate sleeping space with proper ventilation, heating, lighting, and insulation from
noise/vibration
• Sanitary facilities — toilets, showers, washing facilities; separate for male/female
• Recreational room, gym, or library as appropriate to the vessel

• Minimum floor area per person as per flag state rules (approx. 4.5 m² for ratings, more for
officers)
• Food and catering — adequate quantity, nutritional quality, properly equipped galley,
qualified cook for ships > 10 crew
4d. Health Protection, Medical Care, Welfare and Social Security (4 marks)
• Seafarers entitled to free medical and dental treatment onboard and ashore while in service
• Shipowner's liability: Covers medical costs and wages for illness/injury for up to 16 weeks
• Accident prevention: Risk assessments, safety equipment, safety officer/committee on large
vessels
• Welfare facilities ashore: Access to welfare boards, internet, phone, recreational services in
port
• Social security: Minimum 3 branches of social security must be covered by member states
💡 EXAM TIP: For the 16-mark combo, write 4–5 points per sub-topic. Keep answers concise but
technically correct.
