1. AUTOMATIC WATER SPRINKLER SYSTEM
EXAM QUESTIONS: Sketch a typical system, describe operation, sources of water, sprinkler head and its
operation, how temperature rating is determined. (2022/SEP, 2023/APR, 2025/SEP, 2025/NOV)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2, Reg 12 — Mandatory for passenger vessels
throughout accommodation; cargo ships in specific areas
System Components
• Pressurised fresh water tank — immediate supply
• Automatic sea water pump — backup, auto-starts on pressure drop
• Alarm valve / pressure switch
• Distribution pipework throughout accommodation
• Sprinkler heads at ceiling level in each space
• Section stop valves — one per zone
• Alarm bell and indicator panel — bridge and fire station
Operation
1. System kept under pressure at all times
2. Fire raises temperature at sprinkler head — heat sensitive glass bulb shatters
3. Pressure drop in pipework activates alarm (audible + visual on panel)
4. Pressure drop automatically starts sea water pump
5. Water discharges ONLY from activated heads — not entire system
6. Each head operates independently — minimises water damage
Sources of Water
• Pressurised fresh water tank — immediate supply (first ~1 minute)
• Automatic sea water pump — takes over as main supply
• Manual connection to fire main — emergency backup
Sprinkler Head & Operation
• Glass bulb filled with glycerine-based liquid
• Liquid expands when heated — bulb shatters at rated temperature
• Deflector plate releases — water sprays in cone pattern over wide area
• Each head operates independently
Temperature Rating — Colour Code
Colour Temperature Rating Typical Location
Orange 57°C Heated spaces
Red 68°C Accommodation (standard)

Yellow 79°C Higher ambient spaces
Green 93°C Boiler rooms, laundries
Blue 141°C High heat areas
SOLAS Regulations — Key Figures
• Each nozzle covers maximum 16 m² of deck area
• Minimum pressure at nozzle — 2.4 bar
• Water supply sufficient for minimum 30 minutes continuous operation
• Alarm must activate within 30 seconds of water flow
• System must be capable of automatic operation at all times
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Each head works independently — only fire area heads activate, NOT whole system
✓ Alarm shows WHICH ZONE on indicator panel — crew directed to correct location
✓ System is AUTOMATIC — no human intervention needed to start
✓ One liner: Heat breaks bulb → pressure drops → alarm sounds → pump starts →
sea water backs up

2. CO2 TOTAL FLOODING SYSTEM (MACHINERY SPACES)
EXAM QUESTIONS: Sketch and describe a total flooding CO₂ gas system for machinery spaces. Which
valve should be operated first? State periodic maintenance. (2023/FEB, 2023/JUN, 2024/JUL, 2024/DEC)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2, Reg 10 — Fixed CO2 systems mandatory for
machinery spaces on all ships
System Components
• CO2 cylinder battery — stored in dedicated CO2 room outside protected space
• Pilot cylinder — releases first to open main valve automatically
• Master stop valve / Main valve
• Section valve / Distribution valve — directs CO2 to correct space
• Distribution pipework and nozzles throughout machinery space
• Release cabinet — outside protected space, two-step operation to prevent accidental
release
• Time delay device — 20-30 seconds before discharge
• Audible alarm — sounds inside machinery space before release
• Ventilation shutdown interlock — automatically closes dampers and stops fans
• Low pressure alarm — warns if any cylinder loses pressure
How the System Works
• CO2 stored as liquid under pressure in cylinders
• When released — vaporises and expands approximately 450 times its liquid volume
• CO2 displaces oxygen — fire cannot sustain when oxygen drops below 15%
• System designed to achieve 34% CO2 concentration in protected space
• 34% concentration is immediately dangerous to life — hence time delay and alarms
MOST EXAMINED: Which Valve is Operated FIRST and WHY
The SECTION VALVE (distribution valve) to the correct protected space must be opened FIRST.
Correct Operating Sequence:
7. Sound alarm — evacuate machinery space
8. Stop machinery, shut fuel valves
9. Stop all ventilation — close fire dampers
10. Account for ALL personnel — full headcount
11. OPEN THE SECTION VALVE to the correct space FIRST
12. Then operate the main CO2 release (pilot cylinder)
Why Section Valve Must Be First:
• If main release operated first WITHOUT section valve open — CO2 flows to wrong space or
nowhere
• Precious CO2 wasted — recharging takes time, vessel may be lost

• With section valve first — all CO2 goes to correct space, fire extinguished efficiently
Periodic Maintenance
Frequency Check
Monthly Cylinder weight/pressure — recharge if loss exceeds 10% of charge
Monthly Low pressure alarm functioning
Monthly Release cabinet seal — tamper evident seal intact
Monthly Audible alarms inside machinery space
Quarterly Ventilation shutdown interlock — fans stop, dampers close
Quarterly Pipework and nozzles — check for corrosion or blockage
Quarterly Time delay device
Annually Full operational test of alarm and release system (no actual CO2)
Annually All valves — section valve, master valve
Annually Complete pipework inspection
Annually Verify CO2 quantity sufficient for protected space volume
Every 10 years Hydraulic pressure test of all cylinders
SOLAS Regulations — Key Figures
• CO2 concentration required: 34% of gross volume of protected space
• Sufficient CO2 for 30% of gross volume of largest protected space
• Time delay: minimum 20 seconds before discharge
• Recharge trigger: weight loss more than 10% of charge
• Space kept sealed minimum 24 hours after discharge
• Never re-enter without O2 meter — CO2 is colourless, odourless and tasteless
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ SECTION VALVE always opened BEFORE main release — most important exam
point
✓ CO2 is colourless, odourless, tasteless — cannot detect by senses — always use
O2 meter before re-entry
✓ 34% CO2 concentration needed | Oxygen below 15% stops combustion
✓ CO2 expands 450 times — small cylinders flood large spaces
✓ After discharge: sealed 24 hours minimum

3. FIRE IN A GALLEY & MISSING PERSONNEL SEARCH
EXAM QUESTIONS: How to fight a galley fire, how to restrict it as first person on scene. (2025/NOV)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2 — Fire safety requirements for galleys and
accommodation spaces
Types of Galley Fires & Correct Extinguishers
Fire Type Class Correct Extinguisher Notes
Cooking oil / fat fire Class F Wet chemical extinguisher NEVER use water — steam
explosion
Electrical fire Class E CO2 extinguisher Isolate supply first
Ordinary combustibles Class A Water or foam Remove nearby
combustibles
Fighting a Galley Fire — General Procedure
13. Raise alarm immediately
14. Identify type of fire
15. Select correct extinguisher
16. Turn off heat source — gas or electric
17. Fight fire from the DOORWAY — keep escape route behind you at all times
18. Never let fire get between you and the exit
19. If fire cannot be controlled — evacuate and CLOSE THE DOOR
Restricting Fire as FIRST Person on Scene
20. Raise the alarm immediately — shout fire, activate nearest manual call point
21. Turn off heat source — gas, electric cookers, fryers
22. Close all doors and portholes — restricts oxygen, contains fire
23. Close ventilation dampers to galley — stops fresh air feeding fire
24. Attempt initial firefighting ONLY IF: fire is small, correct extinguisher available, escape route
clear
25. If fire too large — evacuate immediately, close door behind you
26. A closed door can hold fire back for 30 MINUTES OR MORE
27. Never re-enter alone without proper equipment
28. Guide fire party to location when they arrive
Finding Missing Personnel in Smoke-Filled Accommodation
Before Entering:
• Never enter alone — always in pairs minimum
• Don BA set (Breathing Apparatus) — essential
• Wear full firefighting gear — protective clothing, gloves, helmet
• Carry a lifeline — connect to team member and fixed point outside

• Carry a torch — visibility near zero in smoke
• Brief the team — assign search areas, agree communication signals
• Safety officer stationed outside — monitors time, holds lifeline
Search Procedure:
29. Systematic search — every cabin and space searched, none skipped
30. Stay LOW — smoke rises, cleaner air near floor level
31. Feel doors before opening — hot door means fire behind it
32. Call out regularly — conscious casualties can respond
33. Use lifeline — guides you back in zero visibility
34. Search in pairs — one searches, one maintains communication
35. Check under beds, bathrooms, behind doors — people collapse anywhere
If Casualty Found:
36. Do not remove BA from casualty if wearing one
37. Check for injuries — if spinal injury suspected, take care
38. Drag to safety using lifeline route — dragging faster than carrying in confined spaces
39. Notify safety officer outside immediately
40. Pass casualty to medical team waiting outside
41. Continue search — there may be more casualties
Withdrawal:
• If BA warning whistle sounds — withdraw IMMEDIATELY
• Never disconnect lifeline until safely outside
• Report search areas covered to incident commander
• Fresh team takes over if required
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ NEVER use water on oil/fat fires — causes violent steam explosion
✓ Closing the door is single most effective action as first person — 30 minutes
containment
✓ NEVER enter smoke-filled space without BA
✓ NEVER search alone — always pairs minimum
✓ Lifeline is mandatory — zero visibility means you can get lost
✓ Stay LOW — smoke rises, cleaner air at floor level
✓ Feel door before opening — hot door = fire behind it

4. CARGO HOLD FIRE DETECTION SYSTEM
EXAM QUESTIONS: Explain cargo hold fire detection system, maintenance procedures, steps when fire
detected. (2025/APR, 2025/JUL)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2, Reg 10 — Fixed fire detection and alarm systems
in cargo holds mandatory
Why Special System Needed for Cargo Holds
• Holds are vast spaces — normal detectors take too long
• Poor air circulation — smoke disperses before reaching detector
• Access restricted when cargo is loaded
• Cannot use standard smoke/heat detectors — too slow for smouldering cargo fires
Sample Extraction Smoke Detection System (SESD)
Components:
• Sampling pipes with small holes — run throughout the hold at various levels
• Suction fan/pump — continuously draws air samples from hold
• Smoke detector unit (photoelectric or ionisation) — located outside hold in accessible space
• Zone indicator panel — shows which hold and which level sample came from
How it Works:
42. Suction fan continuously draws air from sampling pipes in hold
43. Air samples pass through smoke detector unit outside the hold
44. If smoke detected — alarm triggered on bridge and fire control station
45. Panel identifies WHICH HOLD and approximately WHICH LEVEL
Additional Detection Methods:
• CO2 concentration monitoring — rise in CO2 indicates fire or smouldering
• Temperature sensors at various levels
• Observation pipes — crew can visually check or smell air from hold
Maintenance Procedures
Frequency Maintenance Action
Daily Check alarm panel for fault indicators; verify suction fan operating normally
Weekly Test alarm functions; check sampling pipe inlets not blocked
Monthly Introduce artificial smoke into pipes to verify detector response
Monthly Check and clean filters in detector unit; test all alarms including bridge
Annually Full inspection of all sampling pipes for blockage, corrosion, damage
Annually Calibrate detectors; test all isolating valves; record in fire safety logbook

After loading Check sampling pipe inlets not covered by cargo before departure
Steps When Cargo Hold Fire Alarm Activates

Step Action Reason
1 Acknowledge alarm — identify Know exact location before acting
which hold from panel
2 Notify Master — raise general Command informed, emergency response begins
alarm
3 Muster ALL crew — full headcount Safety before any CO2 release
4 DO NOT OPEN THE HATCH Opening introduces oxygen — causes flashover or
explosion
5 Stop ALL ventilation to the hold Starve fire of oxygen
6 Confirm fire — check CO2 levels, Verify before major action
temperatures
7 Check cargo manifest for DG cargo requires different procedures
dangerous goods
8 Boundary cooling Prevent heat spread through bulkheads
9 Prepare CO2 — confirm all Safety critical before release
personnel accounted

11 Maintain watch — 24 hours Prevent reignition
minimum sealed
12 Report to coast guard / port Legal requirement
authority

KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ NEVER open the hatch — most important rule, always state this in exam
✓ System name: Sample Extraction Smoke Detection (SESD) — use this name

5. ELECTRIC CABLE INSULATION & FIRE
EXAM QUESTIONS: Hazards associated with cable insulation in fire, remedies, how fire spread is reduced
by cable installation method. (2023/NOV, 2025/DEC)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2, Reg 3 — Cable specifications; IEC 60332 fire test
standards for shipboard cables
Hazards Associated with Cable Insulation in Fire
• Hazard 1 — Toxic fumes
Burning PVC insulation releases hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas and other toxic gases. More
dangerous than the fire itself — can incapacitate crew quickly.
• Hazard 2 — Smoke
Dense black smoke reduces visibility to near zero — makes evacuation and firefighting extremely
difficult.
• Hazard 3 — Fire propagation
Cables run throughout the ship. If not protected, fire spreads from one compartment to another
along cable runs.
• Hazard 4 — Loss of essential services
Burning cables cause loss of lighting, communications, alarms, pumps — exactly when most
needed.
• Hazard 5 — Electric shock risk
Burning cables may remain live — electrocution risk to firefighters using water.
• Hazard 6 — Re-ignition risk
Smouldering insulation can re-ignite even after apparent extinction.
Remedies
Hazard Remedy
Toxic fumes LSOH cables — Low Smoke Zero Halogen — minimal toxic
gas when burning
Smoke LSOH cables also produce low smoke — better visibility during
evacuation
Fire spread along cables Fire retardant cables — self-extinguishing, do not propagate
flame
Loss of essential services Fire resistant cables — maintain circuit integrity even in fire
Electric shock Isolate circuits before using water on electrical fires
Earthing faults Proper earthing and screening — prevents fault currents
igniting insulation
How Fire Spread is Reduced by Installation Method
• Cable transits through bulkheads MUST be sealed with fire resistant material (ceramic wool,
intumescent compound) — maintains fire integrity of bulkhead
• Separate routing — essential service cables routed separately from non-essential cables

• Fire stops at regular intervals in cable trays — prevents fire running along the tray
• Vertical cable runs avoided where possible — fire travels upward rapidly along vertical
bundles
• Earthing and screening — prevents fault currents that could ignite insulation
• IMO regulations require cables in high-risk areas to meet IEC fire test standards
Three Types of Cables Onboard
Cable Type Property Where Used
Fire Retardant Will not spread flame — self- General use throughout ship
extinguishing
Fire Resistant Maintains circuit integrity even in fire Essential services — pumps,
alarms, emergency lighting
LSOH (Low Smoke Zero Minimal smoke and zero toxic Accommodation, escape routes,
Halogen) halogen gases passenger areas
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Cable transits through bulkheads MUST be sealed — most important installation
point
✓ LSOH = Low Smoke Zero Halogen — not just low smoke, also zero toxic gas
✓ Three cable types: Fire Retardant, Fire Resistant, LSOH — know the difference
✓ Isolate circuits before firefighting — prevents electrocution
✓ Vertical cable runs avoided — fire travels upward rapidly

6. 136-LITRE NON-PORTABLE FOAM FIRE EXTINGUISHER
EXAM QUESTIONS: Sketch, how to operate, two constituents, foam generation time, location onboard.
(2023/JAN, 2024/NOV)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2 — Portable and non-portable extinguishers
required in machinery spaces and high-risk areas
Components
• Outer steel cylinder — contains sodium bicarbonate solution with foam stabiliser
• Inner container — contains aluminium sulphate solution
• Discharge horn/nozzle
• Operating handle / plunger
• Carrying handles on the body
How to Operate
46. Carry to fire location — requires TWO PERSONS (non-portable but carried)
47. INVERT the extinguisher — mixes the two chemicals
48. Direct nozzle at the BASE of the fire
49. Discharge — foam flows out continuously
50. Do NOT invert back during operation
51. Apply foam in sweeping motion to cover burning surface
Two Constituents That Produce Stable Foam
Container Chemical Reaction
Inner container Aluminium sulphate solution Aluminium sulphate +
Outer container Sodium bicarbonate solution (with Sodium bicarbonate →
foam stabiliser)
Result CO2 gas + stable foam CO2 bubbles through foam liquid
creating stable foam blanket
Key Figures
• Volume: 136 LITRES (not kg — common mistake)
• Discharge time: approximately 2 to 3 minutes
• Foam generated: approximately 1000 litres
• Expansion ratio: approximately 8:1
• Effective on: Class B fires (flammable liquids — oil, fuel, paint)
• NOT suitable for: electrical fires
Where Found Onboard
• Engine room — near fuel tanks, purifiers

• Paint store
• Pump room on tankers
• Galley flat / fryer areas
• Any Class B fire risk area
Two Actions of Foam
• Smothering — foam blanket cuts off oxygen supply to burning surface
• Cooling — water content in foam cools the burning surface below ignition temperature
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ 136 LITRES not 136 kg — volume, not weight
✓ INVERT to mix chemicals — do not just tilt
✓ Direct at BASE of fire — not at flames
✓ Two persons required to carry
✓ Class B fires only — NOT for electrical fires
✓ Two actions: Smothering + Cooling

5. Fire Patrol System:
• Watchmen patrol accommodation at regular intervals
• Electronic patrol system — watchman checks in at fixed points using electronic key

• Automatic sprinkler system — primary automatic firefighting in accommodation

9. LOW EXPANSION FOAM FIXED FIREFIGHTING SYSTEM
EXAM QUESTIONS: Sketch line diagram, describe operation, how foam compound and sea water are
converted to foam. (2024/JUN)
SOLAS/Regulation: SOLAS Chapter II-2, Reg 10 — Fixed foam systems for machinery
spaces; IMO MSC/Circ.670
System Components (For Sketch)
• Foam concentrate tank — stores AFFF (Aqueous Film Forming Foam) or FFFP
• Sea water supply — from fire main or dedicated pump
• Foam proportioner/inductor — mixes foam concentrate with sea water at 3% or 6% ratio
• Foam pump — pressurises the foam solution
• Distribution pipework — runs throughout machinery space
• Foam monitors/nozzles — positioned at bilges, fuel tank tops, purifier room, main engine
drip trays
• Release control cabinet — located outside machinery space
• Isolating/section valves — for different areas
• Alarm system — audible alarm before system activation
Operating Sequence
60. Sound alarm — evacuate machinery space
61. Account for ALL personnel — full headcount
62. Stop machinery where safe — shut fuel valves
63. Stop ventilation — close dampers
64. Go to release cabinet OUTSIDE machinery space
65. Open sea water supply valve
66. Open foam concentrate valve
67. Sea water flows through proportioner — Venturi effect draws in concentrate automatically
68. Foam solution flows to nozzles throughout space
69. At nozzles — solution mixed with air to produce finished foam
70. Maintain system running until fire confirmed extinguished
71. Keep space sealed — do not open doors
72. Do not re-enter until safe
How Foam is Produced — The Process
Step 1 — Proportioning (Venturi Effect):
• Sea water passes through proportioner/inductor
• Fast moving water creates low pressure zone — Venturi effect
• Low pressure DRAWS IN foam concentrate automatically
• Concentrate mixes with water at 3% or 6% ratio
• Produces foam solution (premix)
Step 2 — Aeration at Nozzles:

• Foam solution forced through specially designed nozzles
• Nozzles introduce air into the solution
• Air bubbles trapped in solution — creates stable foam
Step 3 — Three Actions of Finished Foam:
• SMOTHERING — foam blanket covers burning surface, cuts off oxygen
• COOLING — water content cools burning liquid below ignition temperature
• SUPPRESSION — AFFF forms aqueous film on fuel surface, prevents fuel vapour escaping
— unique to AFFF
Key Figures
• Foam type: AFFF — Aqueous Film Forming Foam
• Mixing ratio: 3% or 6% foam concentrate to water
• Expansion ratio: 6:1 to 12:1 (low expansion)
• Meaning: 1 litre of solution produces 6 to 12 litres of finished foam
Foam vs CO2 Comparison
Feature Foam CO2
Cooling effect Yes No
Prevents reignition Yes No
Safe for personnel Irritant (safe) Lethal
Electrical fires No Yes
Cleanup required Yes No
Effective on oil fires Yes Yes
KEY EXAM POINTS
✓ Venturi effect: fast water creates low pressure → automatically draws in concentrate
— no separate pump needed
✓ Three actions: Smothering + Cooling + Suppression (aqueous film) — AFFF unique
for film formation
✓ Two ratios to remember: 3% or 6% mixing ratio; 6:1 to 12:1 expansion ratio — these
are DIFFERENT
✓ Foam preferred over CO2 for oil fires: provides cooling + prevents reignition
✓ AFFF = Aqueous Film Forming Foam — not Aqueous Filling

10. HYPER MIST (WATER MIST) FIRE SUPPRESSION SYSTEM
EXAM QUESTIONS: Working principle, difference from traditional water-based systems,
installation/maintenance/testing requirements. (2024/AUG)
SOLAS/Regulation: IMO MSC/Circ.1165 — Guidelines for approval of water mist systems;
SOLAS Chapter II-2
What is Hyper Mist System
• Also known as Water Mist System or High Pressure Water Mist System
• Uses very fine water droplets discharged at HIGH PRESSURE to suppress and extinguish
fires
• Operates at 35 to 200 bar (compare: normal fire hose is only 5-7 bar)
• Produces droplets less than 1mm diameter (compare: normal sprinkler is 3-5mm)
Three Mechanisms of Fire Suppression
1. Cooling (Primary Mechanism):
• Fine droplets have extremely large surface area compared to volume
• Rapid heat absorption from fire and surroundings
• Droplets flash vaporise — absorbing enormous amounts of heat
• Temperature of fire and surroundings drops rapidly
2. Oxygen Displacement:
• Steam produced by vaporisation expands 1700 times its water volume
• Steam displaces oxygen around the fire
• Oxygen concentration drops — fire cannot sustain
• Similar smothering effect to CO2 but using steam — no toxic risk
3. Radiant Heat Blocking (UNIQUE to water mist):
• Fine mist cloud blocks radiant heat from fire
• Prevents fire spreading to nearby combustibles
• Protects personnel and structures near the fire
• This mechanism is NOT possible with normal sprinklers or CO2
Comparison — Hyper Mist vs Traditional Systems
Feature Traditional Sprinkler Hyper Mist System
Water pressure 5-7 bar 35-200 bar
Droplet size 3-5 mm Less than 1 mm
Water consumption Very high Up to 90% less
Water damage Significant Minimal

Suppression mechanisms Mainly cooling Cooling + O2 displacement +
radiant heat blocking
Effective on Class A mainly Class A, B and electrical fires
Safe for electrical equipment No Yes — fine mist less conductive
Safe for personnel Yes Yes — can remain in space
Environmental impact Water damage Environmentally friendly — pure
water
Where Used Onboard
• Engine rooms — replacing CO2 systems on some modern vessels
• Accommodation spaces — replacing traditional sprinklers
• Galleys — effective on cooking oil fires
• Control rooms and switchboard rooms — safe for electrical equipment
• Machinery spaces — around generators, purifiers
• Paint stores
Installation Requirements
73. Nozzle placement — complete coverage, no blind spots, correct spacing and height
74. High pressure stainless steel pipework — corrosion resistant, rated for operating pressure
75. Dedicated high pressure pump — sized correctly, backup pump with auto-changeover
76. Water supply tank — sized for minimum 30 minutes operation — FRESH WATER ONLY
(sea water corrodes nozzles)
77. Pressure vessel/accumulator — provides immediate discharge before pump reaches full
pressure
78. Control panel — monitors status, alarms, controls zones
79. Detection system integration — linked to smoke/heat detectors for automatic activation
80. Approved by classification society — must meet IMO MSC guidelines
Maintenance Requirements
Frequency Maintenance Action
Daily Check system pressure; check water tank level; check control panel for faults
Weekly Run pump briefly; check all valves correct position; test automatic pump start
Monthly Flush system — prevent stagnation and bacterial growth
Monthly Check nozzles for blockage or corrosion
Monthly Test automatic activation from detection system; check pressure relief valves
Annually Full nozzle inspection — remove and check each nozzle
Annually Hydraulic test of pipework; full operational test
Annually Check water quality in tank — treat if necessary

How Regular Maintenance Ensures Effectiveness
• Blocked nozzles — most common failure. Creates blind spot where fire can develop
unchecked
• Pump reliability — regular running keeps bearings and seals serviceable. Idle pump may fail
to start
• Water quality — stagnant water grows bacteria, deposits scale. Flushing keeps pipes and
nozzles clear
• Correct pressure — low pressure produces large droplets, system loses all its advantages
over normal sprinklers
• Detection integration — regular testing ensures automatic activation works. Manual
activation too slow
